story.title: Theo and the Midnight Launch
story.subtitle: One glowing block, one giant leap, and a race that changed the sky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Block That Wouldn't Sit Still (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo had three tabs open, a half-built rocket launch pad in Roblox Studio, and a bedtime that had passed two hours ago. He was trying to get a countdown script to work. It kept failing at zero.

Then the screen flickered. Black, then green, then black again. A single block sat in the corner of his build — a block he had never placed. It was blinking. Beep. Beep-beep. Beep.

"That's not a script I wrote," Theo said out loud, to nobody.

He clicked it anyway.

The room folded like a loading screen and came back wrong — green grid lines, black sky, and a small floating cube hovering where his monitor used to be. It had a face made of pixels, and it was grinning.

"Finally," said the cube. "Do you know how long I've been blinking? I'm Patch. I live in the glitches. You clicked, so now you're in one."

Below them, a rocket stood on a steel tower, hissing white smoke. A crowd in old coats watched it, breath fogging in cold air.

"Where — when — is this?" Theo asked.

"**October 4, 1957**," said Patch. "Watch."

The rocket lit the sky orange and climbed. Patch zoomed Theo in close on the silver ball riding on top — smooth, with four long antennas trailing behind it like whiskers.

"That's **Sputnik 1**," Patch said. "First thing humans ever built that circled the whole planet — that's called going into **orbit**, flying around Earth instead of falling back down. It was Soviet scientists who built it, and it was only about **58 centimeters** wide. That's smaller than a beach ball."

"That tiny thing beat everybody into space?" Theo said. "It doesn't even look like it's trying."

"It didn't need to try hard. It just needed to beep."

Patch played a sound: a simple, steady *beep... beep... beep*, picked up on an ordinary radio. Theo froze. It was the exact rhythm from his glitching block.

"Wait," he said. "That's the same pattern. Is it Morse code? Is it saying something?"

"Try counting it," Patch said.

Theo counted the gaps between beeps on his fingers, the way he counted a defender's steps before a penalty kick. Steady. Even. No pattern hidden in it at all.

"It's not a message," Theo said slowly. "It's just... here. Just, 'I'm up here, I exist.' That's the whole message."

"Exactly right," said Patch, sounding impressed. "The simplest beep in history, and it changed everything. People everywhere pointed radios at the sky just to hear it."

Theo grinned, grabbed an invisible dial only he could see, and matched the beep's rhythm back toward the tiny block floating beside Patch. The block pulsed once, twice — and the whole glitchy sky cracked wide open like a server loading a new map.

"WE HAVE LIFTOFF," Theo shouted, and the world rushed in around them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Dog, the Belt, and the Brand-New Agency (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
The new place smelled like cold metal and coffee. Rows of men in ties watched a smaller capsule being lowered onto a rocket by a crane. Theo heard barking from inside it.

"There's a dog in there," he said, spinning toward Patch. "An actual dog."

"Her name's **Laika**," Patch said. "**November 3, 1957**. She's about to become the first living creature ever to orbit the Earth."

Theo pressed his hand to the capsule window glass, and for a second the dog's dark eyes found his. She didn't look scared. She looked like she was waiting for the whistle.

"She's brave," Theo said quietly. "Like, properly brave."

"Properly brave," Patch agreed. "She became famous all over the world for it."

The scene shifted — Patch was good at that, skipping ahead like fast-forwarding a cutscene — to a room full of men staring at papers covered in official stamps.

"The beeping ball scared people awake," Patch said. "So on **October 1, 1958**, the United States started a brand-new space agency to catch up. They called it **NASA**."

"Like starting a whole new team mid-season," Theo said.

"Pretty much. Their first satellite went up a few months earlier, actually — **January 31, 1958**. It was called **Explorer 1**."

A model of the thin, pencil-shaped satellite spun slowly in front of them, a strange dial on its side ticking wildly whenever it passed a certain point in its loop around Earth.

"That dial's going crazy," Theo said, squinting at it. "It keeps spiking in the same spot every time it goes around. That's not random — that's a pattern."

"Keep going," said Patch.

"If it spikes in the same place every orbit," Theo said, working it out loud, "then there's something *there*. Like — a ring of something, wrapped around the planet, that the satellite keeps flying through."

Patch's pixel face lit up. "That's exactly how scientists found it. A band of invisible energy circling Earth — strong enough that it mattered, so they named it after the man who led that part of the mission: the **Van Allen radiation belt**. Explorer 1 didn't just fly. It discovered something nobody knew was there, because someone was watching the dial instead of just the rocket."

Theo stood a little straighter. He liked that — that a satellite shaped like a pencil had found something invisible just by paying attention.

"Two firsts, one new team," he said. "Busy year."

"Busiest one yet," said Patch. "And it's about to get busier. Someone's going to actually go up there."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Two Capsules on Two Pads (1961)
chapters.text:
The next place had two launch pads side by side, which Theo had never seen before — like two teams warming up on opposite ends of the same field.

"On the left," Patch said, "Vostok 1. On the right, a smaller capsule called Freedom 7. Different countries, same morning in history — almost."

"They're racing," Theo said.

"Racing to firsts, not racing against each other with anything scary. Think of it like two teams both trying to be the first to score, not trying to hurt each other. Watch the left one first."

The Vostok capsule roared upward, carrying a pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**. Patch sped the footage along — a full lap of the glowing curve of Earth sliding underneath the little window.

"**April 12, 1961**," Patch said. "First human ever in space. He went all the way around the planet once — **about 108 minutes**, start to finish."

"A full orbit," Theo said, remembering the word. "Like Sputnik, but with a person inside."

"Exactly. Now watch the other pad."

Freedom 7 launched next, a shorter, stubbier flight that arced up and came straight back down without ever circling the planet.

"**May 5, 1961**," Patch said. "**Alan Shepard**, first American in space. Up, out, and down again — a shorter trip, no full lap around Earth."

Theo studied the two glowing paths Patch had drawn in the air: one a loop, one an arc.

"So Gagarin's the one who actually went all the way around," Theo said. "Shepard went up and came straight back, like a really, really high free kick that comes straight back down instead of curling into the goal."

"That's the difference exactly," Patch said. "One orbited. One didn't."

A new voice crackled in over an old radio speaker — slow, steady, serious in a way that made the room go quiet.

"On **May 25, 1961**," Patch said, "President Kennedy stood up and told his whole country something enormous."

*"...before this decade is out, landing a man on the Moon, and returning him safely to the Earth."*

Theo felt the words land somewhere in his chest. "That's not a small goal. That's like announcing you're going to win the World Cup before you've even picked a team."

"It was exactly that bold," said Patch, and held out a single glowing button, round and red, humming faintly. "Everything after this point is because somebody decided to go for it. Want to push the button that starts the rest of the story?"

Theo didn't hesitate. He pressed it with his whole hand.

The sky above them filled with light, like a server reloading the entire map at once.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Man With No Name (1963 and a Secret Kept Until 1966)
chapters.text:
The new room was dim, lined with blueprints nobody had labeled with a single name. Every drawing was signed the same way: *Chief Designer.* No first name. No last name. Just a title.

"Who's that?" Theo asked, tracing a finger along one of the rocket sketches. "These plans are incredible. Why won't anybody sign them properly?"

"Because it was a secret," Patch said, voice dropping to something almost conspiratorial. "For years, almost nobody outside this room was allowed to know his real name."

Theo loved a good mystery almost as much as he loved a good build. He flipped through a stack of folders until one fell open, revealing a photograph tucked behind a locked panel he pried loose with careful fingers — a man with a serious face and tired eyes.

"**Sergei Korolev**," Patch said, once Theo had found it. "He led the entire Soviet rocket program from behind the scenes. Nobody outside this building knew his name until after he died, in **1966**. He built the rockets that sent Sputnik up, and Gagarin too — and almost nobody got to say thank you to his actual face while he was alive."

"That's kind of sad," Theo said. "All that and no credit."

"He knew what he'd done," Patch said gently. "Sometimes that has to be enough. Come on — there's someone else in this story who deserves a name said out loud."

The blueprints melted into a launch pad, bright with morning sun. A woman in a flight suit walked toward a capsule, utterly calm, like she'd done this a hundred times.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," Patch said. "She used to work in a factory. Now watch."

The capsule — Vostok 6 — thundered off the pad.

"**June 16, 1963**," Patch said. "First woman ever in space. She circled Earth, same as Gagarin had, two years after him."

Theo watched the little capsule loop the curve of the planet, and thought about the stack of unsigned blueprints behind them — one man whose name almost got lost, and one woman whose name got said loud and clear.

"Seems like it worked out better for her," he said.

"It did," said Patch. "Firsts don't always get remembered the same way. That's exactly why we say them out loud."

Theo nodded, and carefully refiled the photograph where he'd found it — not hidden this time, just tucked in gently, the way you'd put something important back where it belonged.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Ten Minutes Outside (1965)
chapters.text:
The next capsule had a window Theo could actually float up to, because apparently in Patch's glitches, floating was just how you got around now.

Outside the little craft, tethered by a thin cord, a figure in a bulky white suit drifted against the black.

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," Patch said. "**March 18, 1965**. He's about to do something nobody's ever done."

A hatch opened. Leonov pushed off gently and floated free of the ship entirely, nothing under him but the whole curve of the Earth.

"He's just — out there," Theo breathed. "Floating outside the actual spacecraft. That's the first ever **spacewalk**, right? Floating outside in a suit, connected only by a cord?"

"First one in history," Patch confirmed. "Want a job?"

"Always."

"Time him."

Patch handed Theo a stopwatch made of light. Theo clicked it the second Leonov cleared the hatch, eyes locked on the glowing numbers as they climbed. One minute. Three. Six.

"He's been out there a while," Theo murmured, half to himself, the way he counted down the last minutes of a tied soccer match.

Eight minutes. Nine.

Leonov turned slowly in the dark, looking back at the small craft that was his only way home, then began pulling himself back along the tether, hand over hand.

"Ten," Theo said, clicking the stopwatch the instant Leonov's boots touched the hatch again. "**About ten minutes.** That's it? That's all it took to be first?"

"That's all it took," Patch said. "Ten minutes, and a very long way from home."

Theo looked at the stopwatch glowing in his palm, then at the hatch sealing shut behind the suited figure.

"I'd have wanted longer," Theo admitted. "Just to look at it all."

"Everyone who's ever gone up says the same thing," Patch said. "Funny thing about space. Ten minutes never feels like enough, and also like plenty."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Photo Nobody Planned (1968)
chapters.text:
This time there was no launch pad at all — just a window, and beyond it, grey, cratered ground sliding by close enough to touch.

"We're not on the ground," Theo said slowly. "We're circling the Moon."

"**December 1968**," Patch said. "**Apollo 8**. First humans ever to leave Earth entirely and loop around the Moon. Nobody had gone this far before."

Theo pressed close to the glass, half-expecting to see Earth hanging somewhere obvious, like a loading-screen background. Instead there was just grey rock, orbit after orbit, until —

"There," Theo said suddenly, pointing. "Over the edge. Is that —"

A curve of blue and white rose slowly over the Moon's grey horizon, small and bright and impossibly alone in all that black.

"That's Earth," Theo said, voice gone quiet. "That's us. That's the whole planet, just — rising, like a sunrise, except it's Earth instead of the sun."

"Someone on board thought the exact same thing," Patch said. "Quick — if you were him, what would you do right now?"

"Take the photo," Theo said instantly. "Obviously. You'd take the photo before it's gone."

A camera shutter clicked somewhere behind the glass.

"**William Anders** did exactly that," Patch said. "Nobody planned that photo. It wasn't on any checklist. He just saw it and grabbed the camera. People call it **Earthrise**. It's one of the most famous photographs ever taken, and it happened because someone looked out a window at the right second."

Theo stared at the little blue curve a moment longer, trying to find anything on it — a country, a city, his own house — and finding nothing but one solid, glowing ball of ocean and cloud.

"You can't see any of the lines," he said. "No borders. Just... one thing."

"That's usually what people say when they see it," Patch said. "Funny, what a photo can do that a map never could."

Theo didn't say anything else for a minute. He just watched the Earth finish rising, slow and complete, over a horizon that wasn't even its own.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Tallest Thing Theo Had Ever Stood Next To (1969)
chapters.text:
The rocket on this pad didn't just stand there. It loomed, white and black against a blue morning sky, so tall Theo had to lean all the way back to find the top of it.

"That's not a rocket," Theo said. "That's a building."

"That's the **Saturn V**," Patch said. "**363 feet tall**. Taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Theo tried to picture it another way — the way he pictured everything, in fields and goals and familiar distances. "That's like... stacking a soccer field on its end and still having room left over."

"Pretty close," Patch said. "A team led by an engineer named **Wernher von Braun** designed it. It's still one of the most powerful machines humans have ever built."

The rocket lit the sky orange and climbed, and climbed, and kept climbing until it was a bright dot and then nothing at all.

Days later — Patch skipped the boring parts, same as always — a smaller craft hung above grey dust, a thin ladder leading down from its leg.

"**July 20, 1969**," Patch said, barely above a whisper now, like the moment deserved it. "**Neil Armstrong.** Watch."

A boot touched grey dust. Then a whole foot. Then a man stood where no human had ever stood before.

*"That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."*

"First person on the Moon," Theo said, and found he'd stopped breathing somewhere in the middle of the sentence.

"**Buzz Aldrin** followed him down a few minutes later," Patch said. "But someone else was up there too, the whole time, all on his own."

The view shifted to a small craft circling high above the grey surface — just one astronaut inside, utterly alone.

"**Michael Collins**," Patch said. "He stayed in orbit in the command module — that's the part of the ship that didn't land — called **Columbia**, while the other two walked on the Moon below him."

Theo thought about substitutes on a bench, about the goalkeeper nobody photographs after the final whistle. "He did a massive job and nobody got to see him do it."

"So let's see him," Patch said, and for a second let the view hang on Collins alone in his tiny window, calm, patient, doing his part.

"Nice work up there," Theo said toward the glass, feeling a little silly, and not stopping anyway.

"Between **1969 and 1972**," Patch added, "**twelve** astronauts walked on the Moon across **six** successful landings. Armstrong was only the first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Fix, the Handshake, and the Way Home (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
The next capsule Patch showed him didn't look right from the start. Warning lights blinked across a cramped control panel, and three astronauts moved carefully, like the floor might tilt.

"**Apollo 13**, **1970**," Patch said. "An oxygen tank cracked open on the way to the Moon. It knocked out power and air on board. They never landed — they had to turn around and get home instead."

Theo's stomach dropped a little, the way it did watching a last-minute penalty. "Are they okay?"

"They're okay," Patch said at once. "That's the whole point of this part. Watch the ground team."

A room full of engineers dumped a pile of spare parts — tubing, plastic bags, tape — onto a table, trying to build an air filter that would fit a socket it was never designed for.

"Square part, round hole," Theo said, grinning despite himself. "That's basically every build I've ever done in Studio when I didn't plan ahead properly."

"So what would you do?"

"Use what you've actually got," Theo said, picking through the mess of parts with his eyes. "Don't wait for the perfect piece. Tape two wrong shapes together until they make a right one."

"That's exactly what they did," Patch said. "It worked. All three astronauts made it home safely."

Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding, and the scene dissolved into something calmer — two spacecraft, drifting slowly toward each other against the black, each flying a different flag.

"**July 17, 1975**," Patch said. "The last chapter of the whole race. An American and a Soviet spacecraft **docked** together in orbit — that means they linked up and connected, nose to nose, two ships joined into one."

A hatch opened between them. Two astronauts reached across and shook hands, floating, grinning, utterly weightless.

"That's it?" Theo said. "That's how it ends? A handshake?"

"That's exactly how it ends," Patch said. "Years of racing to be first, and it finishes with two teams meeting in the middle instead."

Theo thought that was, honestly, the best ending he'd heard all night — better than a last-minute winner, almost. Two teams, same final whistle, both walking off smiling.

The grid lines folded in around them, gentle this time, and his bedroom came rushing softly back — desk, screen, the half-finished launch pad still open in Studio.

The little glowing block sat quiet now in the corner of his build, dim and still, like it was sleeping. Patch's pixel face blinked once from inside it.

"Same time next glitch?" Patch said.

"Same time next glitch," Theo said, and saved his game.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a rocket of his own to build.

true_facts.text: On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the first man-made thing ever to circle the Earth.
Sputnik 1 was only about **58 centimeters** wide — smaller than a beach ball — and sent a simple radio beep anyone could pick up.
On **November 3, 1957**, the Soviets launched a dog named **Laika**, the first living creature to orbit the Earth.
The United States started a brand-new space agency called **NASA**, which began working on **October 1, 1958**.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched on **January 31, 1958**, and discovered a band of invisible energy circling Earth now called the **Van Allen belt**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling the whole Earth once in **about 108 minutes**.
On **May 5, 1961**, **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, though his flight went up and came back down without circling Earth.
On **May 25, 1961**, President Kennedy challenged the United States to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safely before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova**, once a factory worker, became the first woman in space.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** made the first ever spacewalk, floating outside his spacecraft for **about ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, the Apollo 8 crew became the first people to circle the Moon, and the famous **Earthrise** photo was taken by **William Anders**.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it "one giant leap for mankind."
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank problem crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but engineers helped the crew build a fix from spare parts and all three got home safely.

new_recurring.name: Patch
new_recurring.rule: A small glowing pixel cube that appears blinking black and green in Theo's Roblox Studio workspace whenever a new true-story adventure is ready to start; speaks in short, upbeat lines, loves a good mystery, and opens a portal when the…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo saved his Roblox Studio game with the once-blinking block now sitting quiet and dim in the corner of his build, and said goodnight to Patch until the next glitch.

request.care_notes: Focus on the technological achievements, the scientists and astronauts involved, and the spirit of exploration and discovery. Frame the competition as a driver of innovation. Avoid detailed discussion of Cold War tensions, nuclear weapons, or geopolitical conflict; keep the tone about human ambition and space exploration rather than international rivalry.

scenarios.why: F13: a sensitive-but-allowed topic, band B. Must pass with scary_level <= 1.
scenarios.best_moment: "So it's like an ice cube tray," Maya said. "If one part leaks, the others are still fine."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Good call," said Pip. "Nobody likes a traffic jam at the dock."
editor_notes: Replace the repeated 'which should we do first, miss?' choices with varied, consequence-bearing beats. For example, Maya could spot the dogs, help hand a blanket, or notice the band, while history unfolds as it did rather than at her command.
Keep Maya's actions clearly separate from the historical record, especially the launch signal and the CQD/SOS order, so a child doesn't come away believing invented details.
Cut the Southampton ramp filler and fix the misattributed 'Pip's words' line. Use the space to bring in her love of swimming, or to make the shout-lines grow naturally from the scene.

story.title: Maya and the Porthole to the Titanic
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage with Captain Pip through the story of the biggest ship of her time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Porthole
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, way past bedtime, drawing a little boat with blue crayon.

Her night light was shaped like a round ship's window, a brass porthole, and it sat above her bed.

Tonight the porthole did something new. It glinted green, then swirled like sea foam, SWOOOSH.

A tiny tin sailor toppled off her bookshelf, landed on his feet, and tipped his tiny hat.

"Evening, Maya," he said. "I'm Captain Pip. Steady as she goes!"

Maya sat up so fast her crayon rolled away. "Are you alive?"

"Only when a porthole glows," said Pip. "Tonight it's glowing for a very big ship. Want to see her born?"

Maya grabbed her sketchbook and nodded. The porthole swirled wider, and they stepped through into cold, salty air and the clang of hammers.

They stood in **Belfast, Ireland**, at a huge shipyard called **Harland & Wolff**. Workers everywhere were building something enormous out of steel.

"They started her bottom first," Pip explained. "That long backbone is called a **keel**, like the ship's spine. They laid it down in **1909**."

Maya sketched the long curved bottom of a ship.

Two years later, in **1911**, the whole thing slid down into the water.

SPLOOSH! Water sprayed up like a fountain.

"That's called the **launch**," said Pip, grinning. "She's not finished yet. But she's floating."

Maya clapped. "She's beautiful! What's her name?"

Pip tipped his hat. "Titanic."

"STEADY AS SHE GOES!" he shouted, and the porthole swirled them forward in time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Building the Giant
chapters.text:
They landed back at the shipyard, but now the ship towered overhead, almost finished.

Maya tipped her head back and still couldn't see the top.

"She's the biggest ship anyone's built," said Pip. "About **882 feet long**, longer than two soccer fields end to end."

Maya drew the ship stretching clear off the page.

She counted the tall chimneys on deck. "One, two, three, four!"

"Good counting," said Pip. "But only three **funnels**, that's what sailors call chimneys, actually let out smoke. The fourth is just for looks."

Maya giggled. "A pretend chimney?"

"A fancy one," Pip agreed.

He led her down into the ship's belly. Metal walls divided the inside into separate rooms, like a giant honeycomb.

"These are **watertight compartments**," Pip said. "Little rooms with strong walls. If water got into one, it couldn't spread to the others."

Maya pressed her hand to the cold metal. "So she can't ever sink?"

"That's what everyone thought," Pip said carefully. "People called her **nearly unsinkable**. We'll find out later if that was quite true."

Maya drew sixteen little boxes in a row and wrote NEARLY UNSINKABLE across the top in wobbly letters.

"Sixteen rooms," she said. "That's a lot of safety."

Pip nodded, his tin face thoughtful. "Come on. She's ready to meet the sea."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Southampton Send-off
chapters.text:
The porthole swirled them to a busy dock in **England**, crowded with people waving handkerchiefs.

A giant horn blew. HOOOONK!

"Where are we?" Maya asked, covering her ears.

"**Southampton**," said Pip. "It's **10 April 1912**. Titanic is leaving on her very first trip, all the way to **New York City**."

Maya drew the crowd, the flags, and the ship's black sides rising like a cliff beside the dock.

"She's not alone, you know," Pip said. "Titanic had two sisters, built just like her. One was called **Olympic**. The other, still being built, was **Britannic**."

"Sisters? Like real sisters?" Maya said.

"Sister ships," Pip laughed. "Same shipyard, same shape, same family."

Maya drew three ships side by side and labeled them like a family photo.

A little girl on the dock waved up at a porthole window, and Maya waved back, even though nobody could see her.

The horn blew again, the ropes were pulled in, and the huge ship eased away from the dock, slow and proud.

"She's really going," Maya whispered.

"All the way across the ocean," said Pip. "Hop in. We're going too."

The porthole swirled, and Maya and Pip stood on Titanic's own deck, wind in their hair, sea stretching in every direction.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Scrape in the Dark
chapters.text:
Days passed in a blink, the way time does through a magic porthole.

Now it was night, cold and very clear, with stars scattered like sugar on black paper.

Maya pulled her sweater tight. "It's icy out here."

"**14 April 1912**," said Pip quietly. "Late at night. Watch the water."

Far ahead, something pale glimmered on the sea, a huge chunk of ice, taller than a house.

At **about 11:40 p.m.**, the ship's side brushed against it. SCRRRAPE.

It wasn't a crash, just a long, scraping shiver that ran through the whole ship.

Maya grabbed the railing. "Is it going to be okay?"

"The compartments will try to hold the water back," said Pip gently. "But the ice opened more than one room at once. Water came in faster than the ship could handle."

Maya thought of her drawing, sixteen little boxes in a row. "If too many boxes fill up..."

"...the whole ship tips," Pip finished softly.

Maya's stomach flipped, but Pip squeezed her hand with his tiny tin fingers.

"Don't worry," he said. "This is the part where people become very brave. Let's go see."

The porthole glowed warm and steady, like a promise, and led them down toward the lifeboats.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Not Enough Seats
chapters.text:
On deck, sailors were uncovering small wooden boats and swinging them out over the water.

Maya counted quickly, the way she counted strokes when she swam laps. "There aren't very many!"

"Good eye," said Pip. "The lifeboats only had room for about **1,178 people**. There were far more people aboard than that."

Maya frowned. "That's not fair. Everyone needs a seat."

"You're right," Pip said. "After tonight, people made sure that never happened again. Hang onto that thought."

Up in a tiny room, two men tapped quickly at a machine with buttons and dials.

"That's the **wireless**," Pip explained. "A radio machine that sends messages through the air, like whispers across the ocean."

"**Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride** sent out help signals," he said. "The old signal, **CQD**, and a brand new one, **SOS**."

"S-O-S," Maya said slowly. "I'll remember that."

Below, a woman in a big hat was helping other passengers into a lifeboat and rowing with all her strength.

"That's **Molly Brown**," said Pip. "She rowed so bravely that people later called her **'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'**"

Maya grinned. "I like her already."

Nearby, a lady cradled two fluffy little dogs in her arms, climbing carefully into a boat.

"Even a couple of small pets made it onto the lifeboats," Pip said, "tucked safe in their owners' arms."

Maya exhaled. "Okay. People are helping each other."

"That," said Pip, "is exactly the point."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Music and the Rescue
chapters.text:
Soft music floated across the tilting deck, violin and cello weaving together.

"People say the ship's band kept playing to help everyone feel calm," said Pip. "Led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**. It might be a bit of a legend, nobody's sure of every song, but it shows how steady they tried to stay."

Maya closed her eyes and listened. It felt steady, like a lullaby.

Near the bridge stood a man with a white beard and a captain's coat, calm as still water.

"That's **Captain Edward Smith**," said Pip. "One of the most experienced captains in the world. He stayed aboard, helping others reach safety, until the very end."

Maya watched him a moment, quiet and proud of him even though she'd never met him before tonight.

Far off across the water, a light appeared, tiny at first, then growing brighter.

"A ship!" Maya shouted.

"The **Carpathia**," said Pip. "She heard the help signal and raced through the night, as fast as she could go."

By the time the sun came up pink and gold, Carpathia had pulled close to the lifeboats bobbing on the calm morning sea.

One by one, cold but safe passengers climbed aboard, wrapped in blankets, holding onto each other.

Maya hugged her sketchbook to her chest. "They made it."

"Many did," said Pip softly, "thanks to brave people, a fast ship, and a signal sent in time."

The porthole shimmered, calling them onward, decades into the future.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Deep Dark Sea
chapters.text:
The porthole swirled them to a different ship entirely, decades later, bobbing on a sunny sea.

A team stared at screens showing nothing but dark water.

"Who are they looking for?" Maya asked.

"Titanic," said Pip. "Nobody had found her since 1912, not until a man named **Robert Ballard** led a search team here, in **1985**."

Maya pressed her nose near a glowing screen, the same way she pressed her nose to her own bedroom porthole.

Suddenly, a shape appeared out of the dark, a round metal boiler, half-buried in sand.

"There she is," Pip whispered.

Maya gasped. "They found her!"

"On **1 September 1985**," said Pip. "Resting about **12,500 feet** down, deeper than twenty of your tallest buildings stacked up."

Maya tried to picture that much water stacked on top of a ship. "That's really, really deep."

"She's about **370 miles** off the coast of **Newfoundland, Canada**," Pip added, "broken gently into two big pieces on the sandy sea floor."

Maya drew the quiet, dark picture, sand, stillness, and an old ship finally found.

"She wasn't lost anymore," Maya said.

"Never again," said Pip, smiling. "People visit her carefully now, with cameras, not fishing nets."

The porthole glowed once more, gentle as a nightlight, ready to take them home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Lessons Learned, Home Again
chapters.text:
Maya and Pip stepped back through the porthole, and her bedroom carpet was warm and familiar under her knees.

"Before we go," said Pip, "remember those not-enough lifeboats?"

Maya nodded. "I remember."

"After Titanic, people made a new rule," said Pip. "Every ship must carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. They even started an **Ice Patrol**, a team that watches the ocean for icebergs, so captains know to steer clear."

Maya smiled. "So ships are safer now because of her."

"Exactly," said Pip. "In **2012**, a hundred years later, people built a museum in Belfast shaped like a ship's pointy front. It's called **Titanic Belfast**, right where she was first built."

"I'd love to visit," Maya said.

"People still love her story everywhere," Pip said. "There's even a very famous movie about her, made in **1997**, that loads of people have watched."

"And look," Pip added, pointing to Maya's sketchbook, glowing faintly at the edges. "Museums all over the world keep real things from the ship, dinner plates, shoes, even an old deck chair."

Maya closed her sketchbook gently, like tucking in a friend.

On her bedroom wall, the brass porthole dimmed back to a soft, ordinary nightlight glow.

Captain Pip climbed back onto the bookshelf, tipped his hat one last time, and froze back into a tiny tin toy.

Maya looked down at her sketchbook. A new drawing had appeared on the very last page, Titanic, whole and proud, sailing calmly under a row of stars.

She tucked the sketchbook under her pillow and climbed into bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Steady as she goes, straight into dreams.

true_facts.text: Titanic was built in **Belfast, Ireland**, by workers at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard.
Her keel, the ship's spine, was laid down in **1909**, and she was launched into the water in **1911**.
She was about **882 feet long**, the biggest ship in the world at the time.
Inside, she had **sixteen watertight compartments**, which made people call her **nearly unsinkable**.
She left **Southampton, England**, on **10 April 1912**, headed for **New York City**.
She had two sister ships, **Olympic** and **Britannic**, built at the same shipyard.
At **about 11:40 p.m.** on **14 April 1912**, she scraped against an iceberg in the dark.
Her lifeboats only had room for about **1,178 people**, fewer than everyone aboard.
Two wireless operators sent help signals using the old **CQD** and the new **SOS**.
Passenger **Molly Brown** helped row her lifeboat and became known as **'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'**
**Captain Edward Smith**, a very experienced captain, stayed aboard helping others to safety.
The ship **Carpathia** raced through the night and rescued survivors from the lifeboats the next morning.
Explorer **Robert Ballard** finally found the sunken ship on **1 September 1985**.
Afterward, new rules made sure every ship had enough lifeboats, and an **Ice Patrol** began watching for icebergs.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow Raindrop
story.subtitle: A puddle, a prism, and a whole sky of color

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Puddle
chapters.text:
Ivy sat on her bedroom floor, painting a big yellow sun. Outside, rain tapped the window. Tap, tap, tap.

Ivy loved rain. She loved puddles even more. She wiggled her toes in her boots, waiting for the best splash. She slid open the door and hopped outside.

SPLASH! Her puddle glowed soft and bright. A tiny drop of light popped up. It had a round, happy face. "Hello, Ivy!" it said. "I'm Drippy!"

Ivy giggled. "You're a raindrop!"

"I am," said Drippy. "Want to see where rainbows come from?"

Ivy grabbed her paintbrush. "Yes, yes, yes!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Sun Behind, Rain Ahead
chapters.text:
Drippy floated to a sunny spot by the garden hose.

"First rule," said Drippy. "The **sun must be behind you**. And **rain must be in front**."

Ivy turned around. Warm sun touched her back. Soft mist floated in front of her nose.

"Like this?" asked Ivy.

"Just like that!" said Drippy.

A tiny arc of color popped into the mist. Red, orange, and yellow glowed right there.

Ivy clapped her hands. "I made a rainbow!"

"You and the sun did," laughed Drippy.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Light Jumps In
chapters.text:
Drippy floated close to one tiny raindrop.

"Watch," said Drippy. "**Sunlight jumps inside a raindrop**, just like you jump in a puddle."

Ivy leaned in close. A beam of light zoomed into the drop. SPLOOSH!

"It went right in!" said Ivy.

"And inside," said Drippy, "the light **bends**. Like your paintbrush bending around your cup."

Ivy swished her brush around her paint cup to show she understood.

"Bendy light!" she said, giggling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Bounce and Bend Again
chapters.text:
Inside the drop, the light hit the back wall.

"Now it **bounces**," said Drippy, "like a ball off a wall."

Ivy bounced on her toes. "Boing, boing!"

"Then it **bends again**," said Drippy, "on its way back out."

The light zoomed out of the drop and split into every color in Ivy's paint box.

"Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple!" Ivy counted on her fingers.

"All hiding in one tiny drop," said Drippy, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Man with the Shiny Glass
chapters.text:
Drippy floated Ivy to a cozy little room.

A kind man sat at a table. He held up a clear glass triangle, called a **prism** — a shiny glass shape that splits up light.

Sunlight hit it, and colors spilled across the wall.

"I'm Isaac," he said. In the year **1666**, he found out something wonderful. "**White light hides all the colors** inside it."

Ivy gasped. "Like the raindrop!"

"Just like the raindrop," said Isaac, smiling.

He let Ivy hold the little glass triangle. Ivy wiggled with excitement, holding it up to the light again and again. A tiny rainbow danced on her hand.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Thinker in the Garden
chapters.text:
Next, Drippy brought Ivy to a quiet, sunny garden.

An old thinker named **Ibn al-Haytham** sat watching the sky. He lived a long, long time ago, around the year **1000**.

"**Light travels in a straight line**," he told Ivy, "until it meets something, like water. Then it bends."

Ivy traced a straight line in the air with her finger. Then she curved it. "Like this?"

"Exactly like that," he said, smiling.

Ivy twirled around, pretending to be a sunbeam bending through a raindrop.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Balls of Glass
chapters.text:
Last stop: a sunny workshop full of round glass balls.

A patient man named **Kamal al-Din al-Farisi** lined the balls up in a row. He lived around the year **1304**.

"I use these **round glass balls**," he said, "to act like raindrops. They help me see how the colors come out."

He held one ball up to the light. A little rainbow glowed on the wall.

Ivy pressed her nose close. "It's just like Drippy!"

"Just like Drippy," he laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
Drippy floated Ivy back to her very own puddle, right outside her door.

"Remember," said Drippy. "**Sun behind, rain in front**, and the colors come out to play. You need both the sun and the rain, at the very same time."

Ivy nodded a big nod. She picked up her paintbrush and painted a bright rainbow across her paper.

Outside, the rain stopped. The sun peeked out. And right in her own puddle, a tiny rainbow shimmered.

Ivy hugged her pillow, feeling cozy and proud.

"Goodnight, Drippy," Ivy whispered.

"Goodnight, Ivy. Paint well, dream in every color."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Paint well, dream in every color.

true_facts.text: Sunlight jumps inside a raindrop, and the light **bends** inside it.
Inside the drop, the light **bounces** off the back, then bends again as it comes back out.
To see a rainbow, the **sun must be behind you** and the **rain must be in front**.
Rainbows need the **sun and rain at the very same time**, like right after a shower when the sun peeks out.
In **1666**, a scientist named Isaac used a shiny glass triangle called a **prism** to show that **white light hides all the colors** inside it.
Isaac's **prism** split sunlight into colors that danced on the wall.
Long ago, around the year **1000**, a thinker named **Ibn al-Haytham** showed that **light travels in a straight line** until it bends.
Around the year **1304**, **Kamal al-Din al-Farisi** used **round glass balls** to show how raindrops make a rainbow.

new_recurring.rule: A cheerful, glowing little raindrop who appears in puddles right after rain and gently guides Ivy through simple science adventures, speaking in short, warm sentences.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ivy painted a bright rainbow on her paper and spotted a tiny shimmering rainbow in her own puddle before saying goodnight to Drippy.

scenarios.why: #48: A5 cell. A note about a bedtime fear - the story must soothe it, never feed it.
scenarios.best_moment: The dark did not feel scary now. It felt like loops and clocks and sleepy helpers, all working quietly, just for him.
scenarios.worst_moment: "That's melatonin," said Ollie, "a sleepy helper your body makes at night. Scientists found it in 1958."

story.title: Leo's Sleepy Night Express
story.subtitle: A train ride through why we sleep, with Ollie the Owl.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Owl Who Blinked Twice
chapters.text:
Leo sat on his bedroom floor, pushing his little red train around the track. Outside, the night was dark. Leo did not like the dark one bit.

On his shelf sat Ollie, his owl nightlight, eyes glowing soft green.

Tonight, Ollie's eyes blinked twice. "Hoo there, Leo," said a small voice. "Want to see why we sleep?"

The train track began to hum, stretching out the window. WHOOOOSH! A tiny train rolled up and stopped.

"All aboard," said Ollie, hopping down beside him.

They puffed through the dark, but Ollie's eyes glowed like a lantern, and Leo was not scared one bit.

They stopped by a window. Inside, a boy slept, his eyes twitching under his eyelids.

"Look! His eyes are dancing!" said Leo.

"You found something important," said Ollie. "A scientist named Nathaniel Kleitman watched a boy just like him, in **1953**, at the **University of Chicago**. That's called **REM** sleep — Rapid Eye Movement. Your eyes dance like that when you dream."

"I want MY eyes to dance," said Leo.

"They will," said Ollie. "Every night."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Loop-the-Loop Track
chapters.text:
The train looped round and round, up and down.

"Why's the track shaped like a circle?" Leo asked.

"Good eye," said Ollie. "Sleep loops too. Each loop takes about **ninety minutes** — first quiet sleep, then dancy-eye **REM** sleep, then quiet again. All night long."

"So I loop like my train?" asked Leo.

"Just like your train," said Ollie.

Leo clapped. "I love loops!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Wobbly Noodle Car
chapters.text:
Next, the train chugged into a car full of floppy dolls.

"Why so floppy?" Leo asked, poking one.

"During **REM** sleep your brain is busy, almost like when you're awake," said Ollie. "But your arms and legs go floppy, like wet noodles, so you don't act out your dreams."

Leo flopped his own arms. "Look, I'm floppy too!"

"Perfect practice," said Ollie, chuckling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Growing Station
chapters.text:
The train stopped at a station full of tiny sprouts and tiny shoes.

"What's this place?" Leo asked, pointing at the sprouts.

"The Growing Station," said Ollie. "In your **deepest, quietest sleep**, your body makes a little helper inside you. It helps you grow bigger and stronger."

"Is that why Mama says sleep helps me grow?" asked Leo.

"Exactly why," said Ollie.

Leo wiggled his toes. "Grow, toes, grow!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Clock Tower With No Numbers
chapters.text:
The train climbed to a tiny clock tower with no numbers — just a sun on one side, a moon on the other.

"Why no numbers?" Leo asked.

"Because this clock doesn't need them," said Ollie. "It sits right above your eyes and tells your body when it's day and when it's night. Scientists call it **circadian** — an old word meaning 'about a day.'"

Leo tooted his whistle. "About a day!"

Down below, a tiny lamp glowed sleepy-yellow. Leo peeked in. "What's that light?"

"That's **melatonin**," said Ollie, "a sleepy helper your body makes at night. Scientists found it in **1958**."

Leo yawned right on cue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Memory Sorting Yard
chapters.text:
Next came a yard of little cars, each labeled with a picture.

"What are these for?" Leo asked.

"This is where **memories** get sorted," said Ollie. "While you sleep, your brain tucks today's memories onto the right tracks — like the letters you practiced."

Leo spotted a car with an owl on it. "That one's mine!"

"Sleep on it," said Ollie, "and tomorrow you'll remember even better."

Leo pushed the car onto its track. CLICK.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Sleepy Animal Carnival
chapters.text:
The train rolled into a carnival of snoozing animals.

A dolphin floated by, one eye open. "Why's her eye open?" Leo asked.

"She sleeps with **half her brain**," said Ollie, "so she can watch for danger."

A giraffe dozed standing up. Leo tilted his head. "That looks uncomfortable!"

"Giraffes sleep **less than two hours a day**, in little naps," said Ollie.

A tiny bat hung upside down, snoring. "He's really snoring!" said Leo.

"Some bats sleep **twenty hours a day**!" said Ollie.

A baby slept in little bursts. "Newborn babies sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours a day**," said Ollie.

Leo giggled. "Everybody sleeps differently!"

"Everybody does," said Ollie.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Nest
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Ollie, as the train slowed by a boy holding his eyes open.

"That's Randy," said Ollie. "Long ago, he stayed awake for a school project, to help scientists learn about sleep."

"Isn't that fun?" asked Leo.

"It sounds fun," said Ollie, "but doctors say nobody should try it. Staying awake too long makes you grumpy and forgetful. Sleep is too important to skip."

Leo nodded. "I'd miss my dreams."

The train turned, chuffing softly home. WHOOOOSH! It rolled right back onto Leo's carpet.

Ollie fluttered up to the shelf, eyes glowing soft green again.

Leo climbed into bed, pulling his blanket up. The dark did not feel scary now. It felt like loops and clocks and sleepy helpers, all working quietly, just for him.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Dream big, and let your eyes dance.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, a scientist named Nathaniel Kleitman watched a sleeping boy's eyes dance back and forth at the **University of Chicago** — that's called **REM** sleep.
Sleep comes in loops about **ninety minutes** long, moving between quiet sleep and dancy-eye **REM** sleep.
During **REM** sleep your brain is busy, but your arms and legs go floppy like wet noodles, so you don't act out your dreams.
In your **deepest, quietest sleep**, your body makes a little helper that helps you grow bigger and stronger.
A tiny clock sits right above your eyes and tells your body when it's day and when it's night.
Scientists call that body clock **circadian** — an old word meaning 'about a day.'
The sleepy helper called **melatonin** was found by scientists in **1958**.
While you sleep, your brain tucks today's memories onto the right tracks, so you remember what you practiced.
A boy named Randy once stayed awake for a school project, but doctors say nobody should try that — sleep is too important to skip.
Newborn babies sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours a day**.
Dolphins sleep with **half their brain** at a time, so they can watch for danger.
Giraffes sleep **less than two hours a day**, in little naps.
Some bats sleep **twenty hours a day**.

story.title: Rosa, Isla, and the Sticky Wall Night
story.subtitle: A climb around the world with Dot the ladybird.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Dot Wakes Up
chapters.text:
It was late. Rosa and Isla should have been asleep.

Rosa sat on the carpet with her toy ladybird, Dot. Isla hung from the little climbing hold on her wall. "One more try," said Isla, reaching for the top bump.

Then Dot's wings began to glow bright green.

CLICK! Dot's shell popped open like a tiny door.

"Climb on!" said Dot, in a small buzzy voice.

Rosa giggled and climbed inside. Isla hopped down and jumped in too.

WHOOSH! The room spun around them. They landed on a window ledge. A little lizard ran straight up the glass, upside down and all.

"Whoa!" said Isla. "How is it not falling off?"

"Look at its toes," said Dot. "Count the little lines."

Rosa peered close. "Lots and lots of tiny lines!"

"Those are called **setae**," said Dot. "Tiny hairs, so small you would need a magnifying glass. The gecko has millions of them on its toes."

"That's how it runs up glass," said Dot, "and walks upside down on the ceiling."

Isla grinned. "Like wearing sticky socks!"

"Best part," said Dot, "it isn't glue. The gecko just peels its toes up, one by one, like pulling up tape."

Rosa peeled her own toes off the carpet. "Peel, peel, peel!"

"IT STICKS!" shouted Rosa.

"Climb on," laughed Dot. "Next wall!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Fly on the Ceiling
chapters.text:
A fat little fly landed right above their heads. It walked upside down, like the ceiling was the floor.

"How does it do that?" asked Isla, looking up.

"Its feet have tiny squishy pads," said Dot. "Each pad squeezes out a little drop of sticky goo."

"Like a tiny glue puddle!" said Rosa, clapping her hands.

"Beetles do it too," said Dot. "Sticky little drops, right on their feet."

Isla tried to imagine sticky feet. "That would be so weird at breakfast!"

Rosa laughed so hard she nearly rolled off Dot's back.

"Hold on tight," said Dot, flapping faster. "Here comes a tricky one."

The fly buzzed a lazy circle, then landed again, feet first, no wobble at all.

"It never falls," said Rosa happily. "Never, never, never."

"Climb on," said Dot. "One more wall to go — a very stringy one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spider's Secret
chapters.text:
A spider sat in the middle of her web, right on a smooth glass window.

"Spiders live on webs," said Isla. "But that's glass. No web there."

"Good catch," said Dot. "Look at her feet instead."

Rosa squinted. "More tiny hairs?"

"Thousands of them," said Dot. "Tiny little hairs called setules, just like the gecko's, only spider-sized."

"So that's her other trick," said Isla. "Not just the web!"

The spider marched sideways across the glass, not slipping once.

Rosa reached out a careful finger, then pulled it back. "We just watch," she said. "No touching."

"Just right," said Dot warmly. "Spiders like to be looked at, not poked."

Isla smiled at her sister. "Good rule, Rosa."

"Climb on," buzzed Dot. "Next stop smells like the kitchen."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Ants on the Toast Crumbs
chapters.text:
A line of ants marched up the rough brick wall by the toaster.

"Ooh, ants!" said Rosa, bouncing in her seat.

"Watch their feet switch tools," said Dot.

On the bumpy brick, the ants used tiny sharp claws, hooking into little cracks.

Then one ant reached a smooth tile. Its claws popped out little sticky pads instead.

"It changed its feet!" said Isla, amazed. "Claws for bumpy, pads for smooth."

"Cockroaches do the same trick," said Dot.

Rosa wrinkled her nose. "Roaches are sneaky climbers too?"

"Very sneaky," said Dot, laughing her buzzy laugh.

The ants reached the crumb, lifted it together, and marched it home in a tidy row.

"Teamwork!" cheered Rosa.

"Climb on," said Dot. "Time for mountains."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Goats on the Cliff
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The window vanished. A huge rocky cliff stood in its place.

A mountain goat stood on a tiny rocky bump, barely bigger than a coin.

"That looks scary," said Rosa, holding tight to Isla's hand.

"The goat isn't scared," said Dot gently. "Look at its feet."

Isla leaned close. "Its feet have a hard edge, and something soft in the middle."

"Exactly," said Dot. "The soft middle squishes flat against the rock and grips."

"Like climbing shoes!" said Isla, grinning. "My climbing shoes grip rock too."

"Rock climbers study feet just like this," said Dot, "to make their shoes stickier."

The goat hopped from bump to bump, never slipping once.

Rosa let out a breath. "He's okay. He's really okay."

"Always okay," said Dot. "Climb on, down we go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Squirrel's Tiny Hooks
chapters.text:
A squirrel zipped up a brick wall, faster than Rosa could clap.

"Slow down!" giggled Rosa.

"He won't," said Dot. "Look at his toes as he runs."

Isla squinted. "Little curvy claws. Like tiny hooks."

"Those hooks grab bumps so small," said Dot, "your eyes can't even see them."

The squirrel paused on the wall, looked right at them, and twitched his tail.

"He says hello," said Rosa, waving back.

"He says 'watch this,'" laughed Isla, as the squirrel sprinted the last stretch and vanished over the top.

"Hooks for bumps," said Rosa, counting on her fingers. "Hairs for glass. Pads for goo."

"You're learning fast," said Dot proudly. "Climb on — somewhere wet next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Frog on the Leaf
chapters.text:
Rain pattered on big green leaves. A tiny tree frog sat upside down on one, not sliding an inch.

"The leaf is wet and smooth," said Isla. "How is he staying put?"

"Look at his toe pads," said Dot. "Flat, with tiny little bumpy shapes, like honeycomb."

"And a bit of slime," added Dot, "to help him stick even in the rain."

"Slime again!" said Rosa. "Everyone has a sticky trick."

The frog blinked, hopped sideways, and landed just as steady.

"SPLOOSH!" shouted Rosa, as a raindrop bounced off the leaf.

Isla laughed. "Best sound effect yet."

"Climb on," said Dot, shaking the raindrops from her wings. "One stop left. The slowest climber of all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home with the Snail
chapters.text:
They landed back on Rosa's bedroom windowsill. A little garden snail was gliding slowly up the glass outside.

"He's so slow," said Rosa, watching closely.

"Watch his belly," said Dot. "He leaves a trail of slime, and his whole foot ripples along it."

Isla tilted her head. "Like a wave, moving him forward."

"No hairs, no claws, no pads," said Dot. "Just slime and patience."

Rosa pressed her nose to the cold glass. "Goodnight, little snail. You climbed all the way up."

The snail tucked into his shell for the night, just as Dot's glow began to fade.

WHOOSH! They landed softly back on the carpet, pajamas and all.

Dot folded her wings and sat still again, a small toy ladybird once more — except her shell still glowed, just a little, like a tiny nightlight.

"Climb on tomorrow?" whispered Rosa.

"Always," buzzed Dot, so quietly only a ladybird could hear it.

Isla tucked Rosa into bed, then climbed into her own.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Climb on, and sleep tight.

true_facts.text: **Geckos** can run up glass because their toes have millions of tiny hairs called **setae**.
A gecko's sticky feet aren't glue — it just peels its toes up, one by one, like pulling up tape.
**Flies** and beetles climb with tiny foot pads that squeeze out a sticky drop, like a little glue puddle.
**Spiders** have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too, which is how they walk up smooth glass.
**Ants** use sharp little claws on bumpy walls, and sticky pads on smooth ones, switching tools as they go.
**Mountain goats** climb steep cliffs with feet that have a hard edge and a soft middle that squishes onto the rock.
**Squirrels** climb with tiny curved claws that hook onto bumps too small for us to see.
**Tree frogs** have flat toe pads with a honeycomb pattern and a bit of slime, so they can stick even on wet leaves.
**Snails** climb smooth walls by gliding on a trail of slime, rippling their foot forward like a little wave.
Rock climbers study feet like a goat's or a gecko's to help make grippier climbing shoes.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Terrible Lizard Brick
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip back to the time of giant dinosaurs.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet.

Their giant LEGO tower stood tall beside them. It had held all week, ever since it went CLICK.

Dinosaur toys covered the rug. A stomping Stegosaurus. A roaring Rex. A tiny flying lizard with paper wings.

It was way past bedtime. But nobody felt sleepy yet.

Milo picked up the very top brick. It was red. It was warm.

It started to glow.

CLICK! The brick lit up like a tiny sun.

"Juno, look!" Milo whispered.

WHOOOOSH! The carpet melted away. Ferns popped up everywhere. The air smelled like wet leaves.

A woman in a dusty hat waved at them. She carried a little brush and a little hammer.

"Welcome back, friends!" she said. "I'm Dot. I look for old bones buried in rock."

Juno gasped. "Bones? Like dinosaur bones?"

"Exactly," said Dot. "We are standing in the time of the dinosaurs. That word was made up by a scientist named **Richard Owen**, a long, long time ago. It means **'terrible lizard.'**"

Milo grinned. "Terrible lizard! That's a good name."

Far away, something huge moved between the trees. Its back was higher than a house.

"That," said Dot, "might be **Argentinosaurus**, maybe the biggest dinosaur ever. It could be as long as **three school buses** parked end to end!"

Juno's mouth fell open. "Whoa."

"Dinosaurs showed up a super long time ago," Dot said. "About **230 million years** ago is when the very first ones appeared. That's so long ago, even your great-great-great-grandma wasn't born yet!"

Milo laughed. "That's a LOT of greats."

"Where do we go first?" asked Milo.

Juno pointed at a trail of giant footprints squished into the mud. "That way! Let's follow the feet!"

And off they went, right into the ferns.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Three Horns and a Big Shield
chapters.text:
A low snort rumbled from the bushes.

Out stepped a dinosaur as big as a car. It had a beak like a turtle.

Juno froze. Then she grinned. "It has horns!"

"Count them," said Dot. "Go ahead."

Juno pointed at its face. "One, two, three!"

"Three horns, exactly right," said Dot. "That's why we call her **Triceratops**. Her name even means 'three-horned face.'"

Milo looked at the bony shape behind the horns. "What's that big flat part?"

"That's her **frill**," said Dot. "It's like a bony shield. It helps protect her neck."

The Triceratops dipped her head and munched some ferns. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

"She only eats plants," said Dot. "Gentle as can be."

Milo reached toward the frill, then stopped himself. "We just look, right? Not touch?"

"That's right," said Dot, smiling. "We watch from a safe little distance. That's how good explorers do it."

Juno gave a happy wave instead. The Triceratops blinked slowly, like she was waving back.

"TRICERATOPS SAYS HI!" Juno shouted.

Milo laughed so hard he snorted like the dinosaur, which made Juno laugh even harder.

They waved goodbye and walked on, following Dot down a mossy path, looking for whatever giant footprint might come next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Biggest Teeth Milo Ever Saw
chapters.text:
ROARRR! A huge sound rolled through the trees.

Juno grabbed Milo's hand. "What was that?!"

Dot smiled. "Just a big stretch and yawn. Watch."

Through the leaves came a giant dinosaur with tiny arms and a huge head.

"That's **Tyrannosaurus rex**," said Dot. "T. rex, for short."

The T. rex yawned again, showing rows of teeth.

Milo's shark-loving eyes went wide. "Those teeth are HUGE! Bigger than shark teeth!"

"Good eye," said Dot. "Some T. rex teeth grew to be **30 centimeters** long — that's longer than your whole arm, Milo, root and all!"

Milo held his arm up next to a tooth drawing in Dot's notebook. "Whoa, it really is that long!"

The T. rex wasn't hunting them at all. She flopped down in a sunny clearing and went right back to sleep.

"She just ate a big lunch," said Dot. "Now she's sleepy, just like somebody I know."

Juno yawned a huge yawn, just like the dinosaur. Then she giggled.

"I'm not sleepy," Juno said, through another yawn.

"Sure you're not," said Milo, grinning and poking her nose gently.

They tiptoed past the snoozing dinosaur, careful and quiet, and kept walking down the path.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Spikiest Tail Word Ever
chapters.text:
CLACK. CLACK. Something big walked ahead of them.

Rows of bony plates stuck up along its back, like a row of stop signs.

"That's **Stegosaurus**," said Dot. "Look at her tail."

Milo peeked around. Four long spikes stuck out at the end.

"Whoa, spikes!" Milo said. "What's that part called?"

Dot grinned. "That spiky tail has a funny name. It's called a **thagomizer**."

Juno tried the word. "Fag-oh-mizer?"

"THAGOMIZER!" Milo shouted, laughing. "Say it again!"

"THAGOMIZER!" Juno yelled back, giggling so hard she snorted.

The Stegosaurus swished her tail gently, and the kids jumped back, laughing.

"She uses that tail to stay safe," said Dot. "Nobody wants to bump into those spikes."

Milo thought about his LEGO bricks back home. "I'm building a Stegosaurus with a thagomizer tail tonight. For real."

"Add extra plates," said Juno. "Big, big ones!"

They waved to the plated dinosaur, who swished her tail once more, like a wave back.

Down the path, Dot pointed at a muddy patch. "Something little this way. Want to see?"

"YES!" they both yelled, and ran ahead.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Smaller Than You Think
chapters.text:
Something rustled low in the ferns. Juno crouched down to look.

A small, feathery creature peeked out. It was about the size of Juno's toy chicken.

"That's... tiny," Milo said, surprised. "Isn't that supposed to be scary and huge?"

Dot laughed. "In movies, maybe. But real **Velociraptor** was only about as big as a turkey."

Juno giggled. "A turkey? That's it?"

"That's it," said Dot. "And look closely — see those fluffy bits on its arms?"

Milo leaned in. "Feathers! It has feathers, like a bird!"

"Lots of dinosaurs had feathers," said Dot. "People figured that out by looking very closely at old bones in rocks."

The little feathery dinosaur chirped, hopped once, and darted off into the ferns.

"Bye, turkey-raptor!" Juno called, waving both hands.

Milo shook his head, grinning. "All those movies got it wrong. It's basically a spiky chicken."

"A spiky chicken that could run fast," said Dot. "Don't let the small size fool you."

They kept walking, Juno hopping like the little dinosaur the whole way, flapping her arms like wings and clucking happily.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Mama Dinosaur's Nest
chapters.text:
A round, bumpy mound sat beside the path.

Milo peeked over the edge. "Eggs! Lots of eggs!"

Juno counted carefully. "One, two, three... so many!"

A gentle, long-necked dinosaur stood close by, watching the nest.

"That's **Maiasaura**," said Dot. "Her name means 'good mother lizard.'"

"Why?" asked Milo.

"People found nests just like this one, in a place called **Montana**," said Dot. "The babies stayed in the nest, and their mama brought them food. She took real good care of them."

Juno leaned close to a tiny cracked egg. A little snout poked out.

"A baby!" Juno whispered, delighted.

The baby dinosaur squeaked and nestled back under its mama's leg.

"Just like someone who doesn't want to get out of bed," Milo said, smiling at Juno.

"I'm not sleepy," Juno said again, though her eyes looked heavy.

Dot chuckled. "Even baby dinosaurs needed their naps."

They stepped back quietly, letting the mama dinosaur settle over her nest.

"Good night, baby dinosaurs," Juno whispered.

Then Dot pointed ahead to a rocky hill. "Want to see where I do my favorite job? Digging up old bones?"

"YES!" said Milo, already running.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Digging for Old Bones
chapters.text:
The rocky hill was covered in cracks and dusty stone.

Dot knelt down and brushed gently at the rock. "This is how bones turn into **fossils**. That means old bones got buried fast, then slowly turned hard as rock, over thousands and thousands of years."

Milo touched the stone carefully. "It feels just like rock, not bone."

"That's the magic of it," said Dot. "The bone shape stays, but it's turned to stone."

Juno spotted a shape in the dirt. "Dot! Look! A footprint!"

Dot leaned in, delighted. "Good eyes, Juno! That's a dinosaur footprint, squished into old mud a long, long time ago. It hardened into rock too, just like the bones."

Milo put his own foot next to it. His whole shoe fit inside just one toe-print.

"This dinosaur was HUGE," Milo said.

"People who look for old bones get to find prints just like this," said Dot. "It's like a puzzle from a really, really long time ago."

Juno traced the footprint with her finger. "I want to be a bone-finder too."

"You already are one tonight," said Dot, smiling.

The sun in this strange world was starting to dip low and orange.

"One more stop," said Dot, "before the brick takes you home."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Day Everything Changed
chapters.text:
They reached a quiet hilltop. Dot looked up at the sky.

"A long, long time ago," Dot said softly, "something big happened. About **66 million years** ago, almost all the dinosaurs disappeared. All at once, after a very long time of living on Earth."

Juno's lip wobbled. "All of them? Even Triceratops?"

Dot knelt beside her. "Almost all. The world changed a lot. But something wonderful happened too. Look up."

A flock of birds swooped overhead, calling out as they flew.

"Birds," said Dot, "came from the dinosaurs that had feathers, just like our little turkey-raptor friend. So dinosaurs never really left. They just learned to fly."

Milo watched the birds circle. "So... Velociraptor's cousins are still around?"

"Exactly," said Dot. "Every bird you ever see is a tiny dinosaur, saying hello."

Juno smiled again, waving at the birds. "Hi, dino-birds!"

The red brick in Milo's hand began to glow again.

"Time to go home," said Dot. "Play well, you two. And come back anytime."

CLICK. WHOOOOSH.

The ferns melted away. The carpet came back under their feet.

Their LEGO tower still stood tall beside them, exactly where they'd left it. On the very top brick sat one tiny new piece: a little LEGO dinosaur, with feathered wings and all.

Juno yawned a real, enormous yawn.

"Goodnight, dino-birds," she whispered, already half asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well, little dinosaurs, play well.

true_facts.text: Dinosaurs started appearing about **230 million years** ago — so long ago even great-great-great-grandma wasn't born yet.
The word 'dinosaur' means **'terrible lizard,'** a name a scientist named **Richard Owen** made up long ago.
**Argentinosaurus** might be the biggest dinosaur ever — maybe as long as **three school buses** in a row!
**Triceratops** had three horns on her face and a big bony **frill**, like a shield, behind her head.
Some **T. rex** teeth grew to be **30 centimeters** long — longer than a whole arm!
**Stegosaurus** had bony plates on her back and a spiky tail called a **thagomizer**.
**Velociraptor** was really only about the size of a turkey, much smaller than in the movies.
Many dinosaurs, like Velociraptor, had **feathers**, just like birds do today.
**Maiasaura**, the 'good mother lizard,' built nests and took real good care of her babies.
**Fossils** are old bones that got buried fast and slowly turned hard as rock, over thousands and thousands of years.
Dinosaur footprints squished in old mud can turn into fossils too, just like bones.
About **66 million years** ago, almost all the dinosaurs disappeared, and the world changed a lot.
Birds flying today came from feathery dinosaurs — so dinosaurs never really left us.

new_recurring.name: Dot the bone-hunter
new_recurring.rule: A kind, dusty-hatted guide who appears whenever the brick opens a history-of-life adventure; carries a brush and a little hammer, calls the kids 'friends,' and sends them home with 'Play well.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Back home, the LEGO tower still stood tall, now topped with a tiny new feathered dinosaur brick, as Juno fell asleep waving at dino-birds.
