editor_notes: Break the animal-parade structure. Give the night a small through-line, such as Sam trying to earn a 'climbing badge' by copying one trick from each animal. That would make each stop build toward the finale instead of Gordo just announcing the next visitor.

Move more facts from Gordo's explanations into Sam's hands. Let him feel the goat's squishy hoof middle, gently poke a slime trail beside the snail (not the snail itself), or watch the frog's pads through a leaf, so he discovers rather than listens.

Shorten the longer explanatory sentences in Chapters 7 and 9 for a 5-year-old. Cut repeated tics ('creaky little smile', 'leaned in close', 'I love it') and the 'breath he hadn't known he was holding' cliché.

story.title: Sam and the Gecko Who Could Not Fall
story.subtitle: A sticky, slimy, hooved and hairy bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko on the Window
chapters.text:
Sam sat on his bedroom floor in his pajamas. A jar on his knee held a little garden spider. He had said hello to her already. Soon he would let her go.

On the windowsill sat Gordo, a small green gecko toy. His paint was chipped. His eyes were two tiny beads.

Tonight the beads were not black. They were glowing green.

"Ooooh," said Sam.

Gordo's tail gave a little wiggle. TAP. TAP. TAP, went his toes on the glass.

The window did not look like a window anymore. It looked like a big green pond of light.

"Come see how I climb," said a small, creaky voice. It was Gordo. He was talking!

Sam set his jar down gently, spider and all. He walked to the window and touched the glow.

WHOOSH! The glow pulled him right through.

Sam landed on soft, squishy moss. In front of him was a tall glass wall, shiny as a mirror. Running straight up it, quick as a wink, was a real, live gecko.

"That's me," said Gordo, "only bigger, and real, and outside."

"How do you DO that?" Sam asked. "You're not falling!"

Gordo stopped halfway up the wall. Upside down, even.

"Look at my toes," he said.

Sam leaned in close. Each toe had rows and rows of hairs, so small and so many you could never count them.

"Those are my sticky toes," said Gordo. "Millions of tiny hairs. That's my whole secret."

Sam's cheeks hurt from grinning. "Millions? That's more hairs than I have on my whole head!"

"Probably," laughed Gordo. "Want to see them work?"

"YES!" shouted Sam.

Gordo scurried higher, upside down, across the glass ceiling.

"Ready for the next trick?" he called down.

"Ready!" yelled Sam, hopping on his toes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: No Glue, No Mess
chapters.text:
Gordo climbed back down to Sam's level, sticking sideways on the glass like it was nothing.

"My toes are not sticky like syrup," he said. "They don't use glue at all."

"Then how do they stick?" asked Sam.

"Each tiny hair splits into even tinier tips," said Gordo. "So many, many tips. They get super, super close to the glass. That closeness is the whole trick. It just holds on, all by itself."

Sam pressed his own hand flat on the glass. It slid right off. SQUEAK.

"No fair!" he laughed.

"You don't have gecko toes," said Gordo. "Lucky for you, or you'd stick to your blanket every single night."

Sam snorted so hard he had to wipe his nose.

"Here's the best part," Gordo went on. "Since it's not glue, my feet never get sticky or messy. No goo. No mess. Ever."

"Then how do you get UN-stuck?" Sam asked.

Gordo lifted one toe. Then another. Then another, peeling them up one at a time, just like peeling tape off paper.

PEEL. PEEL. PEEL.

"Like that," he said. "One toe at a time. Fast as I like."

Sam tried peeling an imaginary toe off his own hand. "PEEL! PEEL!" he shouted, giggling so hard he nearly fell over.

"Exactly like that," laughed Gordo. "Now follow me. Someone else wants to show off her toes too."

He scurried along the glass wall. Sam ran along the mossy ground to keep up, his bare feet squishing with every step.

"Who?" asked Sam.

"Someone with eight legs," said Gordo. "I think you two will get along."

Sam's eyes went wide. "A SPIDER?"

"A spider," said Gordo, with a creaky little smile.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sam's Favorite Visitor
chapters.text:
On the next wall over sat a spider, calm and patient, her legs neatly tucked.

Sam's whole face lit up. "A spider! I pick up spiders all the time in my yard!"

"I know," said Gordo. "That's exactly why I brought you here."

The spider waved one leg, friendly-like.

"Hello," Sam said softly. He did not touch her. He just looked, the way he always did before letting a bug go home.

"Look at her feet," said Gordo.

Sam leaned in close. On each of her feet were thousands and thousands of tiny hairs, just like Gordo's own toes.

"She has hairy feet too!" Sam said.

"Her hairs are a little different from mine," said Gordo, "but the idea is the same. Tiny hairs, grabbing on tight. That's why spiders can climb smooth glass, just like me."

The spider scurried sideways, quick and light, straight up the wall.

"Go, go, go!" cheered Sam, bouncing on his heels.

She reached the top and gave a little wave with one leg.

"She says thank you," said Gordo, "for never squishing her friends."

Sam beamed. "I would never! I just look, and then I let them go home again."

"That's exactly right," said Gordo. "The best way to say hello to a bug."

A buzzing sound came from around the corner. BZZZZZ.

"What's that?" asked Sam.

"Someone else who climbs walls," said Gordo. "But her trick is a lot wetter. And a lot grosser, honestly."

Sam grinned. "Gross is my favorite kind."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Buzzy Visitor
chapters.text:
Around the corner flew a fat little fly. It landed on the glass with a tiny THUP.

"Flies don't have hairy toes," said Gordo. "They've got something squishier."

Sam leaned close again. Tiny pads sat on the bottom of each foot. A little shine glistened underneath.

"Is that... spit?" Sam asked, scrunching his nose.

Gordo gave his creaky little laugh. "Close! It's a tiny sticky drop. Each pad leaks out a bit of goo, like its own little glue. That's how the fly grips."

"Ewwww," said Sam, grinning anyway. "That's so gross. I love it."

"Most things that climb walls are a little gross," said Gordo. "Or a little weird. Usually both."

The fly buzzed in a happy circle and landed upside down on the ceiling, feet sticking just fine.

"Bet you can't do that," teased Gordo.

Sam went up on his tiptoes and leaned way back. He wobbled, then flopped onto the soft moss. THUD.

"Nope!" Sam laughed, lying flat on his back, moss stuck in his hair.

Gordo scuttled down beside him, shaking his little head. "Good thing you've got me to show you instead."

Sam sat back up, grinning, moss stuck to his pajama sleeve too now.

"What's next?" he asked. "Something with claws, maybe?"

"Funny you should ask," said Gordo. "Follow the scritchy-scratchy sound."

From somewhere nearby came a tiny scritch, scritch, scritch.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Claws AND Sticky Feet
chapters.text:
Sam followed the scritchy sound to a rough brick wall. An ant marched straight up it, quick and busy.

"Ants use tiny claws," said Gordo, "like little hooks, for bumpy walls like this one."

The ant reached a smooth glass patch near the top. It did not slow down one bit. It did not fall.

"Wait," said Sam. "How's it still climbing? That part is smooth!"

"Ants are extra clever," said Gordo. "They've got claws for bumpy walls, AND sticky pads for smooth ones. They just switch, depending on the wall."

"Like changing shoes!" said Sam.

"Exactly like changing shoes," laughed Gordo. "A cockroach does the very same trick."

Right on cue, a cockroach scuttled past, switching smoothly from brick to glass without missing a single step.

Sam clapped his hands together. "Claws for bumpy, sticky feet for smooth! Got it!"

"You got it," said Gordo, giving a proud little nod.

Sam looked up, and up, and up. Above the brick wall stood something much, much bigger: a tall, rocky cliff, way, way up high.

"Whoa," said Sam, his mouth dropping open. "Who climbs THAT?"

"That," said Gordo, "is where we're going next. Don't worry, though. Nobody falls. Not even close."

Sam swallowed, then grinned, already running toward it. "Race you there!"

"You'll lose," said Gordo. "I have sticky toes, remember?"
chapters.shout_line: CLAWS FOR BUMPY, STICKY FEET FOR SMOOTH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Goat on the Cliff
chapters.text:
At the bottom of the rocky cliff stood a mountain goat, calm as could be, chewing something green.

Sam gulped, looking all the way up. "That cliff is SO steep. Is she going to fall?"

"Not this goat," said Gordo gently. "Watch her feet."

The goat trotted straight up the rock face, sure and steady, like it was a flat sidewalk to her.

"Her hooves — those are the hard feet goats have instead of toes — have a hard edge around the outside," said Gordo, "and a soft, squishy middle. That soft part molds right around every little bump in the rock."

"Like a sneaker with grippy bottoms!" said Sam.

"A bit like that," said Gordo. "That's why she never slips."

The goat reached a ledge near the top, turned around, and looked down at them, completely unbothered, still chewing calmly.

"See?" said Gordo. "Safe the whole time."

Sam let out a big breath he hadn't known he was holding, then grinned. "That was so cool. Not scary at all. Well — maybe a little. But mostly cool!"

"Cliffs look scarier than they are," said Gordo, "when you've got the right feet for the job."

A soft ribbit came from a nearby puddle.

"Speaking of feet," said Gordo, "someone wet wants to say hello."

Sam hurried over, moss squishing between his toes. "Another one? This is the best night ever!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Sticky, Squishy Toes
chapters.text:
By the puddle sat a small green tree frog, her toes splayed wide on a shiny wet leaf.

"Frogs climb wet leaves and glass," said Gordo, "without ever slipping at all."

Sam crouched down for a closer look. Each toe ended in a flat little pad, covered in tiny six-sided shapes, lined up neat as tiles.

"Her toes look like bubble wrap!" said Sam.

"Close enough," laughed Gordo. "Those flat pads are covered in a bit of slippery slime, which sounds backwards, but it actually helps her stick to wet things instead of sliding off."

The frog hopped off the leaf, straight onto the glass wall, and stuck there, no slipping at all.

"That's so neat," said Sam. "Wet AND sticky, both at the same time."

"Nature likes doing things its own way," said Gordo.

The frog gave a cheerful ribbit and hopped off into the dark, leaf by leaf.

"One more stop," said Gordo, "before we head home. And this one is extra slow."

"Slow how?" asked Sam, tilting his head.

"You'll see," said Gordo, with a creaky little smile. "Or really, you'll hardly see it moving at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Slowest Climber
chapters.text:
Gordo led Sam to a low stone wall, where a little snail inched her way straight up it, slow and steady.

"No hairs. No claws. No sticky drops," said Gordo. "Just slime."

Sam watched closely. The snail left a shiny, wet trail behind her as she moved, bit by bit.

"She glides on her own slime," said Gordo. "Her whole body is like one big squishy foot. It ripples along, little wave after little wave, and the slime helps her grip the wall."

"That's so slimy and so slow," said Sam, wrinkling his nose happily. "I love it."

"Slow and steady," said Gordo. "She'll get to the top eventually. No rush at all."

Sam watched the snail a moment longer, cheering her on softly. "Go, snaily. You can do it."

The snail, unbothered by fame, kept right on gliding, slow as ever.

"Okay," said Gordo, stretching his tiny legs. "I think it's time we got you home. It's very late, even for a climbing lizard."

Sam yawned a big, wide yawn, suddenly remembering it was way past bedtime. "Will I see you again?"

"Always," said Gordo. "Every gecko's got more walls to climb."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Windowsill
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The green glow pulled Sam back through the window, moss and cliffs and all.

He landed with a soft thump on his own bedroom carpet. His spider jar sat right where he'd left it.

Gordo was small again, back on the windowsill, paint chipped as ever, eyes just two little beads.

"Before I forget," said Gordo, in his small creaky voice, "some clever people who study how things work liked gecko toes so much, they built sticky paddles shaped like a gecko's foot. In 2014, someone used those paddles to climb straight up a glass wall, just like me. No claws. No ropes. No glue."

"A PERSON climbed like a gecko?" Sam gasped.

"A person climbed like a gecko," said Gordo proudly. "And get this — some of those same clever people figured out that if a gecko were as big as a person, it could maybe hold its whole body weight off of just one finger."

"One finger?!" Sam giggled, flopping back onto his pillow. "That's so silly and so cool."

"Most climbing tricks are," said Gordo.

Sam picked up his jar gently and carried it to the window. He opened it just a crack, and the little garden spider climbed out onto the sill, right next to Gordo, then scurried off into the night.

"Goodnight, spider," Sam whispered. "Goodnight, Gordo."

"Goodnight, Sam," creaked Gordo, his eyes dimming back to black. "Stick tight, climb bright."

Sam climbed into bed, thinking of hairy toes and slimy snails and goats on cliffs, and fell fast, happy asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Stick tight, climb bright.

true_facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk upside down on ceilings because their toes have millions of tiny hairs.
Each tiny gecko hair splits into even smaller tips, and getting super close to the wall is what makes them hold on.
A gecko's feet aren't sticky like glue, so they never get messy, and a gecko can peel its toes off one at a time, like peeling tape.
Spiders have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Flies have tiny pads on their feet that ooze a little sticky drop, like their own natural glue, to help them climb.
Ants and cockroaches use little claws for bumpy walls and sticky pads for smooth walls, switching between the two.
Mountain goats climb steep, rocky cliffs using hooves with a hard outer edge and a soft, squishy middle that molds around the rock.
Tree frogs have flat toe pads covered in tiny six-sided shapes and a bit of slime, which helps them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails climb smooth walls by gliding along on their own slime, using their whole squishy foot.
In 2014, scientists built sticky paddles shaped like gecko feet that let a person climb straight up a glass wall.
Scientists figured out that if a gecko were as big as a person, it could maybe hold its whole body weight off just one finger.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Sam returns to his own bedroom, lets his garden spider go free out the window right next to Gordo, and falls asleep happy after Gordo says goodnight with his new catchphrase, 'Stick tight, climb bright.'

story.title: Finn and Nell and the Buzzy Honey Jar
story.subtitle: A sticky, buzzy bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Jar
chapters.text:
Finn licked the last drop of honey off his toast. Sticky and sweet. Yum!

Nell sniffed her yellow flower on the windowsill. "Smells like sunshine," she said.

Then the honey jar on the shelf went GLOW. Soft and gold, like a tiny lamp.

A little wooden bee sticker on the lid began to hum. BZZZZZ. Its wings wiggled.

"I'm Buzzy," said the bee. "Want to see where honey comes from?"

Finn's eyes went wide. Nell grabbed her flower, just in case.

Buzzy puffed a little gold dust. POOF! The room spun. Finn and Nell shrank down, down, down, until they were bee-sized, standing on the windowsill next to a real, huge flower.

A fuzzy bee landed on the petal. She had a long, bendy straw for a tongue.

"That's a **proboscis**," said Buzzy. "A curly straw tongue. She uses it to slurp up **nectar**, the sweet juice inside flowers."

SLURRRRP went the bee.

"Where does it go?" asked Finn.

"Into her honey tummy," said Buzzy. "A special pouch, just for carrying nectar home. Not her eating tummy at all."

Finn patted his own tummy. "I only have one tummy."

"Bees get two," said Buzzy. "Handy, right?"

Nell pointed at the flower. "Can we follow her home?"

That was Nell's idea, and Buzzy grinned. "Hop on my back, little ones."

They climbed on. The bee took off toward a big tree. Finn and Nell held tight and giggled all the way.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Bee Kiss
chapters.text:
The hive buzzed like a thousand tiny engines. BZZZZZZZ.

The nectar bee landed at the door. Another bee rushed over, bumping her with little tap-tap-taps.

"Why's she bumping her?" asked Nell.

"Watch," said Buzzy.

The two bees touched mouths. One passed the sweet nectar straight into the other's mouth, like a tiny, sticky kiss.

"Ewww," said Finn, then, "actually, cool."

"It's called passing the nectar along," said Buzzy. "Every time a bee passes it, a little bit of bee spit mixes in. That spit starts turning the watery nectar into honey."

Nell giggled. "Bee spit makes honey?"

"Just a little bit helps," said Buzzy. "Bit by bit, kiss by kiss."

Finn had an idea. "Can we time how fast they pass it?"

"Go ahead," said Buzzy.

Finn counted. "One, two, three!" The nectar zipped from bee to bee to bee, quick as a wink.

"Three kisses and it's already moving house," laughed Buzzy.

Nell clapped. "Bees are fast kissers!"

A whole line of bees passed the nectar deeper into the hive, mouth to mouth, all the way to the heart of the honeycomb. Finn and Nell followed, ducking under golden wax walls that smelled warm and sweet, like Finn's toast at home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Six Little Sides
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, walls of wax stretched everywhere. Tiny little rooms, all in neat rows.

"Count the sides of one room," said Buzzy.

Finn leaned close and touched the edges with his finger. "One, two, three, four, five... six!"

"Six sides!" said Buzzy. "Every single cell is six-sided, like a tiny stop sign. Bees build them that way because six-sided shapes fit together perfectly, with no squished gaps."

Nell tapped a wall. "It's soft! And warm!"

"That's **beeswax**," said Buzzy. "Bees make it themselves, from their own tummies. Little flakes come out, and the bees chew it soft and build with it."

"Like honey LEGO," said Finn.

Buzzy laughed so hard her wings rattled. "Honey LEGO. I like that."

A house bee spread the nectar into one of the six-sided rooms, smoothing it with her legs.

"That's where the nectar lives now," said Buzzy, "until it turns into honey."

Nell pressed her nose near a cell. "It smells like my flower."

"Flowers and honey are best friends," said Buzzy.

Finn counted five more cells, just to be sure. Six sides, every time. He grinned the whole way through.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Wind Machine Bees
chapters.text:
A strange sound filled the hive. Not buzzing. Something softer. WHOOSH, WHOOSH, WHOOSH.

"What's that wind?" asked Nell, holding her flower tight so it wouldn't blow away.

"Come see," said Buzzy.

A whole row of bees stood by the wet nectar cells, flapping their wings as fast as they could. Their wings moved so fast they blurred.

"Their wings flap about two hundred times every second," said Buzzy. "That's what makes the buzzing sound you hear. Right now they're fanning the nectar to dry it out."

"Like a tiny hair dryer!" said Finn.

"Exactly like that," said Buzzy. "Nectar starts out watery. All that fanning dries it up until it turns thick and sticky. That's how it becomes real honey."

Nell flapped her arms like wings. "Am I helping?"

"Flap faster!" said Finn, flapping too.

They flapped together, giggling, right next to the bees, until Nell got the hiccups from laughing.

"Look," said Buzzy, pointing. The nectar in one cell had gone from runny to thick and golden, right before their eyes.

"It's turning into toast honey!" Finn cheered.

"Almost," said Buzzy. "Just a little more fanning to go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Wax Lid
chapters.text:
One cell stopped being watery. It shone thick and gold, like melted sunshine.

"Is it done?" asked Finn.

A bee walked over and patted a thin cap of wax right over the top, sealing it shut.

"Now it's done," said Buzzy. "That little wax lid keeps the honey safe and clean, like a lid on a jar."

Finn thought of his own honey jar at home. "Just like ours!"

"Just like yours," said Buzzy. "Bees make so much honey because winter is coming. When it's cold, there are no flowers to visit. No nectar to slurp. So the bees eat the honey they saved up instead."

Nell frowned. "So it's like... a lunchbox for winter?"

"A lunchbox for winter," agreed Buzzy. "A very good way to put it."

"Can I help seal one?" asked Finn.

Buzzy nodded, and a friendly bee let Finn pat a soft dab of warm wax over a finished cell, gentle as closing a book.

It sealed with a tiny CLICK.

"I did it!" Finn cheered.

Nell patted the next one too, very carefully, tongue poking out while she concentrated.

Row after row of cells shone gold, each one capped and tucked away, safe until winter came.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Busy Queen
chapters.text:
Deep inside the hive, bees crowded around one very big bee.

"Who's that?" whispered Nell.

"That's the **queen bee**," said Buzzy. "The busy mom of almost every bee here."

Finn watched her lay a tiny white egg into a cell. Then another. Then another.

"She can lay more than a thousand eggs in just one day," said Buzzy.

Finn's mouth dropped open. "A thousand? Can I count them?"

"Go ahead, quick fingers," laughed Buzzy.

Finn counted as fast as he could. "One, two, three... I'm never gonna catch up!"

"Nobody does," said Buzzy. "A hive like this can have twenty thousand bees in summer. Sometimes even sixty thousand."

Nell looked around at all the buzzing wings. "That's SO many sisters."

"Almost all of them are girls," said Buzzy. "Girl bees do the flying, the building, the cleaning, and the honey-making. They run the whole hive."

"Girls rule," said Nell proudly, holding her yellow flower up like a flag.

Finn high-fived her. "Girls rule!"

The queen kept laying eggs, calm and steady, while her busy daughters bustled all around her, humming a happy, buzzing song.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
Outside the hive, a bee landed and began to wiggle. Not a normal walk. A wiggly, waggly dance.

Nell gasped. "She's dancing!"

"She's a **scout bee**," said Buzzy. "She found a great patch of flowers, and now she's telling the others where to go. The wiggle tells them the direction. The dance length tells them how far."

"Can we dance too?" asked Nell, already wiggling.

"Try it," said Buzzy.

Nell wiggled toward the yellow flowers blooming by the fence. Finn copied her, wiggling the exact same way, both of them giggling.

A whole crowd of bees followed their wiggly path, straight to the yellow flowers.

"You did it!" said Buzzy. "You just did a waggle dance."

At the flowers, bees landed and got yellow dust, called **pollen**, stuck to their fuzzy legs.

"Why's she carrying yellow dust?" asked Finn.

"She carries it from flower to flower," said Buzzy. "That helps the flowers grow fruits and seeds. Bees help flowers while they collect nectar. Two good jobs at once."

Nell beamed, holding her own yellow flower next to a bee's yellow legs. "Twins!"

"Best kind of twins," said Buzzy, and the whole patch buzzed happily in the sunshine.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Buzzy, "before bedtime."

A kind beekeeper in a big white hat lifted a wooden lid gently. Finn and Nell peeked from behind a honeycomb wall.

"That's a **beekeeper**," said Buzzy. "She takes care of the hive and only takes a little extra honey, always leaving plenty for the bees."

"That's fair," said Finn.

"Very fair," said Buzzy. "And here's a sweet secret. It takes about twelve bees their whole lives, working together, just to make one teaspoon of honey."

Finn thought of his toast. "One teaspoon? That's a LOT of bee work for my toast."

"A whole team," said Buzzy. "And here's the best part. Honey almost never goes bad, as long as the jar stays shut and dry. Some honey could sit for ages and still be good to eat."

Nell gasped. "Forever honey!"

"Pretty close to forever," laughed Buzzy.

Gold dust puffed again. POOF! The hive spun away, and Finn and Nell landed softly back on their bedroom carpet, full-sized again.

The honey jar sat glowing gently on the shelf, the little wooden bee sticker still and quiet now.

Nell set her yellow flower right beside the jar. Finn gave the lid a happy pat.

"Thank you, Buzzy," they whispered together.

The jar gave one last tiny glow, like a wink, then went dark and ordinary again.

Finn climbed into bed, honey-toast dreams already waiting for him. Nell tucked her flower under her pillow, smiling about her new twin bee.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Sweet dreams, little bees.

Bees keep nectar in a special honey tummy, separate from their eating tummy.

A little bee spit gets mixed in each time nectar is passed along, helping it turn into honey.
Honeycomb rooms always have **six sides**, fitting together with no gaps.
Bees make soft **beeswax** from their own bodies to build the honeycomb.
Bees flap their wings super fast, like a tiny hair dryer, to dry nectar into thick honey.
A bee's wings flap about two hundred times every second, making the buzzing sound.
Once honey is ready, bees seal it with a thin wax lid to keep it safe and clean.
Bees save up honey as a lunchbox for winter, when there are no flowers to visit.
The **queen bee** can lay more than a thousand eggs in just one day.
A busy hive can have twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees in the summer.
A **scout bee** does a wiggly waggle dance to show other bees where good flowers are.

new_recurring.name: Buzzy the Honey Jar Bee

story.title: Omar and the Wheel of Light
story.subtitle: A BMX kid rides two hundred years of bicycles.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Running Machine (1817)
chapters.text:
Omar was supposed to be asleep.

Instead, he lay on his floor, spinning his BMX bike's front wheel with one finger. He was picturing his next big trick for the skate park.

Then the valve cap — the tiny plug where air goes in — began to glow green.

Omar sat up fast. "Whoa."

He twisted the cap. **WHOOSH!** Green light swirled into the shape of a spinning wheel.

Out popped a tiny guide made of shiny spokes and chain, grinning like he'd just landed a trick.

"Name's Spoke," he said. "Want to see where your bike came from? Ride on!"

The wheel of light pulled Omar in. He landed with a THUD in a dusty old square.

A man in a tall hat straddled a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals at all.

"That's **Karl von Drais**," said Spoke. "In **1817**, he built this. People called it a running machine — you push it with your feet, like a scooter."

Omar grinned. "Half scooter, half bike?"

"Exactly," said Spoke. "They also called it a hobby horse."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
Spoke snapped his chain fingers. **CLICK!** The square melted into a bumpy cobblestone street.

A man pedaled past on a machine with pedals bolted right onto the front wheel. His whole body bounced with every bump.

"Ouch," said Omar. "That looks rough."

"It is," said Spoke. "Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement built this in the **1860s**. People nicknamed it the boneshaker."

Omar watched the rider wobble over the stones. "Good name."

"Lallement even got an official American patent for a pedal bike, in **1866**," said Spoke. "That means the idea was officially his."

Omar pointed at the wheel. "The pedals are on the wrong wheel. They should be on the back, with a chain, so your feet don't spin so fast."

Spoke's spokes sparkled. "Hold that thought. Someone else thinks so too — just a bit later."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Penny-Farthing (1870s)
chapters.text:
The street spun away. **WHOOOSH!** Omar landed somewhere sunnier, in the **1870s**.

A rider zoomed past on the strangest bike Omar had ever seen — a giant front wheel, taller than a person, with a tiny wheel behind it.

"That's a penny-farthing," said Spoke. "Named after two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing."

"Big wheel, little wheel," said Omar. "Just like the coins!"

Just then, the rider hit a bump. He tipped forward and tumbled off, landing safely in soft grass.

"They call that taking a header," said Spoke. "Riding up that high was risky."

The man popped up, dusted off his coat, and laughed. "Perfectly fine!"

Omar laughed too, then frowned. "Why not make both wheels smaller — and the same size?"

Spoke's eyes twinkled. "Say that a little louder. Someone's about to agree with you."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885)
chapters.text:
**CLICK!** The scene shifted to a busy workshop, tools everywhere.

A man named **John Kemp Starley** leaned over a new frame. Two wheels, same size. A loop of chain ran from the pedals to the back wheel.

"In **1885**," said Spoke, "Starley built this. He called it the Safety Bicycle."

Omar's jaw dropped. "That's exactly what I said! Same-size wheels, chain on the back!"

"Great minds," said Spoke, bumping Omar's fist with a tiny chain-link hand.

Starley hopped on and pedaled smoothly across the floor. "No more headers!" he called.

"This caught on fast," said Spoke. "Soon bikes everywhere looked just like this — closer to the bike hanging on your wall at home."

Omar looked down at his sneakers. "Can I try it?"

"Patience," said Spoke. "One more stop. Your ride's about to get a lot smoother."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Air-Filled Tire (1888)
chapters.text:
They landed in a yard in Scotland, **1888**.

A man knelt beside a tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around the wheel and filling it with air.

"That's **John Boyd Dunlop**," said Spoke. "He was an animal doctor. He built this tire for his son's tricycle, so the ride wouldn't be so bumpy."

"A tire full of air?" said Omar. "Like my BMX tires?"

"Exactly like your BMX tires," said Spoke. "Before this, tires were solid rubber. Hard as rocks."

Dunlop rolled the tricycle across the gravel. It glided, smooth and quiet, no rattling at all.

"SO SMOOTH!" Omar yelled, and Spoke laughed so hard his spokes jingled.

"His tire company is still around today," said Spoke. "You've probably seen the name."

Omar nodded slowly. "Air tires. No wonder my bunny hops feel so good."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
The yard spun into a busy city street, bikes everywhere — the **1890s**.

Women rode past in a rush, laughing, going wherever they pleased.

"This was the Golden Age of Bicycles," said Spoke. "Millions of bikes sold, all across Europe and America."

"Why do they look so happy?" asked Omar.

"Bikes gave women new freedom," said Spoke. "They could go places on their own, without waiting for anyone. A famous woman named Susan B. Anthony said cycling helped women more than almost anything else ever had."

"That's huge," said Omar.

"It is," said Spoke. "Long skirts were dangerous near bike wheels and chains, so people started wearing looser, safer clothes for riding too."

One rider popped a tiny wheelie on purpose, grinning at her friends.

"She's basically doing tricks already," said Omar.

"Bikes have always been for having fun," said Spoke. "Some things never change."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Bike Shop (1890s–1903)
chapters.text:
**WHOOSH!** They landed in a small shop in Dayton, Ohio, the **1890s**.

Two brothers were fixing bike wheels, spokes gleaming on the workbench.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," said Spoke. "They ran a bike repair shop, right here."

"Wait," said Omar. "Aren't those the airplane guys?"

"Good memory," said Spoke. "They used what they learned building light metal frames and spoked wheels to help build their first airplane, in **1903**."

Omar picked up a wheel, spinning it between his hands. "So bikes basically helped invent flying."

"Pretty much," said Spoke. "Light, strong, and fast. Turns out those rules work in the sky too."

Orville looked up and winked, like he already knew a secret about the future.

Omar grinned back. "Keep fixing bikes. I've got a feeling about you two."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Back to the Ramp (1970s)
chapters.text:
The shop melted into sunshine, dirt trails, and a dusty track — the **1970s**.

Kids zoomed past on small, tough little bikes, popping jumps off dirt ramps.

"BMX bikes," said Spoke. "Riders in the United States built these, inspired by motorcycle dirt racing. Tough frames, made for tricks."

Omar's eyes went wide. "This is basically my bike!"

Nearby, other riders bombed down a rocky hill on bikes with wide, bumpy tires.

"Mountain bikes," said Spoke. "Riders in California built these around the same time, for rough trails."

Omar whooped, watching a rider land a jump clean. "Best stop yet!"

"Every bike tonight," said Spoke, "helped build the one leaning against your wall right now."

The wheel of light opened once more. Omar tumbled back onto his bedroom floor, right where he'd started.

His BMX leaned against the wall, valve cap glowing softly, then fading.

On his pillow sat a tiny chain-link bracelet, still warm.

Omar grinned, pulled up his blanket, and whispered, "Ride on."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ride on.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, **Karl von Drais** built a wooden bike with no pedals — you pushed it with your feet, like a scooter.
People nicknamed his invention a **hobby horse**, and it had handlebars for steering, just like today.
In the **1860s**, Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement bolted pedals onto the front wheel, making the bumpy **boneshaker**.
In the **1870s**, the **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel, taller than a person, and a tiny back wheel.
It was named after two old coins — a big **penny** and a tiny **farthing**.
Riding so high up was risky — falling off the front was called **taking a header**.
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the **Safety Bicycle**, with two same-size wheels and a chain to the back wheel.
The Safety Bicycle was much easier to ride, and bikes everywhere soon looked just like it.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** made a rubber tire filled with air, so rides felt smooth instead of bumpy.
In the **1890s**, bikes gave women new freedom to go places on their own — Susan B. Anthony said cycling helped them more than almost anything else.
**Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran a bike repair shop in **Dayton, Ohio**, in the **1890s**.
They used tricks from building light bike wheels and frames to help build their first airplane, in **1903**.
**BMX bikes** became popular in the United States in the **1970s**, inspired by motorcycle dirt racing.
**Mountain bikes**, with wide bumpy tires, were built around the same time by riders in California.

story.title: Ada and the Fridge Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A CLINK-tastic bedtime trip through pushes, pulls, and tiny invisible hugs.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Letters That Wouldn't Behave
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime, and Ada was still on her bedroom floor.

She had scooped every fridge-magnet letter into one pile. Her toy robot, Bolt, waited beside her for new parts.

Then an **N** and an **S** jumped together with a tiny **CLINK**!

Ada tried to pull them apart. They wouldn't budge. She flipped the **N** around and tried again. This time it zoomed away instead.

"Pushy," said a small voice. The **S** had grown tiny arms and one blinking eye. "I'm Clink. Every magnet has two ends, called poles — north and south."

"Opposite poles pull together," said Clink. "But two norths, or two souths? They push apart."

Ada tested it herself. North to south — **CLINK**! North to north — **WHOOSH**!

"Opposites stick. Same ones don't!" Ada cheered.

"Exactly," said Clink. "Want to see where else that invisible push hides?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Invisible Hug
chapters.text:
Clink led Ada through a swirl of glittery dust, and they landed in her own kitchen — glowing faintly green.

Clink waved a hand over a bowl of paperclips and pennies. The paperclips jumped up and stuck to him. The pennies stayed put.

"Magnets only pull on some things," said Clink. "Iron says yes. Gold and copper, like that penny, say no thanks."

Ada tried it herself. Paperclip — **stuck**! Penny — nothing happened.

"Every magnet has an invisible, stretchy space around it," Clink explained. "It's called a magnetic field. You can't see it, but it can push or pull things nearby."

Ada squinted at the air around Clink. "Can I ever see it?"

"Sprinkle tiny metal bits near a magnet," said Clink, "and they curve into loops, like a secret map only magnets can draw."

Ada tried it — and gasped. "It's like an invisible hug!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: A Million Tiny Dancers
chapters.text:
CLINK! Clink shrank them both down, tiny enough to stand inside a fridge magnet.

Ada gasped. Glowing dots spun everywhere, like the smallest tops in the world.

"Those are electrons," said Clink. "Every tiny bit of everything has them, and each one acts like its own itty-bitty magnet."

"In a magnet," Clink went on, "all those tiny dots spin the same way, lined up like a parade."

"What about my wooden block?" Ada asked. "Is that a magnet too?"

"Nope," said Clink. "In wood, those tiny dots point every which way. No parade, no pulling power."

Ada lined up her toy robots, all facing the same direction. "Like this?"

"Exactly like that," said Clink. "You just built a magnet, Ada-style."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Magic Rock of Magnesia
chapters.text:
Another CLINK, and they landed somewhere old and dusty — ancient Greece, Clink said.

Nearby, a shepherd stared down at his sandal, stuck fast to a rock.

"That's called a lodestone," said Clink. "It's a magnet that grows right out of the ground. People found it near a place called Magnesia."

"Is that why we say magnet?" guessed Ada.

"Probably!" said Clink. "Nobody's totally sure, but most people think that's where the word came from."

Ada patted the lodestone gently. It tugged at a tiny metal bead on her sleeve. "A magic rock, before anybody even knew about electrons."

"The best magic usually is," said Clink.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Needle That Never Gets Lost
chapters.text:
Next stop: a wobbly boat, long ago in China.

A sailor held a floating needle. It spun and spun — then stopped, pointing the same direction every time.

"That's a compass," said Clink. "People floated a magnet needle on water over **2,000 years ago** to find their way."

"But why does it always point there?" Ada asked.

"Because Earth itself is one giant magnet," said Clink. "Deep inside, swirly melted iron makes the whole planet pull like a magnet. The needle just lines up with it."

Ada spun in a circle, arms out like a needle. She stopped, facing the same way each time. "I'm a compass!"

"Best compass I've ever met," said Clink.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: On-Off Magnets
chapters.text:
CLINK! They landed in a junkyard. A crane swung overhead and lifted a whole car — no hooks at all.

"Magnet crane!" gasped Ada.

"An electromagnet," said Clink. "Wrap wire in a coil, run electricity through it, and — boom — instant magnet. Flip the switch off, and it lets go."

"Doorbells use them too," Clink added. "So do loudspeakers, and the little motor inside Bolt."

Ada found a tiny switch on Bolt's arm. **CLICK.** His hand turned magnetic and picked up a paperclip. **CLICK** again, and it let go.

"I CAN TURN MAGNETS ON AND OFF!" Ada cheered.
chapters.shout_line: I CAN TURN MAGNETS ON AND OFF!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Oops, I Broke It
chapters.text:
Back in her room, Ada picked up a bar magnet from her desk and — **SNAP** — it broke in half.

"Oh no, I broke it!" she said.

Clink chuckled. "Try sticking both pieces to a paperclip."

Both halves grabbed paperclips just fine.

"Cut a magnet in half," said Clink, "and you don't get one weak piece. Each new half gets its own north and south, same as before."

Ada grinned with relief. "So it's not broken — it's just two magnets now!"

"Double the fun," said Clink. "Speaking of fast — some trains float right above their tracks on magnets, no wheels touching at all. Just **WHOOSH**."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back Home, Stuck Together
chapters.text:
One more CLINK, and they landed somewhere with beeping machines and kind doctors.

"Hospitals use giant magnets too," said Clink. "A machine called an MRI uses one to take pictures inside somebody's body — no cutting needed, just magnets and pictures."

Then — **CLINK, CLINK, CLINK** — the swirl brought them home, right back to Ada's bedroom floor, fridge letters scattered everywhere.

Ada picked up her **N** and **S** again. They snapped together, soft and bendy.

"Fridge magnets are a little bendy," said Clink, "because they're made with rubber mixed with magnet powder. That's why they bend without ever losing their stick."

Ada yawned a giant yawn.

"Thanks, Clink," she whispered.

"Stick together, sleep tight," said Clink, giving a tiny wave before fading back into the pile of letters.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick together, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: Every magnet has two ends called **poles** — a **north pole** and a **south pole**.
**Opposite poles pull together**, but two of the same poles **push apart**.
Every magnet has an invisible, stretchy space around it called a **magnetic field** that can push or pull.
Magnets get their pull from tiny bits called **electrons**, which act like their own tiny magnets.
When those tiny bits line up the same way, like a parade, they make one strong magnet.
Long ago, people found a magic magnetic rock called a **lodestone**, near a place called **Magnesia**.
More than **2,000 years** ago, people in China floated a magnet needle on water to find their way.
Earth itself is like one giant magnet, because of swirly melted iron deep inside it.
An **electromagnet** is made by wrapping wire in a coil and running electricity through it — and it can switch on and off.
Electromagnets power things like **doorbells**, **loudspeakers**, and giant **cranes** that lift cars.
If you cut a magnet in half, each new half becomes its own magnet, with both a north and a south pole.
Some trains float right above their tracks using magnets, with no wheels touching at all.
Hospitals use giant magnets inside a machine called an **MRI** to take pictures inside somebody's body without any cutting.
**Fridge magnets** are a little bendy because they're made from rubber mixed with magnet powder.

story.title: Priya and Dev and the Rainbow in the Spray
story.subtitle: A squirt-gun science adventure, in every color.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Sparkled
chapters.text:
It was almost bedtime, but Dev was still in the backyard. He had his water pistol loaded for one more squirt.

Priya sat on the porch steps, drawing a purple dragon.

"Last one," Dev said, aiming at the setting sun.

SPLOOSH! A fan of tiny drops flew up and lit into seven stripes of color.

"PRIYA, LOOK!" Dev yelled.

Priya dropped her crayon and ran over. "A rainbow — from your water pistol?"

Right in the middle of the colors, something glowed. A tiny sprite popped out, shimmery as a soap bubble, wearing every color at once.

"Hiya," the sprite said. "Name's Biv. Like the end of Roy G. Biv."

Dev blinked. "Roy who?"

"You'll see," Biv said, grinning. "To make a rainbow, you need the sun **behind** you and water drops in **front** of you — both at the exact same time. Tonight you had both. Grab your squirter. We've got a rainbow to figure out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Bendy Light
chapters.text:
Biv waved a sparkly hand. One floating drop froze in midair, big as a beach ball.

"Climb in," Biv said. "Light does, all the time."

Priya peeked through the drop's curved side. "It bends! Like it turned a corner!"

"Exactly," said Biv. "Light slows down going from air into water, so it bends. Grown-ups call that **refraction** — a fancy word for light taking a turn."

Inside the drop, a sunbeam bounced off the back wall, then bent again on its way out.

Dev squirted another drop to watch it happen twice. "It's like a water slide for light!"

"Best way I've ever heard it," Biv said, laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Rainbow Inside Sunlight
chapters.text:
"Here's a secret," Biv said. "Sunlight looks white, but it's hiding colors inside."

Priya folded her arms. "Prove it."

Biv held up a tiny glass **prism** — a see-through triangle — and let a sunbeam hit it.

A ribbon of colors spilled across the porch: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet.

"A scientist named **Isaac Newton** did this exact trick with a prism, back in **1666**," Biv said. "He proved sunlight holds every color at once."

Priya grabbed her crayon box and lined up six crayons to match. "So which one bends the least?"

"Red bends least, so it ends up on the outside," Biv said. "Violet bends most, so it tucks in on the inside edge."

Dev squirted a quick rainbow to double-check. Red outside. Violet inside. Priya's crayons matched perfectly.

"Nailed it," Dev said, high-fiving his sister.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Whole Circle
chapters.text:
"Hey Biv," Dev said, "why's a rainbow shaped like a smile, not a whole circle?"

"Good eye," Biv said. "Rainbows are actually **full circles**. The ground just blocks the bottom half, so we only see the top arc."

Dev spun around, spraying mist all over himself. A full ring of color flickered — until his sneakers got in the way at the bottom.

"See? Ground," Biv said.

"What if there was no ground?" Priya asked.

"Then you'd see the whole circle," Biv said. "People in airplanes sometimes do, since there's nothing but sky below them."

Dev gasped. "I'm getting a window seat forever now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainbow's Fainter Twin
chapters.text:
Priya squinted upward. "Biv — is that a second rainbow? It looks blurry and backwards!"

A fainter arc glowed above the bright one. Its colors were flipped, violet on the outside this time.

"Sharp eyes," Biv said. "Sometimes light bounces twice inside a drop before it comes out. That flips the colors and makes a second, fainter rainbow above the first."

Dev tried to squirt a triple rainbow. Nothing happened.

"Two's the limit tonight," Biv laughed. "Don't push your luck, squirt-gun boy."

Dev stuck out his tongue, grinning. Priya high-fived Biv instead.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Two Kids, Two Rainbows
chapters.text:
Biv had the kids stand five steps apart.

"Dev, point at the middle of your rainbow," Biv said.

Dev pointed at a spot. Priya pointed too — at a totally different spot.

"Wait, that's not fair!" Dev said. "Mine's over there, not where she's pointing!"

"You're both right," Biv said. "Everybody sees their very own rainbow, made from their own raindrops. It depends on where your eyes are standing. No two people ever see the exact same one."

Priya grinned. "So I've got my own personal rainbow?"

"Yep," said Biv. "And nobody's ever borrowing it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rainbows Everywhere
chapters.text:
"Rainbows don't only live in the sky," Biv said. "They hide in waterfalls, in garden hoses — even in moonlight."

"Moonlight rainbows?" Priya asked.

"**Moonbows**," Biv said. "They're real, but moonlight is so dim they usually look white or gray to your eyes. Cameras can catch the colors though."

Dev tried to run toward the rainbow arching over the yard. His sneakers squelched through the grass — and the rainbow slid sideways, staying just as far away.

"Can't catch it," Biv said. "A rainbow moves whenever you do. You can look, but you can never touch one."

Dev folded his arms. "That's the worst game of tag ever."

"Scientists who study this call it **optics** — the science of how light moves and bends," Biv said. "It's basically a never-ending game of tag. And light always wins."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Old Stories About Rainbows
chapters.text:
"People have told stories about rainbows forever," Biv said, settling onto the porch rail.

"In old Norse tales, a rainbow called **Bifrost** was a bridge to the home of the gods."

"In another old story, a rainbow was a sign of a promise — a gentle reminder that good things follow hard rain," Biv added softly.

Priya tilted her head. "What about the pot of gold?"

"That's an old Irish story," Biv said. "People say a leprechaun hides gold at a rainbow's end. That might be a bit of a stretch, since a rainbow's end moves whenever you do — but it's fun to tell."

Dev grinned. "Guess we'll never dig it up, then."

"Nope," Biv said. "But you two found something better tonight. You figured out how the whole trick works."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Porch
chapters.text:
The glow faded. Biv shrank down to a single sparkle and tucked into the nozzle of Dev's water pistol.

"Give me a squirt whenever the sun's out," Biv's tiny voice said. "I'll be in here, waiting."

Dev looked at his water pistol like it was made of actual magic now. Maybe it was.

Priya picked up her dropped purple crayon. On the back of her dragon drawing, she sketched seven careful stripes: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

Underneath, she wrote: "Our rainbow. Don't touch, Dev."

Dev read it and grinned. "Wasn't gonna."

Upstairs, in pajamas, Dev set the water pistol on his nightstand like a trophy.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Spray well, and dream in every color.

true_facts.text: To see a rainbow, you need the sun **behind** you and rain or spray in **front** of you.
Rainbows need sunshine and water drops at the very same time.
Light goes into a raindrop, **bends**, bounces off the back, and bends again on its way out.
Sunlight looks white, but it's really hiding **every color** inside.
A scientist named **Isaac Newton** used a glass **prism** in **1666** to split sunlight into colors.
The color order in a rainbow goes **red, orange, yellow, green, blue,** and **violet**.
**Red** always sits on the outside of a rainbow, and **violet** sits on the inside.
A rainbow is really a **full circle** — the ground just hides the bottom half.
Sometimes a fainter **second rainbow** shows up, with its colors flipped around.
Every person actually sees their **own** rainbow, made from their own raindrops.
You can never touch a rainbow — it moves away whenever you do.
Some stories say there's a pot of gold at a rainbow's end, but that's just a fun old story — nobody's ever found the real end of one.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Biv the light sprite tucked into Dev's water pistol on the nightstand while Priya drew their very own rainbow on the back of her dragon picture, both kids sure the squirt gun was a little bit magic now.

story.title: Jack and Ellie and the Deep Blue Megatooth
story.subtitle: A bedtime dive through the secrets sharks keep.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glow Under the Flashlight
chapters.text:
Jack sat crisscross on his bed, a flashlight under his chin, making his best shark face. Ellie flopped beside him in her sparkly mermaid-tail blanket, flicking it like a fin.

“Mermaids don’t do that,” Jack said.

“Sharks don’t glow,” Ellie said back.

That was the moment the little tooth around Jack’s neck — a smooth, triangle-shaped tooth he’d found on the beach — started to glow soft blue-green.

Before either of them could say a word, the glow spun into a swirl of light over the carpet, like a whirlpool standing up in the air. It pulled them both in, gently, the way a wave tugs your feet at the beach.

They landed with a soft SPLOOSH inside a giant bubble, floating in open blue water. Something enormous glided past — wider than their school bus, speckled all over with pale spots.

Ellie grabbed Jack’s arm. “Is it going to eat us?”

“Look at its mouth,” Jack said. “It’s barely even open.”

That was the **whale shark**, the biggest fish in the whole ocean, sometimes growing longer than **40 feet**. But instead of chasing them, it drifted by, sipping tiny bits of food called plankton through its huge mouth like a soup strainer.

“It could live past **one hundred years old**,” hummed a small voice — the tooth itself, warm against Jack's chest. “That's older than your great-great-grandma.”

Jack swam closer, carefully, counting the pale spots instead of being scared. Ellie counted along, and by thirty she'd forgotten to be nervous at all.

“See?” Jack said. “Big doesn’t mean scary.”

“Big means GIGANTIC,” Ellie shouted, and the whale shark gave a slow, lazy flick of its tail, as if it agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Shark That Bends
chapters.text:
A grey shark curled around a coral rock like a ribbon, bending nearly in half.

“Sharks don’t have bones like us,” the tooth hummed. “Not hard ones, anyway.”

Jack frowned. “Then how do they not flop around?”

Ellie reached up and gently squeezed her own ear. “It’s bendy, like my ear!”

“Exactly,” said the tooth. “Shark skeletons are made of something called **cartilage** — the same stretchy stuff as the wiggle in Ellie’s ear, not hard bone like in people’s arms and legs. That's why sharks can curl and twist through tight gaps in the reef.”

Jack reached out — slow, careful, never grabbing — and ran one finger along the shark’s side as it passed. “Whoa, it feels like sandpaper!”

“Those are tiny tooth-shaped bumps called **denticles**,” the tooth said. “They let water slide by smoothly, so the shark swims faster with less effort.”

Ellie giggled. “A shark covered in baby teeth!”

“Don’t tell it that,” Jack whispered, and the shark, as if it heard, gave a shimmy and slipped into a crack too narrow for any bony fish to follow.

“See,” Jack told his sister. “Bendy wins.”

“Bendy AND sandpapery,” Ellie corrected, and they both laughed so hard a passing fish startled away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Five Hundred Cousins
chapters.text:
The water ahead was crowded — sharks of every shape drifting past, some long and thin, some flat as pancakes, one no bigger than a hot dog.

“How many KINDS of sharks even are there?” Jack asked, spinning slowly.

“Guess,” said the tooth.

“Fifty?” Ellie tried.

“A hundred?” Jack guessed bigger.

“More than **500 different kinds** of sharks swim in oceans all over the world,” the tooth said. “From that tiny one by your foot to—”

A huge grey shape cut through the crowd, and every smaller shark scattered.

Ellie froze. “Is that one dangerous?”

“That is a **great white shark**,” the tooth said calmly. “It can grow about **20 feet long**, with rows of pointy, saw-edged teeth for catching seals and fish. But it has no interest at all in two kids in a bubble.”

Jack leaned forward instead of back. “Can I see the teeth?”

The great white obliged, mouth opening lazily as it turned, and Jack counted three whole rows before it closed again.

“It isn't even chasing anything,” he said. “It's just cruising.”

Ellie let out a breath. “Okay. Cruising is fine.”

“Five hundred kinds,” Jack said, grinning, “and we just met the most famous one.”

“Famous AND cruising,” Ellie said, and the tooth gave a little warm pulse, like a laugh.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Ellie Finds a Mermaid’s Purse
chapters.text:
Something small and dark, shaped like a little pillow with curly strings on each corner, drifted past Ellie’s nose.

“A purse!” she said, snatching it gently from the water. “A tiny mermaid purse!”

“That’s not—” Jack started, then stopped, because actually, it sort of was.

“Some baby sharks hatch out of cases exactly like that,” the tooth said. “People really do call them **mermaid’s purses**. Other baby sharks don’t hatch from a case at all — they're born live, swimming right out into the water.”

Ellie held hers up to the light, careful not to squeeze it. “Is there a shark baby still inside?”

“Not this one,” the tooth said. “It already hatched and swam off, strong enough to look after itself.”

Jack, meanwhile, had spotted something small and white caught in the sand — a single curved tooth.

“Sharks lose teeth all the time,” he said, remembering. “And new ones just grow in?”

“Thousands, over a shark's whole life,” the tooth said. “Old teeth fall out, new ones slide forward to take their place, like a conveyor belt that never stops.”

“I wish my teeth did that,” Jack said, wiggling a loose one of his own.

“You'll just have to wait for the tooth fairy,” Ellie said sweetly, tucking her purse into her blanket pocket, “like a regular kid.”

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Biggest Shark There Ever Was
chapters.text:
The tooth around Jack’s neck began to glow brighter than before, pulsing like it wanted to tell them something.

“Sharks first swam in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**,” it said. “Before dinosaurs. Before trees. Before almost anything.”

“Before YOU?” Ellie asked, poking Jack.

“Before everyone,” the tooth said, and the water shimmered, pulling them into a swirl of silver light.

When it cleared, the ocean looked the same, but the shark gliding below did not. It was longer than a school bus, with a mouth that could have swallowed a car.

“That,” the tooth said, “is **megalodon**. One of the biggest sharks that ever lived.”

Jack’s mouth fell open. “Is it going to—”

“It's not really here,” the tooth said gently. “This is just a memory. Megalodon isn't around anymore — it disappeared a very long time ago, millions of years before people ever existed.”

Ellie relaxed. “So it's like a ghost shark?”

“More like an old photograph,” the tooth said. “And this tooth you're wearing, Jack? It's one of megalodon's actual teeth, kept safe in the ground for millions of years. Soft bendy parts like cartilage almost never last that long, but hard teeth do — so teeth as long as your hand are almost all scientists have ever found of megalodon.”

Jack held the tooth up proudly. “So I've basically got one of the oldest teeth in the world.”

“A very polite one,” said Ellie, “that doesn't bite.”

The megalodon's shape faded like smoke, and the silver light swept them onward.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Shark That Walks
chapters.text:
They landed in shallow water over a coral reef, and something small and spotted was... walking. Actually walking, using its fins like little paddles, across the sand between rock pools.

“Wait,” Jack said, leaning so close his nose nearly touched the bubble wall. “Is that shark WALKING?”

“That's an **epaulette shark**,” the tooth said. “It uses its fins like paddles to walk across reefs and shallow pools. It can even survive for hours with very little air to breathe, in a tide pool that would make most fish give up.”

“IT WALKS!” Jack yelled, loud enough that Ellie clapped both hands over her ears, grinning anyway.

Nearby, another shark lay completely still on the sandy bottom, not moving a single fin.

“Is that one okay?” Ellie asked, suddenly worried.

“Perfectly,” the tooth said. “That's a **nurse shark**. Most sharks have to keep swimming to breathe, but a nurse shark can pump water over its gills while it rests, so it gets to just lie there.”

“Like a nap?” Ellie said.

“Exactly like a nap.”

Jack nudged his sister. “You'd make a great nurse shark.”

“You'd make a terrible one,” Ellie shot back. “You never stop moving.”

The walking shark paddled right past them, unbothered, off toward its own tide pool, and Jack laughed so hard he nearly let go of the bubble's edge.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Super Senses
chapters.text:
A shark with a head shaped like the end of a hammer swung slowly side to side, scanning the sand.

“Its head is called a **cephalofoil**,” the tooth said. “It's wide and flat, and it spreads the shark's eyes far apart, almost like wearing glasses on each side of its head. That gives it an almost all-around view to spot hidden fish.”

“How does it find fish buried IN the sand, though?” Jack asked. “It can't see through sand.”

“Good question,” the tooth said. “Sharks have tiny jelly-filled holes on their snouts that feel the tiny electric signals every living thing makes, even through sand. You can just think of them as a shark's secret sense for finding hidden things.”

Ellie gasped. “Like a metal detector, but for fish!”

“Exactly like that.”

A streak of silver shot past them so fast it left a trail of bubbles — there, then gone.

“Whoa! What was THAT?” Jack said.

“A **shortfin mako**,” said the tooth. “The fastest shark in the ocean, built for quick bursts of speed to catch fast fish like tuna.”

“Race you to that rock,” Jack told Ellie, kicking off.

“You're not a mako, Jack,” Ellie called, paddling after him anyway, mermaid tail blanket and all, and for one glorious second, neither of them noticed they were losing badly to a fish.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A woman in an old-fashioned diving mask floated nearby, utterly calm, scribbling notes on a slate while a shark circled her politely, as if waiting its turn.

“That's **Eugenie Clark**,” the tooth said. “People called her the ‘Shark Lady.’ She spent years studying how sharks behave, and she showed something important — sharks are curious, and they can even learn tricks, like a very large, very toothy dog.”

Ellie tilted her head. “Aren't people scared of sharks, though?”

“Lots of people used to be,” the tooth said. “But a shark biting a person is actually very rare. Far more sharks get hurt by people than the other way around.”

Jack watched the shark nudge Dr. Clark's slate, gentle as a cat asking for breakfast. “She's not scared of it at all.”

“She knew sharks sit at the top of the ocean's whole food chain,” the tooth said. “They help keep everything else balanced and healthy, which means a healthy ocean actually needs them.”

“So they're not monsters,” Ellie said. “They're just important.”

“Important,” the tooth agreed, “and worth looking after.”

Dr. Clark looked up, smiled at them both as if she'd known they were there all along, and gave a small wave before the water shimmered, folding softly back into silver light.

“I like her,” Ellie said.

“Me too,” said Jack. “Best job in the whole ocean.”

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The silver light folded around them once more, and then — SPLOOSH, not into water this time but into blankets — they tumbled back onto Jack's bedroom carpet.

The tooth around Jack's neck had gone quiet and dark again, just an ordinary little tooth.

Except Ellie's blanket pocket wasn't empty. She reached in and pulled out the small leathery mermaid's purse, still a little damp.

“It came WITH us,” she whispered.

Jack grinned, clicking his flashlight back under his chin. “Guess the ocean wanted you to keep a souvenir.”

“Better than a seashell,” Ellie said, setting it carefully on her nightstand, right next to her mermaid dolls.

“Five hundred kinds of sharks,” Jack murmured, flopping back onto his pillow, “and we only met, what, eight?”

“Nine, if you count the Shark Lady,” Ellie said through a yawn.

“She doesn't count. She's not a shark.”

“She's basically a shark,” Ellie mumbled, eyes already closing. “She just swims with legs.”

Jack laughed quietly and set the tooth on his own nightstand, where it gave one last, tiny glow, like it was saying goodnight too.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.

true_facts.text: The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the ocean, sometimes longer than **40 feet**, but it mostly eats tiny bits of food called plankton.
Some whale sharks can live past **one hundred years old**.
A shark's skeleton is made of **cartilage**, bendy stuff like the stretchy part of your ear, not hard bone.
More than **500 different kinds** of sharks swim in oceans around the world.
The **great white shark** can grow about **20 feet long** and has rows of pointy, saw-edged teeth.
Some baby sharks hatch from leathery cases nicknamed **mermaid's purses**, while others are born live.
Sharks lose and regrow **thousands of teeth** over their whole life, new ones always sliding forward.
Sharks have been swimming in the ocean for more than **400 million years**, since before dinosaurs.
**Megalodon** was one of the biggest sharks that ever lived, but it isn't around anymore.
Because soft cartilage doesn't last underground, **teeth as long as a hand** are almost all scientists have found of megalodon.
The **epaulette shark** can walk across reefs using its fins and survive for hours on very little air.
A **hammerhead shark's** wide, flat head spreads its eyes apart for an almost all-around view.
**Eugenie Clark**, nicknamed the Shark Lady, studied sharks for years and showed they are curious and can learn tricks.
A shark biting a person is actually very rare, and far more sharks are hurt by people than the other way around.

story.title: Nora and the Wandering Tessera
story.subtitle: A night trip to Pompeii, tile by tile

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Tile
chapters.text:
Nora knelt on her bedroom floor, tiny glass squares spread out around her knees. She was gluing them onto cardboard, one by one, building a blue wave for her mosaic project. It was way past bedtime, but she couldn't stop. The hallway light was off. Her lamp was the only glow left in the house.

Then one tile would not sit still. It buzzed, warm, right under her thumb. It glowed gold, brighter than her lamp, brighter than anything on the floor.

"That's new," Nora whispered.

The tile hummed louder. A tiny voice popped out of it, squeaky and bright. "Hello! I'm Tessie. I'm a **tessera** — that's just a fancy word for a tiny tile, like the ones in your hands."

Nora blinked. "Tiles don't talk."

"This one does," said Tessie. "Want to see where tiles like me come from? Hold tight."

Gold light filled the room. **WHOOSH!** The floor dropped away.

When the light cleared, Nora stood on a sunny stone street. Carts rattled past. Someone shouted about fresh fish. The air smelled like warm bread and salty sea.

"Welcome," said Tessie, "to **Pompeii** — a busy Roman town, near where the Italian city of **Naples** stands today."

Nora looked down. Rows of flat stones poked up out of the street, like stepping-stones across a puddle, except there was no puddle at all.

"Why are there rocks in the middle of the road?" Nora asked.

"Guess," said Tessie.

Nora thought hard. "So people don't get their feet wet? And carts can still roll right between them?"

"Exactly right," said Tessie. "This town once had about **eleven to fifteen thousand people**, and the streets got messy. These stones kept feet dry while cart wheels rolled through the gaps."

Nora grinned and hopped from stone to stone like a game. "I love this town already."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Painted Walls and a Name
chapters.text:
They turned a corner into a square full of noise. Painted words covered every wall, red letters on white, some new, some half-washed by rain.

"What's all that writing?" Nora asked, pointing.

"Ask it," said Tessie.

Nora walked closer. One sign showed a loaf of bread. Another had big block letters, bold as a shout.

"Is that... an ad?" Nora guessed. "Like a sign for a bakery?"

"Spot on," said Tessie. "People painted messages right onto their walls — ads for shops, and even votes for town leaders. It was Pompeii's version of a billboard."

Nora laughed. "Walls were like phones."

"Kind of," said Tessie. "Come see the water."

They stopped at a stone fountain shaped like a lion's face. Water trickled from its mouth into a stone trough.

"This town had pipes running everywhere," said Tessie, "bringing water to fountains like this one, all over town."

Nora cupped her hands under the cool water. "Fancy."

"Speaking of fancy," said Tessie, "do you know what the name **Pompeii** might mean?"

Nora shook her head.

"Some people think it comes from an old word, **pompe**, meaning **five**. Maybe because five little villages joined together to make one big town."

Nora held up five fingers. "Five friends, one town."

"That's the idea," said Tessie, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Roar of the Amphitheater
chapters.text:
A roar rolled across the rooftops. Nora jumped. "What was that?!"

"Follow it," said Tessie.

They ran toward a huge round building made of stone, bigger than Nora's whole school. Thousands of people sat on its curved benches, cheering, stamping their feet.

"This is the **amphitheater**," said Tessie — "a giant round stone theater, built for watching big shows."

"What kind of shows?" Nora asked.

"Gladiator games," said Tessie. "**Gladiators** were fighters who trained hard and performed for the crowd, right down there on the floor."

Nora peered over the edge at the oval ground below. "It's like a giant stadium."

"It is," said Tessie. "And a very old one, too. Built around **70 BC** — one of the oldest amphitheaters anyone has ever found."

The crowd roared again, louder this time. Nora covered her ears, then grinned and dropped her hands.

"ROAR!" she shouted along with them, cupping her hands like a megaphone.

"ROAR!" Tessie's little voice echoed back, and they both laughed so hard Nora nearly slipped off the stone step.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Mountain Across the Bay
chapters.text:
Tessie tugged Nora toward the edge of town, where the ground began to rumble, soft and low.

"Did you feel that?" Nora asked.

"This town felt plenty of rumbles," said Tessie. "It sits right next to a **volcano** — a mountain that can burst open with hot melted rock and ash."

Nora looked up. Past the rooftops stood a tall green mountain. "That's a volcano? It looks so calm."

"For now," said Tessie. "A young writer named **Pliny the Younger** once stood across the bay and watched that very mountain, **Mount Vesuvius**, turn wild. He wrote two long letters describing everything he saw — so carefully that scientists today still call this kind of big, sudden volcano burst a '**Plinian eruption**,' after him."

"He was like a reporter," said Nora.

"Exactly like one," said Tessie. "Want to hear what he saw?"

Nora nodded, a little nervous.

"Don't worry," said Tessie gently. "It happened a long, long time ago, and plenty of people got away safely. I'll tell it slow."

Nora took Tessie's glowing edge in her hand. "Okay. I'm ready."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Gray Snow
chapters.text:
On one bright morning, **August 24, in the year 79**, the mountain cracked open. A tall gray cloud shot into the sky, shaped like an umbrella pine tree.

Nora watched from a safe hilltop with Tessie glowing beside her. "Is everyone okay?"

"Many people saw the cloud early and hurried away to safety," said Tessie. "One brave sailor named **Pliny the Elder** even steered his ships toward the mountain to help people escape."

Ash began to fall like gray snow, soft and silent, settling onto rooftops, carts, and streets.

"It kept falling," said Tessie, "for hours and hours, until it was as deep as **twenty feet** in some places — taller than two grown-up giraffes stacked on top of each other."

Nora gasped. "The whole town got a blanket."

"A very thick one," said Tessie. "And that blanket is exactly why we can visit this town today."

Nora tilted her head. "Because it protected everything?"

"Precisely," said Tessie. "Keep that thought. It gets good."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Baker's Bread
chapters.text:
The gold light shimmered, and suddenly they stood in a quiet house, sunlight slanting through a gap in a stone wall.

"Where are we now?" Nora whispered.

"Many years later," said Tessie, "after people dug the ash away and found this town again."

Nora peeked into a little room. A loaf of bread sat inside a stone oven, round and cracked on top, exactly how it was left.

"That bread is really old?" Nora asked.

"Almost **two thousand years old**," said Tessie. "The ash fell so fast, it froze everything in place — even this baker's bread, still marked with lines from his knife."

Nora turned to the wall. Bright painted pictures covered it: people dancing, a goat, swirling patterns in red and gold.

"Those paintings," Nora breathed. "They're almost like a mosaic of colors, like mine!"

"They're called **frescoes**," said Tessie — "paintings made right onto wet wall plaster. Some of the fanciest ones are in a house called the **Villa of the Mysteries**, full of pictures nobody has fully explained."

Nora traced a swirl with her finger, careful not to touch. "A mystery painting, in a mystery town."

"You could say that," said Tessie, glowing a little brighter.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Volcano Hugs
chapters.text:
They hopped again, this time landing near the sea, where waves lapped at dark sand.

"Smell that?" asked Tessie. "Salt and pine. We're in **Herculaneum** now — a smaller town by the water, buried by that very same eruption."

Nora looked around at wooden beams still holding up a balcony. "Wait, wood? I thought everything turns to dust."

"Good catch," said Tessie. "Herculaneum got covered by a different kind of hot volcanic mud, not ash like Pompeii. That mud sealed everything up so tightly, it even kept wooden furniture and paper **scrolls** — those are just old rolled-up books — safe for centuries."

Nora touched a wooden shutter, soft with age but still standing straight. "So Pompeii and Herculaneum are like twins with different coats."

"Exactly," said Tessie. "One got a snowy blanket of ash. The other got a warm, sealed hug of mud."

Nora giggled. "Volcano hugs."

"Only this kind," said Tessie. "Never the touching kind. Just the learning kind."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Blue Wave
chapters.text:
One more **WHOOSH**, and they stood on a grassy hill above two half-dug towns, ropes and little signs marking careful paths.

"This is now," said Tessie. "Well — a now from not too long ago."

"People found this place again?" Nora asked.

"In **1748**," said Tessie, "workers digging in the dirt hit old walls and statues, and everyone remembered Pompeii was real."

Nora looked at tiny brushes and buckets near a roped-off house. "Are they still digging?"

"Only about **two-thirds** of the town has been uncovered so far," said Tessie. "The rest is still waiting under the ground."

"Like a present nobody's opened yet," Nora said.

"These days," Tessie added, "**millions of visitors** come every single year to walk these same streets you just ran across."

Nora smiled. "I was here first, though."

"You certainly were," Tessie laughed.

The gold light spun around them both, and the hill, the ropes, and the buckets melted away. **WHOOSH!** Nora landed back on her own bedroom floor, tiles scattered around her knees.

The little tile in her hand had gone cool and quiet, just an ordinary glass square now.

Nora pressed it onto her cardboard, right in the middle of her blue wave. It fit perfectly, like it had always belonged there. **CLICK.**

"IT FITS!" Nora whispered, grinning at her own knees.

She pulled her blanket up to her chin, the last bit of lamplight catching on the glass tiles.

Somewhere, tiny and golden, a small voice yawned. "Not bad for one night, tile-finder."

Nora smiled into her pillow. "Not bad at all, Tessie."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tiny piece tells a story.
