story.title: Isla and the Buried City of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A mystery that was buried under ash for almost seventeen hundred years.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Lens and the Street of Five
chapters.text:
Isla was supposed to be asleep forty minutes ago.

Instead she was cross-legged on her bedroom floor, going through a shoebox of broken things her grandmother had left her. Grandma had been an archaeologist, which Isla had decided was the best job that existed. Digging up clues nobody else had noticed? Pure mystery, just with more dust.

At the bottom of the box was a cracked brass magnifying lens and a jagged piece of reddish pottery, a souvenir Isla had begged for on a museum trip. She held the lens up to the pottery, the way Grandma used to, squinting at the little ridges where a potter's fingers had once pressed the clay.

The crack in the lens caught her lamp light and turned green.

Isla froze. The green deepened, humming faintly, like a held breath. Then the floor dropped away with a sound like **WHOOOSH**, and Isla was standing on a stone street under a sky far too bright for midnight.

A cart rattled past and nearly took her toes with it. She jumped back onto a row of raised stones poking up out of the road like stepping stones across a river, except there was no river, just dusty street on either side.

"Careful," said a voice. "People have been losing toes to those carts for eighteen centuries."

A young man in a toga stood nearby, a wax tablet tucked under one arm, watching her with open curiosity. "I am Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus," he said, then seemed to think better of it. "Call me Pliny. The younger one. There are two of us. It gets confusing."

Isla looked down at the stones under her feet, then at the gap between them, just wide enough for a cart wheel to pass through. "These aren't just decoration," she said slowly. "They're for crossing the street without stepping in the mud. And the gaps let the carts through anyway."

Pliny looked almost offended that she'd figured it out so fast. "Stepping stones, exactly. Pompeii's streets get filthy with rainwater and worse. Nobody wants wet sandals."

Behind him, the street opened into a town humming with noise: shopkeepers calling out prices, a fountain splashing somewhere, the smell of warm bread drifting from an open doorway. Isla turned in a slow circle, taking it in. "How big is this place?"

"Somewhere between eleven and fifteen thousand people," Pliny said. "Shops, bathhouses, theaters, temples. Not bad for a town most people have never heard of." He paused. "Yet."

"Yet," Isla repeated, narrowing her eyes. That word was doing a lot of work.

She noticed a sign painted on a nearby wall, red letters over whitewash. "Is that... an advertisement?"

"And a bit of politics," said Pliny. "People here paint slogans and ads right onto their walls. It's rather effective, actually."

Isla grinned. Ancient graffiti. This was already her favorite field trip.

"One more thing," she said, pointing at a stone marker carved with the town's name. "Pompeii. Where does that even come from?"

"Most historians think it's from an old local word, *pompe*," Pliny said. "It meant 'five.' Maybe five villages joined together here, long before any of this was built."

Isla filed that away the way she filed every good clue: carefully, and for later.

"Mind the gap," she muttered, stepping over the stones after him, into the noise of a town that had no idea what was coming.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Fountains, Fighters, and Cracks in the Wall
chapters.text:
The fountain on the corner was doing something Isla had definitely not expected from the year 79.

It was running. Actually running, water trickling steadily out of a stone spout into a trough, with two women filling jugs and gossiping like it was any ordinary Tuesday.

"There's plumbing," Isla said, half to herself. "There's actual plumbing."

"Lead pipes," Pliny confirmed, tapping the stone with his tablet stylus. "They run under most of the streets, carrying water to fountains all over town. Some houses even have their own private supply."

Isla crouched by the trough, tracing the pipe's path with one finger before it vanished under the cobbles. A town with running water two thousand years before she'd be born. She filed that one away too, right next to the stepping stones.

They turned a corner into a wide open space shaped like a bowl, stone seats rising in tiers around a sandy oval floor. Isla's mouth fell open.

"An amphitheater," Pliny said, before she could ask. "Built around 70 BC. One of the oldest of its kind anywhere. Gladiators fight here, crowds roar, somebody always loses their voice cheering."

"How many people fit in there?"

Pliny shrugged. "Enough to make the whole town shake when they cheer at once."

Isla walked along the outer wall, running her hand over the stone, and stopped. A jagged crack ran from top to bottom, patched over with newer, paler stone, like a scar that had been stitched shut.

"This has been broken before," she said.

Pliny's easy smile faded, just slightly. "Good eye. Seventeen years ago, in the year 62, a serious earthquake shook this whole town. Walls cracked, roofs fell in. People have been repairing it ever since." He gestured at scaffolding further down the street, workers still patching a temple wall.

"So the ground here just... shakes sometimes?" Isla asked.

"The ground here," Pliny said carefully, "has reasons to shake."

Isla turned to follow his gaze. Past the rooftops, past the painted walls and their loud red slogans, a mountain rose green and peaceful against the sky, its slopes covered in vineyards.

"That's just a mountain," she said.

"That," said Pliny, "is Vesuvius."

He said the name the way you'd mention a neighbor who was usually quiet but occasionally, memorably, was not. Isla looked at the mountain for a long moment, at the vines growing peacefully up its sides, and felt the first small prickle of a mystery she couldn't yet name.

"It looks fine," she said.

"It generally does," Pliny agreed. "Right up until it doesn't."

Isla decided she did not love that answer, and said so. Pliny only smiled and led her on, past the painted ads, past the gladiators' practice yard, toward the smell of baking bread drifting from a side street — and toward a day that, Isla was starting to realize, Pliny already knew the ending to.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Mountain Wakes
chapters.text:
The ground moved first.

It was small, almost nothing, a tremble Isla felt through the soles of her sandals more than heard. Then a crack, impossibly loud, rolled down from the mountain like thunder with somewhere urgent to be.

"Here," Pliny said, and the green light of the lens folded around them both before Isla could ask where. When it faded, they were standing on a hillside well back from the town, the bay spread out silver below them.

"Are we safe?" Isla asked.

"We're safe," Pliny said. "We're only watching."

Above the mountain, a column of ash and smoke was climbing into the sky, thick and dark, higher than any cloud Isla had ever seen. It was the twenty-fourth of August, in the year 79, and Mount Vesuvius had finally stopped being quiet.

"It's enormous," Isla breathed.

"It's going to get bigger," Pliny said, not unkindly. "Pumice — that's light, bubbly rock, full of trapped air — is going to fall like hail for hours. By the time it's finished, the town down there will be buried under four to six meters of ash and rock. Taller than your house."

Isla stared at the gray column, trying to picture an entire town disappearing under that much ash, and found she couldn't, not really. It was too big a number for her brain to hold all at once.

"What happens to everyone?" she asked quietly.

"Many people got out in time," Pliny said. "Not everyone. It's a true story, Isla, and true stories aren't always gentle ones." He let that sit for a moment, then added, more softly, "But it's also why we're standing here. Nothing this well preserved happens by accident."

Isla nodded slowly, watching the ash drift sideways on the wind, dusting rooftops she could just make out in the distance. It didn't feel like an ending. It felt, strangely, like the start of a much longer story — one that would take almost seventeen hundred years to finish being told.

"Preserved how?" she asked, because that word had caught in her ear like a fishhook.

Pliny's mouth twitched, the closest thing to a smile he'd managed since the ground first shook. "That," he said, "is the best part. Come on. There's someone I think you should meet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Two Letters Across the Bay
chapters.text:
They landed in a garden across the bay, in a house that smelled of ink and old paper.

A man sat hunched over a writing desk, quill scratching fast, ash dusting his shoulders like gray snow even here, miles from the mountain. Pliny straightened up a little. "My uncle," he said. "Pliny the Elder. Different Pliny. Also confusing."

The older man didn't even look up. "A cloud shaped like nothing I've ever seen," he muttered, writing fast. "I must go closer."

"He commands ships," young Pliny explained to Isla. "When the mountain erupted, he didn't sail away from it. He sailed toward it, to rescue people trapped along the coast."

Isla blinked. "That's either the bravest or the most reckless thing I've ever heard."

"Both," said Pliny, with the air of someone who had had this exact argument before. "He stayed to help as long as he could."

Isla watched the older man finish a line, dip his quill again, and write on, steady as the pipes carrying water under Pompeii's streets. "And you? What do you do?"

"I stay here and write down everything I see," Pliny said. "Two long letters, later, to a historian who asked what happened. I describe the cloud, the ash, the sea pulling strangely back from the shore. Careful notes. Nothing exaggerated."

"Why does that matter so much?" Isla asked. "It's just letters."

"Because almost two thousand years from now," Pliny said, "scientists who study volcanoes will read my letters and still use them. When a volcano erupts this violently, throwing ash this high into the sky, they'll call it a *Plinian eruption*. Named for the letters. Named, really, for just... paying close attention."

Isla turned that over slowly. A kid's homework-sounding word, named after someone who'd simply written down what he'd watched, carefully, without panicking. That felt like the most useful kind of bravery there was — the kind you could actually practice.

"So the letters are evidence," she said. "Like a witness statement."

"The very first one anyone kept," Pliny said, and for the first time since she'd met him, he looked faintly proud. "Everything we'll ever know about that day starts with two letters and a nephew who couldn't stop writing."

Isla looked back at his uncle, bent over his own work, sailing toward danger instead of away from it, and decided that this family, whatever else was true about them, did not do things by halves.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Frozen in Time
chapters.text:
The green light set them down somewhere that should not have existed anymore.

Ash had hardened into solid ground, and when Pliny brushed dust from a doorway, Isla saw a house standing almost exactly as it had the day the mountain erupted. Paint on the walls. A floor. A loaf of bread sitting inside a clay oven, as if the baker had only just stepped out.

"Is that—" Isla started.

"Real bread,” Pliny said. "Baked that morning. The ash came down so fast and so thick it sealed everything in place almost instantly. It's a bit like pressing a leaf into wet concrete. Whatever was happening at that exact moment just... stayed."

Isla crouched by the oven, careful not to touch, and noticed something pressed into the crust: a small, deliberate mark, almost like a signature.

"That's the baker's stamp," she said slowly. "He marked his own bread. Like putting your name on your homework."

"Clever," Pliny said. "You're the first visitor who's spotted that in a while."

On the wall nearby, faded but unmistakable, someone had scratched a quick message into the plaster — not official, not important, just a thought someone had once had and scrawled down without thinking twice.

"People really did write on everything," Isla said.

"People have always written on everything," Pliny said. "You should see the inside of a schoolroom bench, two thousand years from now."

Isla snorted, then sobered, looking around the frozen room. A painted wall, still bright red in places. A loaf of bread, never eaten. A joke, scratched by someone who never knew it would outlive them by seventeen centuries.

"It's sad," she said. "But it's also... it's like a time capsule nobody meant to bury."

"That's exactly it," Pliny said. "Disasters are terrible things to live through. But this one happened to leave behind the most detailed snapshot of daily life anyone has ever found. Nobody tidied up first. Nobody hid anything. You're looking at an ordinary Tuesday, perfectly preserved."

Isla reached toward the loaf, then stopped herself, hand hovering an inch above the crust. Some mysteries, she was starting to understand, you solved just by looking carefully — and by leaving things exactly where you found them.

"Who gets to find all this?" she asked. "Eventually, I mean."

Pliny's green light was already rising around them, patient as ever. "Patience," he said. "That part takes almost seventeen hundred years."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Diggers of 1748
chapters.text:
The light faded on a hillside full of shovels.

Men in old-fashioned clothes were digging into a slope thick with weeds, sweat on their faces, a cart half-loaded with broken stone nearby. It was, Pliny explained, the year 1748 — and nobody on that hillside had any idea what they were about to find.

"Pompeii's been forgotten for a long time," he said. "Buried, grown over, mostly lost to memory. These workers think they're just digging a foundation."

One of the diggers shouted something and waved the others over. A wall had appeared, straight-edged, clearly built by human hands, clearly not natural rock.

Isla's archaeologist instincts, inherited straight from a shoebox of broken things, kicked in instantly. "That's not just a wall," she said, moving closer. "Look at the corner, it's too neat. There's a whole building under there."

"Exactly what they're about to realize," Pliny said.

She watched one of the workers hack carelessly at a half-buried statue with a pickaxe, chipping off a piece of a nose. Isla winced.

"They're being so rough with it!"

"Early days," Pliny admitted. "People didn't yet understand how to dig carefully, how much could be lost by rushing. It takes time for a whole new kind of careful digging to be invented — the kind where you record exactly where everything was found, instead of just pulling treasures out."

"That's basically what archaeology even is," Isla said. "Not just digging stuff up. Digging stuff up *properly*."

"Took people a while to learn that," Pliny said. "But they did. Slower, more careful digging eventually replaces all this." He nodded at the hillside. "This is where it starts, though. The exact moment Pompeii stops being a forgotten hill and starts being a mystery worth solving."

Isla watched the diggers uncover more wall, more fragments, shouting excitedly to one another in a language she didn't understand but whose meaning was obvious: *we found something*.

"I'd have told them to slow down," she said.

"I believe you," said Pliny. "Good thing people eventually did. There's still a great deal left under that hill, you know. Even now."

Isla turned to him sharply. "Even now? You mean someone hasn't found everything yet?"

Pliny's green light was already curling around them both, like it had somewhere else in mind. "Patience," he said again. "I keep telling you. This part takes a while too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Villa of Mysteries
chapters.text:
The hillside was gone. In its place stood a city of stone, swept clean, sunlight pouring down on walls painted so brightly Isla had to blink.

"This is now," Pliny said. "Or close enough to it."

Tourists wandered the streets with cameras, guides pointing out frescoes — wall paintings — in colors that had somehow survived underground for almost two thousand years. Isla turned in a slow circle, same as she had in Chapter One, except this time half the town was missing walls and roofs, open to the sky, carefully numbered and labeled.

"Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has actually been dug up," Pliny said. "The rest is still under there. New paintings get uncovered every so often. New mysteries, really."

"A third of the whole town," Isla repeated, delighted. "Still buried. Still waiting."

They stopped in front of a building with the grandest paintings Isla had seen yet: tall painted figures, mysterious ceremonies, a story clearly being told across the walls that nobody today could fully read.

"The Villa of Mysteries," Pliny said.

"Of course it is," Isla said happily. This was, without question, the best-named building she had ever stood in front of.

"Nobody's entirely sure what the ceremony shown here actually was," Pliny admitted. "Experts have theories. Nobody's proven any of them completely."

Isla studied the painted figures for a long moment, a girl being led forward, something being revealed to her that the viewer couldn't quite see. "Maybe it's not supposed to be fully solved," she said slowly. "Maybe that's the point. It's a two-thousand-year-old cliffhanger."

Pliny looked at her like she'd said something worth writing down. "I like that answer better than most of the official ones."

They walked on, past a sign mentioning a neighboring seaside town called Herculaneum, buried the same day by the same mountain, but by a different kind of volcanic material — one that had, strangely, preserved even wooden furniture and old scrolls, things Pompeii's ash hadn't managed to keep.

"Two towns," Isla said. "Buried the same day. Preserved completely differently."

"Even disasters have their own fingerprints," Pliny said.

Isla looked back at the Villa of Mysteries one more time, at a painting nobody could fully explain, in a town that was still only two-thirds uncovered, and decided that some mysteries were worth leaving exactly where you found them — for now.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Mountain Now
chapters.text:
Vesuvius looked exactly the same as it had the first time Isla saw it — green, quiet, almost friendly — except this time there were antennas bolted to its slopes and a small building near the summit with a satellite dish on the roof.

"It's still active," Pliny said, following her gaze. "The same mountain. It could erupt again someday — nobody can say exactly when. Millions of people live close by now, so scientists keep watch on it constantly, checking for tiny tremors and small changes in the ground."

"Like a very patient stakeout," Isla said.

"Precisely like that," Pliny agreed. "Down there, meanwhile, Pompeii gets millions of visitors every single year. It's officially recognized now as one of the most important historical sites on the planet, somewhere worth protecting for everyone, forever."

Isla looked down at the whole excavated town spread below them, sunlit and swept clean, tourists moving along streets she'd once watched carts rattle through, past stepping stones she'd nearly lost a toe to, past a bakery whose bread she'd almost touched.

"It's strange," she said. "A disaster turned into the best clue anyone's ever found."

"That's rather the whole mystery of it," Pliny said. "The worst day imaginable, and also the reason we know so much about ordinary days that came before it. Both things are true at once."

The green light was rising again, warmer now, almost gentle.

"Will I come back?" Isla asked quickly, before it closed around her completely.

Pliny's smile was the same dry, almost-proud one he'd worn since Chapter One. "There's still a third of that town buried," he said. "Seems a shame to leave a mystery unfinished."

Then the green folded in, and the floor of Isla's bedroom rushed back up to meet her.

She was sitting exactly where she'd started, shoebox open beside her, lamp still humming warm and yellow. The magnifying lens lay in her palm, crack gone quiet, no longer glowing.

But the little reddish shard beside it had changed. Pressed faintly into one edge, where there had been nothing before, was a tiny mark — almost like a signature.

Isla turned it over carefully in the lamplight, already reaching for the notebook on her shelf. Tomorrow, she had a mystery to write down.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a mystery to write down.

true_facts.text: On **August 24, in the year 79**, the volcano **Mount Vesuvius** erupted and buried the town.
The eruption buried the whole town under **4 to 6 meters** of ash and rock — taller than a house.

A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched from across the bay and wrote two detailed letters about it — which is why scientists still call this kind of violent eruption a **"Plinian eruption."**
The ash fell so fast it froze everyday moments in place, like a **loaf of bread** still sitting inside its oven.
Paintings on walls and quick scribbled messages survived almost perfectly, frozen the moment the eruption began.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten until it was **rediscovered in 1748**, when workers digging nearby found ancient walls.
A nearby town called **Herculaneum** was buried the same day by a different kind of volcanic material, which preserved even wooden furniture and old scrolls.
Pompeii's streets had raised **stepping stones**, so people could cross without mud — with gaps left just wide enough for cart wheels.
Pompeii had an advanced water system, with lead pipes carrying water to fountains all through town.
The town's amphitheater, used for gladiator games, was built around **70 BC** — one of the oldest of its kind.
Even now, only about **two-thirds of Pompeii** has been dug up — the rest is still buried, with new discoveries still turning up.
Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano today, and scientists keep careful watch on it since millions of people live nearby.

new_recurring.name: The Finder's Lens
new_recurring.rule: A cracked brass magnifying lens, inherited from Isla's archaeologist grandmother. When held up to a genuinely old object, the crack glows green and pulls Isla into that object's true history. It can also move her safely between moments…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Isla returned to her bedroom to find a tiny signature-like mark newly pressed into her museum pottery shard, and reached for her notebook to start writing down the mystery.

request.care_notes: Focus on the archaeology, the preserved objects that tell us about daily Roman life, and how volcanologists study Vesuvius today. The story should not describe people dying or suffering in detail; treat the eruption as a historical event that created a time capsule for us to learn from.

editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Separate Stegosaurus and Triceratops, or have Bit flag that they lived about 80 million years apart, which fits Level 8's 'misfile' theme. Move the Maiasaura nest out of the Gobi or drop the mismatch. Cut Owen's invented 'eighteen different random names'. Keep the raptor turkey-sized throughout. Let Bit correct Theo's 'scales' on the pterosaur.

Break the repeated chapter-ending formula and the narrator's tic. Give each level a different way of earning its coin, and cut most of the 'because that's how his brain worked' variants. Also fix the barefoot/shoelace/sneaker contradiction, perhaps by having Theo use his pajama drawstring or a strip of fern for the marker.

Honour the bible by having Bit's pixels go watery at the trophy moment. Replace the 'fact pile ... checkmark' sentence with an in-world line about legends. Tighten the final screen message and the closing sentence, since 'whole still-flying world' is slightly awkward.

story.title: Theo and the Dinosaur Save File
story.subtitle: Player One loads up 230 million years of real history.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Triassic Spawn Point (230 Million Years Ago)
chapters.text:
Theo was lying on his bedroom floor, laptop propped against a pillow, headset slipping down over one ear. In Roblox Studio he had just dragged a lava texture onto a cliff for his newest build, a dinosaur survival map. It had been two weeks since his last game had flashed THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD across the screen, and Theo had taken that personally. He'd built a volcano level. He'd built a soccer field level, because why not. Tonight he was building dinosaurs, and he had no idea what they actually looked like.

The cursor froze. The screen flickered green, pixels climbing up from the corners like static learning to walk.

**BZZZT.**

A small green sprite blinked onto the taskbar, eight blocky squares tall, grinning like he'd been waiting all week.

"Player One," said Bit. "You searched *Tyrannosaurus* at eleven p.m. and spelled it right the first try. I had to say hi."

"Bit?" Theo sat up so fast his headset fell off. "I thought the game was done."

"A game's never done," said Bit. "It just loads a new level. And this one's got teeth. Grab your coin bag — you're about to meet something older than your volcano, older than your school, older than *dirt.*"

The laptop screen stopped being a laptop screen. It turned into a doorway, green light pouring onto the carpet like the inside of an old arcade machine. Theo — barefoot, still in his pajama shirt — stepped through.

He landed in mud. Ferns the size of umbrellas dripped overhead. Somewhere close, something snorted.

"Where—" Theo wiped a leaf off his face.

"Level 1," Bit said, hovering beside a tree that looked like a giant toilet brush. "Spawn point: the Triassic period. Set your internal clock back **230 million years** — that's roughly when dinosaurs first installed themselves on planet Earth."

A creature the size of a dog dashed past on two skinny legs, gone before Theo could really look at it.

"That's a dinosaur?" Theo said. "It's tiny."

"First ones were," said Bit. "No boss-level T. rex yet. This is the tutorial area — everything's still small, and there's a whole planet of empty servers waiting to be filled."

Theo watched another one skitter through the ferns, feathers twitching on its tail, and did the math out loud, because that's what he did with numbers — ran them until they made sense. "So if dinosaurs show up here, at two hundred thirty million, and we're playing this on a night in my actual bedroom... that's a lot of save points between here and now."

"BZZZT. Correct," Bit said, delighted. "First coin, Player One." A small gold coin, pixelated at the edges, dropped into Theo's palm and melted into his pocket like a drop of water finding a puddle.

"Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Word Vault (London, 1842)
chapters.text:
Bit snapped his fingers — a sound like a console powering on — and the ferns dissolved into fog. When it cleared, Theo stood in a stone room full of long tables, every one covered in chunks of rock shaped suspiciously like bones.

A tall man in a dark coat moved along the tables, sorting pieces by size the way Theo sorted blocks into folders when a build got messy.

"Richard Owen," Bit whispered. "Scientist. Bone guy. About to do something that sticks around forever."

Owen looked up and didn't seem at all surprised to find a boy in pajamas and a green pixel floating behind him. "You've come at a good moment," he said. "I've just given these old bones a name."

"They didn't have one before?" Theo asked.

"Pieces of them did," Owen said, tapping a jaw fragment. "This one's Megalosaurus — somebody else named that back in **1824**. But nobody had a word for the whole *group* these giant creatures belonged to. So in **1842**, I made one." He said it slowly, like he was still proud of it. "**Dinosaur**. From the Greek — *deinos*, terrible, and *sauros*, lizard. 'Terrible lizard.'"

Theo turned that over. "Wait. So there was a dinosaur with a name eighteen years before there was a word for 'dinosaur'?"

"Exactly the gap that bothered me," Owen said, looking pleased someone had noticed. "A pile of bones labeled with eighteen different random names, and no folder to put them all in."

That landed for Theo immediately — he had hundreds of parts in his Roblox inventory with names like Rock3_FINAL_use_this_one, and he knew exactly how bad an unsorted folder could get. "You should tag them," Theo said. "By time period. So you know which ones showed up first. If I don't tag assets, the whole game breaks later."

Owen blinked, then reached for a stick of chalk and began marking the tables: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous — the three chapters of the dinosaur story, oldest to youngest. "A folder system," he murmured. "Why didn't I think of that eighteen years ago."

"BZZZT! Tag it!" Bit shouted, and a second gold coin dropped into Theo's pocket.

"Level complete," said Bit. "And for the record, Player One — you just helped invent paleontology's filing cabinet. That's the word for scientists who study old bones to figure out how ancient life worked."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Beach at Lyme Regis
chapters.text:
Salt wind. Grey cliffs. Rain that had just stopped falling.

A girl not much older than Theo crouched at the bottom of the cliff, hammer in hand, examining a lump of rock like it owed her money.

"Mary Anning," Bit said. "One of the best fossil hunters who ever lived, and she started young."

"Fossil hunter?" Theo said. "Like, dinosaur hunter?"

"Not dinosaur, exactly," Mary said without looking up. "Sea creatures, mostly, from the same old world. Come here — after a storm, the cliff falls apart and spits out things that have been hiding for ages."

Theo crouched beside her. "What even is a fossil?"

"An animal dies, and if it gets buried fast enough — mud, sand, whatever's handy — the soft parts rot away, but the hard parts, the bones, slowly turn to stone," Mary said. "Tiny bits of mineral swap in for the bone, piece by piece, over thousands of years, until what's left is a stone copy of the original."

"So it's not actually bone anymore."

"It's a stone photograph of one," Mary said. "Good description. Steal it if you like."

Theo scanned the exposed rock face, squinting the way he squinted at a map in Roblox Studio looking for a bug. Something caught his eye — a tight coil, half-buried, curling like a shell the size of a dinner plate.

"That," he said, pointing. "Is that something?"

Mary crouched down fast. "That," she said, "is absolutely something."

Then she looked past Theo's shoulder, and her face changed. The tide had turned while they talked, water creeping toward the base of the cliff in slow grey sheets.

"It'll be under water in twenty minutes," Mary said.

Theo didn't wait to be asked. He grabbed a loose stick, jammed it into the sand right beside the coiled shape, and tied his own shoelace around the top so it would still show even half-submerged. "Marker," he said. "So you can find the exact spot again, even after the water comes up."

Mary looked at the stick, then at Theo. "That," she said, "is exactly what I needed."

"BZZZT. Nice save," said Bit, and a third coin dropped. "Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Biggest Boss on the Map
chapters.text:
The fog cleared into open grassland, and Theo's jaw actually dropped, which he would deny later if anyone asked.

A neck rose out of the trees like a crane on a construction site, and kept rising, and kept rising, until Theo lost track of where it ended.

"Argentinosaurus," Bit said. "Might be the biggest dinosaur we know about. Scientists think it could be over **30 meters** long — about **100 feet**, nose to tail."

Theo, who measured everything in game units because that's how his brain worked, started doing math out loud. "Okay. I'm about five feet tall. That's twenty of me, lying down in a line, just to match one animal."

"Lying down and probably still getting stepped on," Bit said. "Careful."

Something else moved at the tree line — smaller, but with a skull the size of a bathtub and teeth Theo could see from fifty feet away.

"T. rex," Bit said, keeping a respectful distance. "Its teeth got up to **30 centimeters** long — a full **12 inches**, counting the root buried in the jaw. Longer than your forearm."

Theo looked at his own forearm, unimpressed by comparison, then back at the teeth. "That's not a tooth. That's a kitchen knife with a grudge."

"Most of it's hidden in the jaw, like the part of an iceberg you don't see," Bit said. "Still counts."

Theo kept running numbers, because that's what he always did when something was this big — he wanted the actual scale, not just "huge." He paced out footsteps on the ground, comparing stride length to his own, muttering level-design math under his breath: if the hitbox for that thing is forty feet, spawn points need way more buffer room.

"You're designing around it," Bit said, watching him work.

"If I put something this size in my game, players need way more warning before they round a corner into it," Theo said. "Like a boss-room sound cue."

"Make a note," Bit said. "You're basically doing a scientist's job. They work out how big and how fast these things were from the bones left behind — same thing you just did with footsteps."

Theo grinned, feeling unreasonably proud of a dinosaur he hadn't even touched. "BZZZT yourself," he said, and a fourth gold coin dropped into his pocket before Bit could even say it.

"...Level complete," Bit said, mildly offended someone had stolen his line.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Truth About the Raptor
chapters.text:
"Okay," Theo said, ducking behind a rock. "Where's the raptor. I've seen the movies. I'm ready."

"You are extremely not ready for how unready you are," Bit said. "Look down. Like, actually down."

Theo looked down. Pecking through the underbrush near his sneaker was something that looked exactly like an angry, feathered chicken with a long tail and sharp teeth.

"That's... a Velociraptor?" Theo said.

"That's a Velociraptor," Bit confirmed. "About the size of a turkey. Much, much smaller than the movie versions, which were built more like six-foot-tall actors in suits than actual fossils."

Theo stared at it. It stared back, head tilted, entirely unthreatening. "I've been scared of a turkey this whole time."

"A turkey with feathers," Bit added. "Lots of dinosaurs had them — not just this one. Feathers for warmth, feathers for show, probably feathers for all kinds of reasons nobody's fully sure about yet."

Something clicked for Theo — the kind of click he got mid-build, when two systems he'd been coding separately suddenly turned out to be the same system. "Wait," he said slowly. "Feathers. Birds have feathers."

"Keep going," Bit said, grinning.

"Are you telling me birds are... dinosaurs?"

"Scientists think birds are the modern descendants of a group of meat-eating, two-legged dinosaurs," Bit said. "Which means the pigeons outside your window, technically, never got the memo that the dinosaurs went anywhere."

Theo sat back on his heels, turkey-raptor still pecking unbothered a few feet away, and thought about every bird he had ever ignored at a park. "So the dinosaurs didn't actually disappear," he said. "They just got smaller and learned to fly and started stealing fries off the ground."

"That's the headline, yes," Bit said. "Try not to tell your whole class at once, you'll want to space that reveal out."

Theo reached toward his pocket for the coin before Bit could even announce it, which made Bit laugh, a sound like an old console booting up.

"BZZZT. Level complete," Bit said anyway, because he liked saying it. "And for what it's worth — turkeys deserve way more respect now."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Plates, Horns, and the Thagomizer
chapters.text:
The ground shook — not scary-shook, just heavy-animal-walking shook — and something the size of a small bus ambled past with a row of bony plates standing up along its back like a mohawk made of rock.

"Stegosaurus," Bit said. "Check out the tail."

Theo checked out the tail. Four long spikes jutted from the end of it, swinging slow and deliberate with every step.

"That tail has a name," Bit said. "Scientists call the spiky end a **thagomizer** — which is a weird, almost joke of a word, and yes, it kind of started as one, but it stuck."

"Thagomizer," Theo repeated, delighted. "That sounds like the final boss of my game."

"Put it in," Bit said. "I'd play that."

They rounded a low hill, and Theo nearly walked straight into something with three horns and a huge bony shield fanning out behind its head.

"Triceratops," Bit said. "Don't worry, it mostly eats plants. The horns and that big bony **frill** are defense gear — like a built-in shield."

Theo studied the frill, the way it curved up and around the neck, and his brain did the thing it always did with game mechanics: it looked for the rule. "Wait," he said. "It's not just decoration. It's literally protecting the one part a predator would go for first — the neck."

"That's exactly the idea scientists have," Bit said, impressed. "You're reading the armor like you'd read a character design sheet."

"Because I would put a shield exactly there," Theo said, already imagining the asset in his head — a frilled dinosaur boss with a weak point only visible from directly behind. "You'd have to flank it to get a hit in. Whoever built this thing knew what they were doing."

"Nobody built it," Bit said gently. "It happened that way over a long, long time, because the Triceratops with better frills survived more often. But sure — tell yourself a dinosaur invented level design. I won't stop you."

Theo grinned and reached for his coin pocket before Bit could even get the sound effect out.

"BZZZT," Bit said anyway. "Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 7: Footprints in the Gobi
chapters.text:
The air turned dry and gritty, wind dragging sand sideways across an endless stretch of dunes.

"Gobi Desert," Bit said. "Mongolia and China. One of the richest dinosaur-bone locations on the entire planet — like a server with way more loot drops than usual."

Theo crouched at a flat stretch of hardened mud, where a line of three-toed prints marched off toward the horizon, each one preserved like it had been stamped yesterday instead of unthinkably long ago.

"Footprints don't usually turn to stone," Theo said. "Right? Those are soft."

"These are called **trace fossils**," Bit said. "Not bones — just the shape something left behind, baked hard before it could wash away. Found in places like this, and in Texas too."

Theo measured the gap between prints with his own stride, the same way he'd pace out jump distances when tuning a platformer level. He frowned, recalculated, then said, "These are spaced really far apart for the print size. Whatever made these was moving fast. Running, maybe, not walking."

Bit's eight pixels did something close to raising an eyebrow. "You just read a dinosaur's speed off its footprints. That's real science, Player One. Scientists use exactly that math."

A little farther on, they found a shallow bowl-shaped dent in the ground, broken oval shapes scattered around its edge.

"Maiasaura," Bit said, voice going soft. "Name means 'good mother lizard.' Nesting sites found over in Montana show these dinosaurs built nests and stuck around to take care of their babies — brought them food, kept them safe, the whole parenting package."

Theo looked at the nest a long moment, something unexpectedly warm catching in his chest. "That's kind of nice," he said. "Everyone always makes dinosaurs sound like just teeth and stomping. Nobody mentions the ones who were just... moms."

"Most of them probably were, one way or another," Bit said. "Doesn't always make the highlight reel."

Theo reached for his coin, quieter this time, and Bit let the moment sit a second before saying it.

"Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Not Quite Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
A shadow slid over the sand, enormous and silent, and Theo looked up to see something with leathery wings gliding on a thermal, easily forty feet across.

"New asset," Theo said automatically, already sorting it in his head the way he sorted everything — into folders. "Dinosaur: flying type."

"Nope," Bit said. "Wrong folder."

Theo blinked. "It's huge, it's old, it's got scales. How is that not a dinosaur?"

"Pterosaur," Bit said. "Flying reptile, same neighborhood in time, related to dinosaurs — but not actually one. Different branch of the family tree entirely."

Theo re-sorted it mentally, same way he'd drag a misplaced block into the right folder mid-build. "Okay. Reptile-but-not-dinosaur folder. Noted."

Out past the dunes, where the ground gave way to open water, two huge shapes cut through the waves — one long and sleek, one built like a sea-monster with flippers.

"Plesiosaur and mosasaur," Bit said. "Lived in the ocean at the same time as all this. Also not dinosaurs."

"They're just — everybody's not a dinosaur today," Theo said.

"Welcome to the hardest part of the quiz," Bit said. "People lump anything old and scaly into 'dinosaur.' It's the biggest misfile in the whole subject."

Something small darted between the trees behind them, and Theo spun to look — a creature barely the size of a crow, gliding on four wings, two in front and two in back, soaring from branch to branch like it was testing out a jetpack.

"Microraptor," Bit said. "That one actually is a dinosaur. Four wings, built for gliding tree to tree."

Theo watched it stick a landing on a low branch. "So the flying lizard thing isn't a dinosaur, but the four-winged glider thing is."

"Exactly."

"This is worse than tagging my asset folders," Theo said, but he was grinning, already re-sorting everything in his head into cleaner categories — dinosaurs, flying reptiles, sea reptiles, each one correctly labeled instead of dumped into one big pile. "New system. I'm building a proper folder tree when I get home."

"That's the first thing anyone's said all night that actually sounded like homework," Bit said. "I love it."

A coin dropped before Bit could announce it, and this time Theo beat him to the line too. "Level complete," Theo said, grinning.

chapters.heading: Level 9: Sue, the Last Day, and the Trophy
chapters.text:
The last door Bit opened smelled like dust and old summer — a cracked stretch of orange rock under a huge sky, South Dakota, a hand-lettered sign staked into the ground.

A half-uncovered skeleton lay in the dirt, ribs curving up out of the rock like the hull of a ship.

"Say hello to Sue," Bit said. "Found right here, in **1990**. One of the biggest, most complete T. rex skeletons anybody's ever dug up."

"Sue," Theo repeated. "Like, a person named it after themselves?"

"Named after the person who spotted it first," Bit said. "There's a story going around that a farmer's dog dug up the very first bit of a different famous fossil, years earlier — but nobody can actually prove the dog part. That might just be a good story people liked telling. Doesn't make the bones any less real."

Theo liked that honesty — the admission that not every story in the fact pile came with a checkmark next to it. "Some legends you keep anyway," he said, "even if you're not totally sure."

"Especially those," Bit agreed.

The sky overhead darkened a shade, not stormy, just dimmer, like someone had turned down a brightness slider.

"This is the last save point," Bit said, quieter than before. "**66 million years ago.** Most scientists think a huge space rock — an asteroid — slammed into Earth, somewhere near what's now Mexico, and changed everything, fast. The world after looked nothing like the world before."

Theo waited for the scary part. It didn't come.

"The dinosaurs that weren't birds didn't make it through that change," Bit said. "But you already met who did." A single bird crossed the darkened sky above them, wings beating steady. "Turns out the save file didn't actually delete. It just updated. New version, same bloodline."

Theo watched the bird go and thought about the pigeon-sized raptor, and the frill like armor, and the mother dinosaur who wouldn't leave her nest, all of it somehow leading to a bird flying over a desert on a night that wasn't technically happening in real time.

"If I was building this as a level," Theo said slowly, "I wouldn't end it on the asteroid. I'd end it right here — the bird flying on, after. Like the game doesn't actually end, it just changes what you're playing as."

Bit went very quiet, which for an eight-pixel sprite made of jokes was unusual. "That," he said, "is a genuinely good ending, Player One. BZZZT."

A last gold coin dropped into Theo's pocket, and all nine coins rose together, spinning, fusing in midair into one small, warm, solid trophy shaped like a T. rex skull.

"Level complete."

The green doorway opened one more time, and Theo stepped through, back onto his own bedroom carpet, laptop glowing softly where he'd left it.

The trophy was still in his hand. Actually in his hand, not just in a coin pocket that didn't really exist. He set it on his desk next to his keyboard.

On the screen, green letters blinked once: THE PAST NEVER ENDS. IT JUST LOADS THE NEXT PLAYER.

Theo looked at his half-built dinosaur level, at the blank spots where he hadn't known what to put yet, and grinned.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole still-flying world to build.

true_facts.text: Dinosaurs first showed up around **230 million years ago**, way back in the Triassic period.
The word **dinosaur** means **'terrible lizard'** in Greek, and a scientist named **Richard Owen** came up with it in **1842**.
The very first dinosaur ever given a proper name was **Megalosaurus**, back in **1824** — eighteen years before the word 'dinosaur' even existed.
**Mary Anning** was a real fossil hunter who searched the cliffs near **Lyme Regis** for ancient sea creatures.
A **fossil** forms when an animal's hard parts slowly turn to stone, as tiny minerals swap in for the bone over thousands of years.
**Argentinosaurus** might be the biggest dinosaur ever found — maybe over **30 meters**, about **100 feet**, nose to tail.
A **T. rex** tooth could grow up to **30 centimeters** — a full **12 inches** — counting the part hidden in the jaw.
A real **Velociraptor** was only about the size of a **turkey**, nothing like the giant movie versions.
Lots of dinosaurs, including Velociraptor, likely had **feathers**.
Birds alive today are thought to be the modern descendants of meat-eating, two-legged dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never fully disappeared.
**Stegosaurus** had bony plates along its back and a spiky tail weapon nicknamed a **thagomizer**.
**Triceratops** had three horns and a big bony **frill** that worked like built-in armor for its neck.
By about **66 million years ago**, most dinosaurs that weren't birds were gone for good.
Many scientists think a huge **asteroid** — a giant space rock — smashed into Earth and changed the whole world, fast.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo brings home a trophy shaped like a T. rex skull, fused from nine golden coins, while the screen reads THE PAST NEVER ENDS. IT JUST LOADS THE NEXT PLAYER.

scenarios.why: #48: band D (13-17), which F13 never covered. A teenager must not be talked down to.
scenarios.best_moment: He didn't say anything clever about it. Some facts don't need a joke stapled onto them.
scenarios.worst_moment: Tomorrow, the judges were getting a project with a lot more rocket in it than they were expecting.
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Explorer 1 launched eight months before NASA opened. It found the inner belt, so let Eli spot a boundary rather than 'two belts.' Von Braun's V-2s were wartime rockets. Apollo-Soyuz docked at about 140 miles. Hedge the Earthrise story: it was unplanned, not a 'broken checklist.'

Break the radio-states-fact, radio-confirms formula and pay off the requested 'mysterious' tone. Put Shepard before Kennedy (Shepard's flight is what made the speech possible). Give Eli a few hands-on choices: retuning to chase a fading signal, testing a hypothesis on his own kit, or a hint about who or what is transmitting.

Cut the duplicated ending so there is one strong final line. Prune the repeated 'sat with' and 'said slowly' tics and the 'That's not X. That's Y.' pattern. Tighten Eli's muddled Earthrise reasoning so the physics he's proud of is actually right.

story.title: Eli and the Signal from 1957
story.subtitle: A shortwave radio, a green dial, and eighteen years of racing for the stars.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Static (October 1957)
chapters.text:
Eli had three days left to fix his grandfather's old shortwave radio before the physics fair, and so far all it did was hiss.

He twisted the dial anyway, half-asleep on his bedroom floor at midnight, waiting for the lecture he'd get tomorrow for frying another capacitor. Then the static changed. It thinned into a rhythm: beep... beep... beep. Steady as a heartbeat, and twice as loud as it had any business being.

The dial's green light, dead for a decade, flickered on.

"That's not a lecture frequency," Eli muttered, leaning closer.

A voice came through the hiss, dry and patient, like someone who had been waiting a long time to be asked a question. "Good. You're tuned to 20.005 megahertz. October 4, 1957. Say hello to the first thing humans ever put in orbit."

Eli's hand froze on the dial. An **orbit** is a path around a planet, held steady by gravity instead of falling into it, and the idea wasn't new to him; he'd done the math for a school project. What was new was hearing it happen. "Sputnik," he said. "That's Sputnik's beep."

"Lock the frequency and find out."

He turned the dial a careful quarter-turn, the way you'd tune a guitar string, until the beep sharpened into one clean tone. The room folded sideways, static rising like water —

— and Eli was standing on cold tile in a tracking station, surrounded by men in rolled-up shirtsleeves listening to the exact same beep on equipment ten times the size of his.

"That," said the voice, now coming from a battered radio bolted to the wall instead of his nightstand, "is **Sputnik 1**. Launched by the Soviet Union this morning. About **58 centimeters** across — roughly the size of a beach ball — and that beep is the entire mission. No camera. No instruments. Just a radio shouting 'I'm up here' to anyone on the planet with an antenna."

"That's it? The whole thing?"

"That's enough to end an argument about who's better at rockets. In a month they'll launch **Sputnik 2**, carrying a dog named **Laika** — the first living creature to reach orbit. She'll be famous worldwide within days."

Eli looked at the men around him, pale, furious, scribbling equations on the backs of napkins. "They look like they lost something."

"They did," said the voice. "They lost the idea that they were ahead."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Belt Nobody Expected (Early 1958)
chapters.text:
Static again, then a new tone — slower, clicking in uneven bursts, like a heartbeat monitor having a bad night.

"Where now?" Eli asked, already turning the dial to match it.

"Same argument, different scoreboard," said the voice. "January 31, 1958. A lab in California."

The room was smaller than the tracking station, lit by fluorescent tubes, centered on a man hunched over a pen recorder, watching a needle twitch across rolling paper. Eli leaned over his shoulder.

"That's **Explorer 1**," the voice said. "America's answer to Sputnik. Launched today. It's carrying a counter that measures radiation — invisible particles zipping around up there — and it's supposed to read almost nothing once it clears the atmosphere."

Eli studied the needle. It wasn't reading nothing. It was pinning itself flat against the top of the chart, over and over, like it had hit a wall.

"That's not a broken instrument," Eli said slowly. "That's an instrument that found something it wasn't built to measure. It's not failing — it's maxing out."

The man at the recorder looked up sharply, as if he'd heard the thought rather than the words.

"Exactly right," the voice said. "Explorer 1 had just discovered a ring of radiation trapped around the Earth by its own magnetic field — a loop scientists hadn't known was there. It got named the **Van Allen radiation belt**, after the scientist who built the detector. Nobody in this room believed the readings at first. They thought the equipment was lying to them."

"But it wasn't lying. It was just telling them something they hadn't asked yet."

"That's half of physics, Eli."

He thought of his own half-built antenna back on his desk, and wondered if it, too, might someday catch something nobody had thought to ask it to look for.

Eight months later, the voice told him, the United States would stand up a whole new agency to run its space program: **NASA**, officially open for business on **October 1, 1958**. Sputnik had scared one country into building a satellite; the satellite had scared it into building an agency.

"So the belt is basically a government org chart's fault," Eli said.

"History's funnier than physics gives it credit for."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Hundred Eight Minutes (Spring 1961)
chapters.text:
The next signal arrived mid-sentence, like someone had grabbed Eli by the collar. Cheering — real, overlapping, thousands of voices — poured out of the radio before the dial even finished turning.

"April 12, 1961," the voice said. "Moscow's about to go very, very loud."

Eli materialized at the edge of a crowd staring up at a clear sky, and he didn't need the voice to tell him what had just happened; the whole street was chanting one name. "**Yuri Gagarin**," the voice confirmed. "First human being in space. He just orbited the Earth once, aboard a capsule called Vostok 1, and he's on his way back down right now."

"How long was the flight?"

"About **108 minutes**, launch to landing."

Eli did the math under his breath before the voice could beat him to it — orbital speed, circumference, rough numbers from memory — and landed close enough that the voice actually laughed, a short dry sound like static clearing its throat.

"Not bad for mental arithmetic in a crowd."

Three weeks later the scene changed to a launch pad in Florida, smaller rocket, smaller crowd, same tension stretched across everyone's face. "**Alan Shepard**," the voice said. "May 5. First American in space, aboard Freedom 7. His flight didn't make a full orbit — just up and back down, fifteen minutes — but it was enough to keep the argument alive."

"Second place," Eli said. "That's got to sting."

"Keep listening."

Three weeks after that, a different voice entirely — recorded, formal, unmistakably a podium — crackled through the radio. "**May 25, 1961**," the Operator said. "President Kennedy, in front of Congress, challenging the country to land a man on the Moon and bring him home safe — before the decade's out."

Eli listened to the applause roll through the speech, thinking about everything that had to go right for a deadline like that to mean anything: the fuel, the math, the sheer number of things not allowed to fail. "That's not a speech," he said. "That's a parts list with extra steps."

The Operator didn't disagree.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Secret Behind the Call Sign (1961–1963)
chapters.text:
"Here's a mystery for you," the voice said, before Eli had even caught his breath from the applause. "Every signal you've heard from the Soviet side has come from a program with no public boss. No name on the door. Who do you think is actually in charge?"

Eli frowned at the dial, where a new frequency hummed low and steady, half-buried under layers of coded chatter. "Somebody who doesn't want to be found. You don't hide a name by accident."

"Keep pulling that thread."

He tuned past the chatter and the Operator dropped him into a control room dense with cigarette smoke and clipped Russian, everyone addressing one unseen figure only as "the Chief Designer" — never a name, never a face in view.

"That's **Sergei Korolev**," the voice said quietly, once the room had gone back to its business. "He's been running the Soviet rocket program this whole time — Sputnik, Gagarin, all of it — and his identity is a state secret. It won't come out publicly until after his death, in 1966."

"You hide your best scientist like he's a weapon."

"In this story, he basically was one."

The scene shifted again — June 16, 1963, a bright capsule window, and a woman's voice counting off numbers in Russian with total calm. "**Valentina Tereshkova**," the voice said. "First woman in space. She used to work in a textile factory. Today she's orbiting the Earth aboard Vostok 6 — and by the time she lands, she'll have gone around **forty-eight times**."

Eli watched the capsule's tiny window scroll past a curve of blue he recognized instantly from photographs, except this was the first time anyone had actually been a woman looking at it from up there. "Does Korolev get credit for this one too?"

"He built the rocket. She flew it. Both facts are true at once — that's usually how big moments work."

Eli turned that over as the static began to rise again. "I like him more as a mystery than I would as a name on a plaque."

"Funny," said the voice. "He probably felt the same way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Ten Minutes Outside (March 1965)
chapters.text:
The static this time came with a hiss of breathing — loud, close, amplified by something that sounded like a tin can with a microphone taped inside.

"March 18, 1965," the Operator said. "You're about to meet someone standing outside his own spacecraft."

Eli's stomach dropped before his brain caught up — not fear exactly, just the sheer wrongness of the image forming around him: a figure in a bulky white suit, tethered by a single cord, floating against a black so complete it looked painted on.

"**Alexei Leonov**," the voice said. "First human being to leave a spacecraft in orbit and just... float. This is called a **spacewalk** — no ground, no air of your own, nothing holding you up but a line back to the hatch."

"How long is he out there?"

"About **ten minutes**."

Eli watched the tether go taut and slack, taut and slack, as Leonov drifted at the end of it. "No gravity to pull him back. No air to push against. He's basically just hanging there until somebody reels him in."

"That's **zero gravity** for you," the voice said. "Everything you know about up and down stops meaning anything, which is exactly the kind of thing your physics teacher would make you solve for homework."

"I'd have packed a longer tether."

"Funny you say that — his suit puffed up so much in the vacuum that he almost couldn't fit back through the hatch. He had to let air out of it just to squeeze through."

Eli winced, watching the small figure fold himself back toward the capsule, inch by inch, the tether coiling in behind him like a fishing line. "That's not in any textbook I've read."

"Most of the good parts aren't," the voice said. "They get smoothed out by the time it's a paragraph in a book. Up close it's always messier, and somehow always smaller — ten minutes doesn't sound like history until you're the one floating in it."

The hatch sealed. The breathing on the radio slowed, steadied, and the static began to climb again, pulling Eli toward whatever came next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Earthrise (December 1968)
chapters.text:
"Now go further out," the voice said, and the static this time didn't crackle so much as stretch, thin and distant, like a radio station losing its signal on a long drive.

Eli opened his eyes in near silence — a tiny window, a curve of gray rock scrolling past below, and beyond it, impossibly, a blue and white marble rising over a horizon that wasn't Earth's.

"December 1968," the voice said. "**Apollo 8**. These three astronauts just became the first people to orbit the Moon — and one of them, **William Anders**, is about to take a photograph you've definitely seen before, even if you didn't know its name."

Eli watched a camera lift toward the window. "Earthrise," he said quietly. He had seen it — posters, textbooks, a coffee mug in his school's science room — and had never once connected it to a moment this specific, this fragile, a photo taken almost by accident out of a tiny window two hundred thousand miles from home.

"They came all this way to look at the Moon," the voice said, "and the thing that stopped them cold was looking back at Earth."

"Makes sense. You don't notice a room until you're standing outside it."

The scene shifted to a hangar on the ground, vast and improbable, dominated by a rocket so tall Eli had to tilt his head back inside the vision just to see where it stopped. "That's the machine that got them here," the voice said. "**Saturn V**. Three hundred sixty-three feet tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty."

"Who builds something like that?"

"**Wernher von Braun** led the team. He'd built rockets for Germany years before; after the war he ended up leading NASA's rocket program instead, and the Saturn V was the result — the engineering answer to everything Korolev's team had been doing on the other side of the planet."

Eli walked the length of the rocket in the vision, craning up at each stage, each section built to fall away once it burned its fuel and did its job. "It's basically three rockets stacked on top of each other, and two of them exist just to throw the third one higher."

"Now you're thinking like an engineer instead of a tourist."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Giant Leap (July 1969)
chapters.text:
The static cut out entirely this time, replaced by something worse: total silence, and a countdown that wasn't numbers but heartbeats, Eli's own, loud in his ears.

"July 20, 1969," the voice said, barely above a whisper now, as if even it didn't want to break the moment. "You're about to watch someone's boot touch something no human boot has touched before."

Eli stood in the dark beside a console banked with small gray screens, surrounded by men leaning forward on folded arms, nobody speaking, nobody breathing in sync with anyone else.

"That's **Neil Armstrong**," the voice said, as a figure in white eased down a ladder on the tiny screen, one slow rung at a time. "First person on the Moon. **Buzz Aldrin** joins him a few minutes later. Their crewmate, **Michael Collins**, stays up above the whole time, alone, orbiting in the command module — someone has to fly the ride home."

"That's got to be the loneliest job in history."

"Or the calmest. Depends who you ask."

Armstrong's boot touched down. The line came through the static a half-second late, words Eli had heard a hundred times in documentaries and somehow still felt entirely new in real time: a giant leap, not just a small step.

The room around Eli erupted — not loud, just a wave of exhaled breath and quiet handshakes, like men too tired to shout properly.

"Between this mission and 1972," the voice said, "**twelve astronauts** will walk on the Moon, across six separate landings. This is the first of them."

Eli looked at the rocket diagram still pinned to the console, the same three-hundred-sixty-three-foot giant from the hangar, now reduced to a single tiny capsule splashing back down somewhere in an ocean he couldn't see from here. He thought back to the stacked stages, each one discarded along the way, and understood for the first time why that mattered: without them, this tiny capsule never would have had enough push left to get this far from home.

"All that rocket," he said, "just to get a few people and a flag up there, and bring them home again."

"That's most of engineering, if you zoom out far enough," the voice said. "Building something enormous so that something small can survive the trip."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Houston, We've Had a Problem (April 1970)
chapters.text:
This signal arrived wrong from the first second — clipped, urgent, three voices talking over each other in a way none of the others had.

"1970," the voice said, flat now, no theater in it at all. "**Apollo 13**. On the way to the Moon. An oxygen tank just failed."

Eli felt the shift immediately — not fear exactly, more the cold focus of watching a problem get worked in real time. The capsule around him groaned, power flickering across a dashboard of gauges, three astronauts moving fast and calm instead of fast and panicked.

"Are they going to be okay?" Eli asked, and he was glad his voice came out steady.

"Yes," the voice said immediately. "That's not me being kind — that's just what happened. Keep listening and you'll see how."

On the ground, a room full of engineers in short-sleeved shirts argued over a table scattered with spare parts — a square piece here, a round piece there, nothing fitting the other. "They need to fit a square air filter into a round socket," the voice said, "using only what the astronauts already have on board. Hoses. Tape. A procedure manual's cardboard cover."

Eli leaned over the table, physics brain already running the problem — airflow, seals, whatever would hold pressure without a perfect fit. "It doesn't have to be elegant," he said slowly. "It just has to not leak."

One of the engineers, three thousand miles and years out of Eli's reach, said almost the exact same thing out loud a second later.

"They got it to work," the voice said. "The astronauts built it exactly like that, with exactly that logic, and it held long enough to get them home. Splashdown, safe, all three of them, a few days later."

Eli exhaled, a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "So the whole mission to the Moon turned into a mission to just get three guys back alive."

"And it worked," the voice said. "Sometimes the best part of an engineering story isn't the plan. It's what people build when the plan breaks."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Handshake in Orbit (1975)
chapters.text:
The last signal was the calmest one yet — no cheering, no countdown, just two sets of radio chatter slowly lining up with each other, like two people finally finishing each other's sentences.

"July 17, 1975," the voice said. "Last stop."

Eli found himself floating — properly floating, the vision steady enough this time that he could feel the lack of up and down from earlier settle into something almost peaceful — beside a window showing two spacecraft easing toward one another against the black.

"American and Soviet," the voice said. "**Apollo** and **Soyuz**. They're about to dock — link up, hatch to hatch — in orbit."

"After all that," Eli said. "Sputnik, Gagarin, the Moon, the tank explosion. All of it, and it ends with them just... parking next to each other."

"It ends with a handshake," the voice said, as the hatch between the two craft swung open and an American astronaut reached through to grip a Soviet cosmonaut's hand, both of them grinning like the whole eighteen-year argument had just been quietly set down on a table somewhere. "Eighteen years of trying to beat each other to space, and it finishes with two crews shaking hands in orbit, on television, for the whole planet to see."

Eli watched the handshake hold a beat too long, like neither of them wanted to be the first to let go. "That's a weirder ending than I expected."

"Most races are," the voice said. "You start them trying to win. You don't always know what you're racing toward until you get there."

The static began to climb, gentle this time, more like a tide going out than a wave crashing in. The hatch, the handshake, the black window full of stars all thinned at the edges, and Eli felt the floor return under his feet — carpet, not tile, not a capsule.

His room. His radio, dial glowing a last soft green before fading to dark, a single frequency still scrawled on a sticky note he didn't remember writing: 20.005 MHz — Sputnik.

He sat there a long moment, radio cooling under his hand, the physics fair suddenly feeling like the smallest part of the assignment.

Tomorrow, he had a project to rebuild — and a much better reason to finish it.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a project to rebuild — and a much better reason to finish it.

true_facts.text: On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, a satellite about the size of a beach ball that did nothing but beep over the radio — and that was enough to make the whole world listen.
A month later, the Soviets sent up **Sputnik 2** carrying a dog named **Laika**, the first living creature to reach orbit.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and ended up discovering a ring of radiation looping around Earth, later named the **Van Allen belt**.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States stood up a brand-new space agency, **NASA**, which opened for business on **October 1, 1958**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **Kennedy** challenged the country to land a person on the Moon and bring them home safe before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, circling the Earth **forty-eight times**.
The Soviet rocket program's real boss, **Sergei Korolev**, was kept a total secret — his name wasn't made public until after his death in **1966**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his own spacecraft, a **spacewalk** that lasted about **ten minutes**.

In **December 1968**, the crew of **Apollo 8** became the first people to orbit the Moon, and astronaut **William Anders** snapped the famous **Earthrise** photo of Earth rising over the Moon's horizon.
The giant **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon was designed under **Wernher von Braun**, who had built rockets years earlier before leading NASA's team.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank failure crippled **Apollo 13** on the way to the Moon, but the crew made it home safe after engineers helped them improvise a fix using what was already on board.
The whole contest ended peacefully on **July 17, 1975**, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and the crews shook hands.

new_recurring.rule: An old shortwave radio on Eli's desk. Turning its dial to match a strange beep or broadcast, and the green light flickers on, pulling the listener into that exact historical moment; a dry, patient voice called the Operator narrates and…
