story.title: Mia and the Deep Stats of the Beautiful Game
story.subtitle: A stoppage-time tour through two thousand years of the world's game.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Stoppage Time
chapters.text:
Mia had the laptop balanced on a pillow and the lamp turned down low, the way you do at eleven-forty on a school night when you are absolutely not still awake. On the screen: a spreadsheet of her club's last six matches, every shot logged, every pass mapped, an expected-goals model she had built herself. **Expected goals** — a number that guesses how likely a shot was to go in, based on thousands of shots like it before. Her team should have scored four goals on Saturday, the model said. They scored one.

She tabbed back through the formula for the ninth time, muttering about unlucky bounces, when the screen went black, then a flat stadium-floodlight green, a center circle pulsing in the middle of it like a heartbeat.

A shape stepped out of the glow: assistant-referee flag under one arm, a scoreboard where a face should be, numbers scrolling across it like a ticker. '0 - 0,' it said, by way of hello. 'Oldest scoreline in the sport. We'll get to that. I'm Nil. Think of me as your data analyst for history.'

Mia did not scream, because screaming felt like an overreaction to a man made of a scoreboard, and also because he had excellent posture for a hologram. 'You're telling me soccer has a stats guy.'

'Soccer has had a stats guy since before it had a name,' said Nil. 'Shall I show you the first fixture on record?'

The green light swallowed the bedroom and set them down in noise and dust — a wide dirt field ringed by cheering crowds, players in loose tunics chasing a stitched leather ball between two poles.

'China,' said Nil, 'more than **2,000 years ago**, during the Han dynasty. This game is called **cuju** — it means "kick the ball" — and it is the earliest known ancestor of the sport you play every Saturday.'

Mia watched a player flick the ball up off one shoulder without using a single hand. 'That's a better first touch than half my team.'

'Keep watching,' said Nil. 'Possession stats were terrible back then. Nobody was logging them.'

'Someone needs to,' Mia said, already reaching for a notebook that wasn't there.

'Someone will,' said Nil. 'Give it about two thousand years.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The King Who Banned the Game
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them into a narrow London street, and immediately something large and inflated came flying at Mia's head.

She ducked. Behind her, a crowd of grown men sprinted full tilt after the same ball, shoulder to shoulder, shouting, knocking over a fruit cart.

'This is **mob football**,' said Nil, stepping neatly out of the path of a man in a very old-fashioned hat. 'No rules, no field lines, sometimes no limit on players at all. Whole villages against whole villages, and the ball could end up anywhere — a field, a river, somebody's front door.'

'This looks less like a sport and more like a reason to call the police,' said Mia, watching the fruit cart get righted by its remarkably patient owner.

'**King Edward II** thought the same thing,' said Nil. 'In **1314**, he banned it in London — too much noise, too much chaos, too many broken fruit carts. Didn't work. People kept playing anyway, for centuries, mostly by ignoring him completely.'

Mia grinned. 'A king lost to a ball game. Put that on the scoreboard.'

The light shifted, and the street became a cold stone room inside **Stirling Castle**, in Scotland. Hidden inside a wall, forgotten for hundreds of years, sat a round leather ball, flattened and ancient.

'Found hidden here,' said Nil. 'Probably from the **1540s**. Stuffed with a pig's bladder for bounce, which is exactly as unglamorous as it sounds. Some call it the oldest football in the world.'

Mia crouched to look at it properly, then nudged it with one finger, half expecting it to still bounce. It didn't — four hundred years inside a wall will do that to a ball. 'No panels like mine,' she said. 'Just leather and hope.'

'Different ball every century,' said Nil. 'Same obsession every century.'

'So the oldest ball we've got was hidden in a wall,' Mia said. 'Somebody's coach confiscated it and never gave it back.'

'That,' said Nil, 'is the single best theory anyone in four hundred years has come up with.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Rulebook
chapters.text:
They landed in a tidy office in London, and immediately everything felt more organized — more Mia's kind of chaos.

A man with an enormous mustache was hunched over a desk covered in crossed-out paper, writing something by candlelight.

'Who's winning an argument with himself?' Mia asked.

'**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**,' said Nil. 'Founding member of something called the Football Association, and about to write football's first official rulebook. Before this, every school and every town played by its own version of the rules. Some let you carry the ball. Some didn't. Games between schools were basically arguments about what counted.'

'That's not a sport,' Mia said. 'That's a dataset with no shared units.'

'Exactly the problem some Cambridge students had tried to solve fifteen years earlier,' said Nil. 'In **1848**, they wrote the **Cambridge Rules** — one attempt at a single shared rulebook. It didn't fully catch on. Morley's version did.'

On **26 October 1863**, in a London tavern, Morley and ten other club representatives founded the **Football Association** — the FA — and agreed on one enormous, controversial rule: no more picking the ball up and running with it. Carrying was out. Kicking was in. Rugby split off to do its own thing.

Morley looked up from his draft, caught sight of the two of them, and frowned at Mia like she'd wandered into a meeting she hadn't been invited to.

'He wrote the actual **Laws of the Game** himself,' Nil went on. 'Pen, ink, one very patient committee.'

Mia leaned over his shoulder, reading upside down the way she read a teacher's grade book. 'Rule four,' she read aloud. 'No carrying the ball with the hands.'

Morley tapped the paper without looking up, as if confirming a fact to someone who should already know it, and kept writing.

'He doesn't talk much,' Mia said.

'He's about to invent the most-played sport on the planet,' said Nil. 'Let the man work.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Oldest Cup, The First Draw
chapters.text:
'Favorite stat in the whole sport,' Nil said, as the office dissolved into a stone-walled stadium hung with old banners. 'Oldest trophy still being played for, anywhere in the world.'

The **FA Cup** had started in **1871-72**, a straight knockout tournament for English clubs — win or go home, no second chances, no group stage to soften a bad night.

'No cushion,' Mia said. 'One bad game and you're done for the whole year. That's brutal.'

'That's also why people have watched it for over **150 years**,' said Nil. 'A single mistake means something here. Your expected-goals model would hate it.'

'My expected-goals model would respect it,' Mia said. 'There's a difference.'

The scene shifted again, this time to a muddy pitch in Glasgow, thin crowds standing three and four deep around a rope. Two teams in long-sleeved shirts lined up, breath steaming in the cold.

'**1872**,' said Nil. 'Scotland against England. The first-ever official international match between two national teams.'

Mia watched ninety minutes of careful, scrappy, extremely polite football, and not one single goal. The final whistle went. Both sides shook hands like it had been a triumph anyway.

'That's it?' Mia said. 'Nobody scored. Nobody at all.'

'**0-0**,' Nil confirmed. 'The scoreline I introduced myself with, if you remember. First international fixture in history, and the stat line is just two zeroes.'

Mia pulled a face. 'My coach would have benched both strikers at halftime.'

'Your coach,' said Nil, 'would have had to bench an entire country.'

She watched the two captains walk off still deep in conversation, clearly already planning a rematch, and found she didn't mind the nil-nil so much after all. Some numbers tell you less about the game and more about how new it still was — like a model with only one match logged. You don't judge it yet. You wait for the sample size, and you let the data grow up a little.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A League, A Letter, A World Body
chapters.text:
'Quick question,' Mia said, as a crowded Victorian street market rose up around them, newspaper sellers shouting scores. 'Why do you call it "soccer"? Everyone else just says "football."'

'Good catch,' said Nil. 'Officially, the sport was called **association football**, to separate it from rugby football. English schoolboys in the **1880s**, who apparently could not be bothered to say four syllables, shortened "association" to "assoc" and then to "soccer." Both names have always meant the exact same game.'

'So it's not a different sport,' Mia said. 'It's a nickname that got famous in one country and stuck.'

'Correct,' said Nil, 'and you will still argue about it at family dinners for the rest of your life.'

They moved on, into a smoky meeting room where a man named **William McGregor** was arguing — cheerfully, loudly — that clubs needed a proper schedule instead of whatever games they could arrange that week.

'In **1888**,' said Nil, 'McGregor organized the **Football League** — the first organized football league anywhere in the world. Fixed fixtures, a proper table, a season that actually meant something.'

Mia's eyes lit up the way they did at a good spreadsheet. 'A table. Points. Standings. That's it, that's the whole appeal of sports, right there.'

'Sixteen years later,' Nil said, 'the sport needed a referee bigger than one country.'

The scene shifted to Paris, 1904, where delegates from seven countries sat around a table signing papers nobody in the room could have guessed would end up governing a sport played by half the planet.

'**FIFA**,' said Nil. 'Football's world governing body, founded in Paris in **1904**. Seven nations at the start. A great many more by the time you're watching it on your phone.'

Mia looked around the modest little room — no trophy cabinet, no stadium, just some ink and some ambition. 'This is where it all got official. It looks like a tax meeting.'

'Most important moments do,' said Nil.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Ban That Should Never Have Happened
chapters.text:
The green light set them down on the edge of a packed English stadium, bigger than any crowd Mia had seen yet, every seat full.

'Fifty-three thousand people,' said Nil, 'come to watch women's football.'

On the pitch, a tall, fearless-looking forward was running at defenders like they weren't there.

'That's **Lily Parr**,' said Nil. 'Star player for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular teams in England at the time. She could apparently shoot harder than most of the men's players anyone had seen.'

Mia watched Parr beat two defenders and smash a shot past the keeper, and the crowd noise hit her like weather. 'This is bigger than my league's championship game.'

'It was,' said Nil, and something in his voice changed. 'Then, in **1921**, the FA banned women from playing on its member clubs' grounds. No real football reason given. The teams kept going anyway, on whatever fields they could find, for fifty years, without proper grounds, proper funding, or proper credit.'

Mia's jaw tightened. 'Fifty years. That's not a rule, that's a punishment for being good at something.'

'No argument from me,' said Nil. 'Here's where it turns, though.'

The light jumped forward. The stadium emptied, refilled, modernized — new seats, a new year glowing in the corner of a scoreboard: **1971**.

'The FA finally lifted the ban,' said Nil. 'Fifty years late. Still — lifted.'

Another jump, China this time, a packed stadium under the kind of floodlights Mia recognized from World Cup highlights she'd watched a hundred times. **1991**. The first official **Women's World Cup**, trophy held up by the winning team.

'The United States,' said Nil, 'won the very first one.'

Mia watched the celebration, confetti catching the floodlights, and thought about the fifty empty years in between. 'They should've never had to wait,' she said. 'But I'm glad they got it back.'

'So is every stat sheet since,' said Nil. 'There's a lot more data now. Lily Parr would have loved that part.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Eleven Countries, One Trophy
chapters.text:
'Uruguay,' Nil announced, as the scene became blazing sun, a brand-new concrete stadium, and flags Mia didn't recognize snapping in the wind. 'July, **1930**. Thirteen countries, one trophy, and absolutely no idea yet that this would become the biggest sporting event on Earth.'

'This is the first World Cup,' Mia said, already scanning the crowd for anything that looked like a stats board and finding nothing but hand-painted signs.

'The man who made it happen is standing right there,' said Nil, nodding toward a neat, serious-looking official near the tunnel. '**Jules Rimet**, president of FIFA. He'd spent years pushing for one single tournament that would crown a true world champion, instead of a dozen countries all claiming the title separately. This stadium is the result of that argument finally being won.'

Mia watched the host nation storm onto the field to roars that shook dust loose from the stadium railings. 'Home advantage,' she murmured. 'Never underestimate home advantage. It shows up in every data set I've ever built.'

It held. **Uruguay beat Argentina in the final** to win the very first World Cup, and the stadium came apart with noise, strangers hugging strangers in the stands.

Nil produced, from somewhere inside his scoreboard chest, a small golden statue of a winged figure holding up a ball. 'The original trophy,' he said. 'Named after **Jules Rimet himself**. It would travel the world for the next forty-four years, handed from champion to champion.'

Mia turned it over in her hands — lighter than she expected, for something that would end up meaning so much to so many people who'd never even touch it. 'Forty-four years is a long career for a trophy.'

'Wait until you hear what happens to it,' said Nil, taking it carefully back before she got any ideas about souvenirs.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Dog Who Found the Cup
chapters.text:
'London, **1966**,' said Nil, and the scene became a glass display case, roped off, a small crowd of worried-looking men in suits standing around it. 'The World Cup trophy — the actual Jules Rimet trophy — on display before the tournament. And then, one morning, gone. Stolen clean out of its case.'

Mia blinked. 'Someone stole the World Cup?'

'For about a week, yes,' said Nil. 'Police searched everywhere. Then a man out walking his dog near London noticed his dog sniffing at a package wrapped in newspaper under a hedge.'

'The dog found it?'

'The dog found it,' Nil confirmed. 'His name was **Pickles**. National hero, several newspaper covers, at least one celebratory biscuit.'

Mia laughed so hard she had to sit down on an invisible bench of light. 'A dog solved a national emergency and nobody even trained him for it.'

'Pickles retired undefeated,' said Nil. 'Months later, **England hosted that same World Cup — and won it.** Their only title to date.'

The scene shifted again, sun and samba drums now, a different decade, different flags. 'Brazil,' said Nil, 'has won the World Cup a record **five times** — **1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002**. And one player was on the squad for three of those wins.'

A small, electric forward danced through four defenders like they were cones at practice, and finished with a touch so soft it barely looked like effort. '**Pele**,' said Nil. 'Only player ever on three World Cup-winning squads — **1958, 1962, 1970**.'

Mia watched him glide past another defender. 'That's not a stat line. That's a cheat code.'

A whistle blew sharply nearby — a referee reaching into his pocket and pulling out two bright squares of card, one yellow, one red, holding them up like he was presenting evidence.

'**Ken Aston**,' said Nil. 'Invented yellow and red cards, after sitting at a traffic light and thinking, you know, that's actually a very clear system. Debuted at the **1970 World Cup**.'

'Red means off, yellow means careful,' Mia said. 'Honestly the most useful idea in this whole trip.'

'One more,' said Nil, as a new golden trophy appeared in his hands, a different shape from the first one. 'Since Brazil kept the original trophy for good after that third title, FIFA needed a replacement. New World Cup Trophy, **1974**. Still the one lifted today.'

Mia held it up to the light. 'Heavier than the last one.'

'History usually is,' said Nil.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Full Time
chapters.text:
The green light folded back into her bedroom exactly where it had started, laptop still glowing, spreadsheet still open, the little error in her expected-goals model still blinking red in one cell.

Nil stood by the desk, flag under his arm, scoreboard face gone quiet and soft-lit instead of blazing.

'Same room,' said Mia. 'Different me, slightly.'

'That's generally how this works,' said Nil.

She looked at the spreadsheet with new eyes — four goals expected, one goal scored, and for the first time all night it didn't bother her the way it had at eleven-forty. A two-thousand-year-old game that had survived a royal ban, fifty years of a ban that should never have happened, a stolen trophy, and a dog named Pickles could survive one unlucky Saturday.

'You know what the stats never tell you?' she said.

'Go on,' said Nil.

'How long it took to even agree on the rules. How many people had to argue about a rulebook before any of this counted.' She tapped the trackpad, closed the spreadsheet, opened a blank page instead. 'I think I want to build something different. Not just what should've happened. What actually did — all the way back.'

'That,' said Nil, 'is a much better model than the one you had open at eleven-forty.'

The scoreboard face flickered once, dimmed, and folded itself back into the laptop screen, which returned to its ordinary, unremarkable blue. Nil was gone, the way he'd arrived — mid-sentence, no fanfare, like a final whistle nobody quite hears coming.

Mia sat for a second in the quiet, then opened a new document and typed one line at the top: *The Full History, All the Way Back.*

Saturday's game suddenly felt like a very small part of something enormous. She went to sleep already working out where chapter one would start.

story.ending_line: Saturday couldn't come soon enough — she finally had the whole data set.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a kicking game played in **Han dynasty China** more than **2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's oldest known ancestors.
Mob football got so wild that **King Edward II banned it in London in 1314**.
A leather ball stuffed with a pig's bladder, found hidden inside **Stirling Castle** and maybe from the **1540s**, might be the oldest football in the world.
The **Football Association** was founded in London on **26 October 1863**, and its first big rule was: no more carrying the ball.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote football's first official rulebook, the **Laws of the Game**, in **1863**.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world.
The first-ever international match was **Scotland versus England in 1872** in Glasgow, and it ended **0-0**.
The nickname **"soccer"** comes from English schoolboys in the **1880s** shortening "association football" to "assoc."
**FIFA**, soccer's world governing body, was founded in **Paris in 1904** by seven countries.
**Lily Parr** was a star player for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular teams in England in their day.
The FA finally lifted its ban on women's football in **1971**, fifty years after it had started.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **China in 1991**, and the **United States** won it.
The first **World Cup** was played in **Uruguay in 1930**, and the host country beat Argentina in the final.
In **1966** the World Cup trophy was stolen in London, and found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.

story.title: Noah and the Midnight Patch Notes
story.subtitle: A bedtime adventure through the science of sleep

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Boy Who Blinked (1953)
chapters.text:
It was 1:47 a.m., the kind of hour that exists only for people who should be asleep. Noah was propped against his headboard, thumb flicking through highlight clips of a match he'd already watched twice, when his phone did something it had never done before.

The screen went black, then flashed a sick, static green — the color of an old computer that had forgotten what decade it was. Letters crawled across it: LOADING LEVEL 1.

Before Noah could lock the screen, a figure climbed out of it. Small, blocky, pixelated, wearing a nightcap two sizes too big. It saluted.

"REM-9," it said. "Sleep guide, patch notes pending. You're up late, player one."

"You're a glitch," Noah said.

"I'm a *feature*," REM-9 said. "Question: you ever wonder why your eyes twitch when you dream?"

Noah hadn't, particularly, but he wasn't about to admit that to a sprite. "Enlighten me."

REM-9 pulled up a flickering image: a sleep lab, **1953**, University of Chicago. A scientist named **Nathaniel Kleitman** and his grad student **Eugene Aserinsky** were watching a boy sleep, and noticed his eyes flicking back and forth under closed lids, fast, like he was watching a tennis match no one else could see.

"They called it **REM sleep** — Rapid Eye Movement," said REM-9. "Found it in 1953. Kleitman basically invented the whole field. People still call him the father of modern sleep research."

"So the eyes move because..."

"Because the brain's wide awake behind them. Dreaming. Guess what the body does to stop you from acting it out."

Noah guessed. "Shuts it down?"

"Ding," said REM-9, and the floor dropped away like a loading screen.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Ninety-Minute Lap
chapters.text:
Noah landed on what looked like a racetrack with no finish line, just a loop that repeated, glowing blue, then violet, then blue again.

"Sleep isn't one long level," REM-9 said, riding what appeared to be a hoverboard made of a pillow. "It's laps. About **ninety minutes** each. Quiet laps, called non-REM. Loud laps, called REM, where the dreaming happens. Back and forth, all night."

Noah clocked the pattern, same as a difficulty curve. "So it's not just... off?"

"Never off. Just switching modes." REM-9 pointed at a sleeping avatar jogging in place on the track, arms loose, totally limp. "During REM, your brain's almost as busy as it is right now, scrolling clips at one in the morning. But your muscles go slack — basically paralyzed — so you can't punch your way out of a dream."

"That's actually kind of a genius patch," Noah admitted. "What happens if it glitches?"

"Then you get sleepwalkers. But that happens in the quiet laps, not the dreaming ones. So whoever's up wandering the kitchen isn't acting out a dream. They're just, weirdly, somewhere else entirely."

Noah watched the loop a moment longer, timing it like a cooldown meter. "Ninety minutes. That's basically two ranked matches."

"Everything's ranked matches to you," REM-9 said, and shoved him toward the next loop before he could argue.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Growth Patch
chapters.text:
The next room was dim and padded, like a server room built out of sleeping bags. Deep in the loop, things got quieter — the slowest part of the lap.

"This is the deep stage," REM-9 said. "Deepest part of non-REM sleep. This is where your body dumps out the most **growth hormone** — the stuff that tells you to get bigger, repair muscle, heal up."

Noah thought about the ache in his shoulder from gym class. "So this is the patch that fixes everything."

"Pretty much. It's a big reason growing kids need more sleep than, say, a sprite, who does not grow, technically, ever." REM-9 struck a small pose.

"So every time I stay up till two scrolling clips—"

"You're skipping the patch notes," REM-9 said. "No deep stage, less repair. Your body doesn't care how good the clips were."

Noah frowned, filing that away next to things he was definitely going to ignore at 1 a.m. tomorrow anyway. "Noted."

"Sure it is," said REM-9, utterly unconvinced, and the floor dimmed further, pulling them both toward a clock the size of a building.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Master Clock
chapters.text:
The clock had no hands, just a soft pulsing light, mounted right behind two glowing threads that crossed like the strings on a guitar.

"Those threads are your eye nerves," REM-9 said. "And that little patch of brain sitting right above where they cross? That's the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. Say it five times fast."

"Absolutely not," said Noah.

"Fair. Call it the master clock. It runs on a roughly **24-hour cycle**, telling the rest of you when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake. There's a word for that kind of clock — **circadian**. It comes from old Latin words meaning **'about a day.'**"

Noah looked at the pulsing light, then at his own phone, dark now in his back pocket. "So when I'm up till two scrolling, I'm basically yelling at my own clock to shut up."

"Precisely. Light from a screen is extremely good at telling that clock it's still daytime. The clock believes it. The clock is not a critical thinker."

"Harsh."

"Accurate," said REM-9, and the master clock gave a single slow pulse, like a heartbeat agreeing with it.

chapters.heading: Level 5: Trophies
chapters.text:
A wall of what looked suspiciously like achievement trophies lit up ahead, except each one had a tiny portrait on it.

"Trophy room," REM-9 said. "In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, basically science's biggest trophy, for figuring out the actual genes that keep that master clock ticking."

"Genes," Noah repeated. "Like, instructions built into you."

"Exactly. And over here—" REM-9 tapped a smaller, older-looking trophy, slightly dusty "—**1958**. A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team pulled out a hormone called **melatonin**, the chemical your brain releases to make you feel sleepy, from the pineal glands — a little gland in the brain — of animals."

Noah made a face. "That sounds like a boss-fight ingredient."

"It's a sleep signal, not a spell component. Your own brain makes it every night, once it's dark enough and your screen isn't arguing with your master clock about what time it is."

"So the trophies are just biology nerds who found the cheat codes."

"The *correct* cheat codes," REM-9 said. "Unlike whatever you're doing at one in the morning."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Rinse Cycle
chapters.text:
The next space looked like the inside of a washing machine crossed with a filing cabinet, which, REM-9 explained, was exactly the point.

"Two jobs happen here every night," it said. "First: filing. Sleep sorts today's mess into long-term memory. Whatever you practiced, learned, or embarrassed yourself trying — sleep decides what sticks."

Noah thought about the guitar riff he'd been grinding for a week, and the boss pattern he'd finally nailed at midnight only to forget half of it by morning practice. "So if I'd actually slept instead of trying to nail it at 2 a.m.—"

"You'd probably remember more of it. Second job," REM-9 went on, gesturing at a slow, rhythmic wave moving through the walls, "is the rinse. Scientists call it the **glymphatic system** — basically a nightly wash cycle that flushes waste out of your brain while you sleep."

"My brain needs laundry."

"Your brain needs laundry," REM-9 confirmed. "Skip the cycle enough nights in a row, and the mess doesn't get washed out. You get foggier. Moodier. Worse at the very games you're staying up to play."

Noah opened his mouth to argue and found, annoyingly, that he had nothing.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Eleven-Day Run
chapters.text:
The last room before home looked like a scoreboard, and at the top of it was a name Noah didn't recognize: **Randy Gardner**.

"San Diego, **1964**," REM-9 said. "Seventeen years old. Science-fair project. He decided to just... not sleep. For about **eleven days**. One of the longest stretches anyone's ever managed, on record."

Noah sat up a little. "That's insane. That's basically a world record."

"It is. It's also not one you get a trophy for trying to beat. Doctors have looked at it since, and the verdict's unanimous: going without sleep wrecks your mood, your attention, your memory, fast. Randy's stunt taught scientists a lot. It is not a challenge."

"Relax, I'm not staging a reenactment," Noah said. "I just want to beat Marcus's stats, not break my brain."

"Noted and appreciated," said REM-9. It flicked to a smaller display, almost a bonus round. "Speaking of extremes — bottlenose dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time, one eye open, so they don't drown or get eaten. Giraffes sometimes get by on under two hours a day. Certain bats sleep something like twenty hours."

"Bats basically live the dream. Pun intended."

"Horrifying pun intended," REM-9 said. "Here's the real scoreboard, though: across a whole life, most people spend something like a **third of it** asleep. It's not wasted time. It's maintenance."

The scoreboard dimmed, and the floor began, gently, to rise.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Logging Off
chapters.text:
Noah landed back in his own room so smoothly it barely counted as landing. His phone sat face-up on the blanket, screen dark, no green static anywhere.

REM-9 perched on the headboard, smaller now, like the level was closing out. "One more file before you log off," it said. "Way back in **1899**, a scientist named **Sigmund Freud** wrote a whole book arguing dreams were secret messages about hidden wishes."

"Is that true?"

"Mostly not, by today's research — most of that specific theory didn't hold up. But it got people seriously studying dreams for the first time, which isn't nothing."

Noah glanced at the clock. 2:03 a.m. Somewhere between the master clock and the rinse cycle and Randy Gardner's terrible idea, his thumb had completely forgotten about the highlight clips.

"So the moral is: go to sleep."

"The moral," REM-9 said, already fading back toward the phone's dark screen, "is your brain's got a whole night shift waiting on you to clock out. Growth, memory, laundry, all of it. It can't start the shift if you won't stop scrolling."

Noah set the phone face-down on the nightstand, which felt, for some reason, like an actual achievement.

"Catch the next level tomorrow?" he asked, not sure if anyone would answer.

The screen gave one last small green flicker, like a wink, and went properly dark.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow night, the clips could wait.

true_facts.text: Scientists **Nathaniel Kleitman** and **Eugene Aserinsky** discovered **REM sleep** in **1953** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch.
A night's sleep is built from repeating **ninety-minute** laps that switch between quiet sleep and dreaming REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when awake, but the muscles go limp so the body can't act out the dream.
The deepest stage of quiet sleep triggers the biggest release of **growth hormone**, one reason growing bodies need extra sleep.
A tiny part of the brain called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** acts as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
The word **circadian** comes from old Latin words meaning **'about a day.'**
In **2017**, scientists **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep the body's clock running.
In **1958**, scientist **Aaron Lerner**'s team isolated **melatonin**, the hormone that makes you feel sleepy, from animal pineal glands.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memory, which is why good sleep helps you remember what you practiced.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' called the **glymphatic system** flushes waste out of the sleeping brain.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** of San Diego stayed awake for about **eleven days** as a science-fair project, one of the longest stretches on record.
Doctors don't recommend trying to break that record — going without sleep quickly hurts mood, attention, and memory.
Across a lifetime, people spend roughly a **third of their life** asleep.
In **1899**, **Sigmund Freud** wrote that dreams reveal hidden wishes, an idea most scientists today don't fully accept, though it got people seriously studying dreams.
